Easily the best fishing game out there and not because there aren't many fishing games out there but because the game does a great job at immersion with beautiful visuals and audio and you can just relax.
Of course by relaxing, I don't mean that the game is easy, if you want to go for small fish go ahead, that's easy, but if you want some nice largmouth bass you gotta work for it!
The game is full of small little awesome details. Like I only realized recently that there are actual fishes in the lake! I always thought that the game was random and it assigned a fish to your hook (based on location and bait etc...) when you caught one, but no that's not how it works! You can see them if the water is clear and shallow! They move around your bait, poke it, hit it and if you're convicing enough, they'll bite it!
First thing I'd like to mention is that, you don't need to have any actual fishing experiences in real life to be able to play and enjoy this game!
The game can be hard at first, specially after you level up once or twice, all the new equipments that unlock can be overwhelming. There's a tutorial at the beginning of the game but it doesn't cover a lot of the stuff you'll need to catch bigger fish later in the game. So you'll have to look up tutorials and read item descriptions to figure out how to work with the new rod you just bought.
Although there are some pop up tutorials here and there after you level up, catch a new fish or buy something new, I'm not sure exactly how they are triggered, but they give you some essentional info about for example how to catch a new type of fish.
Also there isn't an element of randomness to this game when it comes to catching fish, by that I mean that the game uses a fuzzy logic recognition system.
What does that mean?
It means that when you're trying to catch a fish by for example a retrieval method like Stop&Go (there are multiple retrieval methods in the game), your consistancy in luring the fish determines the quality of the fish. That's not randomness, that's as close as you can get to real life simulation! I love these devs!
Speaking of the devs, they are great and they know what they're doing. They are active and constantly fixing the game and notifying about the server's status etc...
It's an awesome fishing game, with some suprising great little details. Try it, you won't regret it!

VERY FUN!  This highly addictive FPS from the creator of the Counter Strike Series is like the spiritual successor to the original games.  There are the classic game modes we know and love: Bomb Defusal and Hostage Rescue.  However there are several new gamemodes: VIP Escort (Drive the VIP to an extraction point), VIP Escort On Foot (Lead the VIP to the extraction point on a close quarters map on foot), Team Death Match (10 second respawn close quarters combat), and the newer hostage rescue which is the one I mentioned above (Capture hostages as a Terrorist for a few rounds and then contain them or capture hostages from the Terrorists and attack as a COunter-Terrorist).  This game has many features the old Counter-Strike did not have like: RPGs and M320 Grenade Launchers, cars, new loadout and purchasing systems, fast roping down the sides of buildings, levolution when a bomb detonates, new guns, pick up ammo off of a dead teammate or dead enemy, heal your teammates, new knife, new player animations and new NPC animations and AI, the ability to look down and see your legs, better graphics, more video display options and power saving options, perks, kill streaks, attack dogs, character customization, new maps, new voting systems, private server creator and much more!  All in all, this is a very impressive game, all we need are more amped graphics while the current graphics are good and the ability to aim on all weapons since technically this is not Counter-Strike and it helps bring a whole new level of skill to the game.  So in the end, YES! I would recommend this game.

This game is very deserving of its reputation as a horror gem. It does something that very few horror games today (F.E.A.R., Dead Space, etc.) are willing to do: take away your ability to defend yourself. Because of this, you spend so much time huddled in a corner doing your best to blend into the stonework while you imagine what lumbering horror is after you.
Lighting in Amnesia is somewhat sketchy. Protagonist Daniel lacks the lung capacity to blow out a candle so while immovable, candles that let you save lantern oil can potentially be your downfall if a monster stumbles in and there are no dark corners present. This is doubly annoying in room with puzzles where you stand long enough to warrant lighting a candle or two to preserve sanity as monsters love to spawn outside these rooms. The game also has odd definitions on what counts as dark.
That might be a little harsh though. The game paces itself well and the atmosphere is such that you will feel drawn to keep playing.

Every once in a while there comes a game that strikes me, and makes me think if it's even possible for a game like this to exist.
Just like Oblivion and Skyrim did when they came out and I was used to playing corridor based games and knowing what to expect.
Or Metal Gear Solid where you can do everything you can think of, not being restrained by game mechanics.
Arma is not a game in the classical term. It is a massive military sandbox. Meaning that your experience is determined by your ability and creativity. Lack of this ability can quickly turn any sandbox into a boring walking simulator ruining your fun.
Every new idea can turn arma into a completely new game that you need to learn.
A good example of this is Dayz. A mod that became popular and evolved into a standalone game.
It has one of the the largest and most dedicated modding communities.
You will soon realise that every knowledge you acquired in real life you can use in arma and vice versa.
This game changed my way of thinking and made me learn topographic map navigation, celestial navigation, use of compass, bearing, pace counting, ballistics and many other things.
Again, any of these skills you can quickly test in Arma and learn from your mistakes.
Arma can easily replace many other games, because it feels like many games are contained inside Arma.
Tank sim, helicopter flight sim, casual airplane flight sim, you will have second thoughts about buying other games once you played Arma. Or even find that Arma has ruined many other games for you.
Be prepared to learn. Learning curve is very steep, especially if you have never
played sim games, altho arma is more a game than a sim it is a sim none the less.
The Controls are complex, be prepared to memorise and customise your whole keyboard.
The game engine suffers from some bottlenecks that are being worked on.
This is not battlefield/CoD. You can compare it by theme, but not by genre.
If something goes wrong 90% its your fault.
If you are easily frustrated again it's your fault.
New player starting a new game? Change AI in difficulty options to 35or less. You can
always buff them later.

And then it happened. Chased through the pitch black, hideous howls and gnashes behind me, heart pounding as I flew along in a blind panic, turned in the hope of slamming a door on my assailant... and confronted with a total monstrosity of a being two inches from my face. I screamed. Loudly.

This is a good expansion on the Portal universe. Uses the same dynamics and gameplay that we all know and love. I do have some issues with it so far (see cons)
Pros
-Good story
-Familiar gameplay
-Closest we'll get to Portal 3
Cons
- Levels can be a bit trickier to figure out. Between testing areas there are not always a clear cut way to get to the next area. At times I've had to look up guides to get on to the next section because it's not always so apparent as it was in the original games. Can be a bit tedious because of this. I like solving puzzles, not running around a giant room for 10 minutes looking for the spot to portal to. The layout of these puzzles makes it feel more like a grind that the original games. This is also due in part to the next point.
- The voice acting seems a bit flat. I know this is fan made, but it's not very well written if you ask me. I found myself snickering at many of the jokes and snide remarks of the first two games, not so much this one. The redundancies of the "you're fired" jokes from Cave Johnson, and the mediocre and not so cleaver insults from Virgil make the fan made aspect all the more apparent. I know it's hard to live up to some of the most iconic quotes in video game history "the cake is a lie, When life gives you lemons, etc" but it wasn't humorous at all for me. The voice for Virgil is very annoying in my opinion. Sort of takes away from the experience, as part of the fun of the originals was the moments of levity between the tedium of testing. This falls short on that.
All in all I do recommend this mod, as it's free and you'd have to be brain dead to not download something that's free. However, with the frustrations of the game layout and the poor dialogue I honestly wouldn't pay more than 5 bucks for this mod if I had to.
*Edit*
After trying to play more I just can't recommend this game. The transitions between "testing sites" is too much. There are no clear or apparent ways to get through, and without looking at walkthroughs it's annoying. With the original games, you'd see a clear place to portal to. This one it's like, oh, drop 50 feet down to that shaded pipe to a ledge that you can't see in the shadows to get to an elevator that doesn't even take you where you need to go. It doesn't make sense. Not to mention all of the puzzles are the same or so it seems. use a cube to open an area, spread gel in that area to get to section 3, find a way to portal back to grab the cube to open the door to leave the area. Since all mods as of now are free, I just can't recommend it.

Amnesia: The Dark Descent is the best horror game I've ever played, none other has ever made me so scared.
Content:
The main story is pretty short, clocking in about 4-6 hours and there’s not much replay value other then to see more then one of the endings. Justine (a side story) takes about an hour or so but I can't be sure because I really cannot beat it (it's sooo scary). However, the replay value comes in when you go online and download custom stories. There are some great ones out there so that’s where I spent most of my 70 or so hours in this game.
Graphics and Performance:
The graphics do a great job of setting the mood. However, some textures can look pixelated at times but it's not really that immersion breaking. The other complaint I have is that you're likely to play this game in a dark room (please do) and when you experience flashbacks the screen will turn white for a second or two and it can hurt your eyes. Performance-wise, I've always had framerate problems, at least the graphics options are very customizable so chances are you will find a set-up that will get you a constant 60fps.
Sound and Music:
The sound and music department is great, always setting the horror mood. You will hear floors above you creak, chains rattling, water flowing, basically anything that can make the room seem more scary than they actually are.
Mechanics:
This is where I think the game is weakest. Every monster encounter is scripted (except in Justine where they patrol, but still spawn to a script) so playing through the game enough I have memorized where every encounter will be. There is little patrol and some encounters can be easily waited out to wait for them to despawn. The monsters are also pretty dumb, but they easily get the job done. The physics engine is also pretty solid, but sometimes weird things can happen.
Final Thoughts:
Even though now that the sequel is out, I think this is the better one of the two and highly recommend you play this one instead, though both are great games. But despite Amnesia: The Dark Descent's many flaws, it is my most favorite horror game I have played and I think you should too.

Its pretty good, my first play through was in Story Mode and several of the puzzles are of higher difficulty than standard Portal 2 maps.  Some were of quality that if someone told me they were official maps I wouldn't doubt it.
A few maps though break away from some of the principles of the maps made by Portal's developers though.  The biggest one is using the destruction of a cube to trigger a cube respawn or respawning a cube to trigger a cube's destruction as required step in the solution of some puzzles.
I also felt like some of my solutions to the puzzles seemed a bit more like exploits than solutions in the Story Mode.
Either way, once I beat it on story mode, I went back through on advanced mode.  And some puzzles I felt were easier on advanced mode, most were much more difficult and required a lot more thought and planning to come to the correct solution.  None of my solutions in advanced mode felt exploity to me, so I'm fairly sure I found legitimate solutions to all of the puzzles in advanced mode.
All in all, I felt both modes gave a decent amount of replay value and the puzzles were well thought out and frustrating to a point, but never frustrating long enough to make it lose its fun.  The story is well told and I'm really pleased with the quality of the mod.
And for the price... any Portal fan would be stupid to not play this game.

So, what the developer essentially did was take Megaman, Duck Tales (NES), Super Mario Bros 3, and Zelda II and threw them into a couldron. Then, they proceeded to add their own ingredients until this game surpassed (dare I say it?!?!) most of the games I mentioned.
While this game may be a love letter to the old days of a dpad and two buttons, it is very much its own game and has successfully carved itself a place amongst classics for me. The platforming is very tight, the level design is wonderful and different, there's a lot of humor in the game, and some touching moments too. This is just a VERY good game. I...I can't think of anything that's wrong with it. It was very clear in what it set out to do and it did it. In that regards, the game is of extremely high quality. It didn't falter in any way or in any of its mechanics.
10/10. Now, let me explain. This isn't the same experience you're going to get with, say, a game from Valve or Blizzard or another big company name. This game deserves a perfect score because it accomplished what it set out to do. It delivered on all fronts and gave us great platforming with a retro style. There is not one category that I can say it fell short in. There is simply nothing wrong with this game.
If you like platformers, sidescrollers, metroidvanias, or the NES, I'm incredibly surprised you haven't picked it up yet. Go buy it, you dolt.

Rainbow 6 Siege is a 5v5 first person shooter set in multiple completely destructible maps. It requires you to be calculating, smart, dependant on your team, and a good shot.
And it is the best multiplayer FPS I have ever played. I know that most people don't like Ubisoft or Uplay but Ubisoft actually has a very good game here. I daresay one of their best. It has lots of defending and attacking operators (characters) which are all quite balanced. The only time they are really "overpowered" is if a chosen operator is in the hands of someone who knows how to play it. All the DLC that Ubisoft releases for this game is free. You heard me correctly. Free. The season pass owners only get automatic access to the new operators (all maps are available to all players), renown (in-game currency) boosters, and extra daily challenges to make them more money. All players can buy the new operators though they are quite expensive and require alot of grinding. But that is ok because the game is by no means a chore to grind through. You can queue up with friends. You have skins and charms and things for the operators but you do not need to pay money for most of them.
All in all it really is an amazing game. I really don't have any complaints.
Word of warning to you, they game comes with a built in voice chat system which allows players to be tactical in game without an outside source. And sometimes... every once in a while... you have toxic players that scream into their mics or play awful music or do something to be extremely irritating. However you won't run into them often and most players are quite nice and helpful. Every playerbase has their share of toxicity as this one does. And this player base is almost entirely helpful and kind.

The point of this game is to use plants to attack zombies and defend your house. A variety of zombies exist ranging from Michael Jackson-like zombies doing the Thriller dance as they attack you, to pogo stick-bouncing zombies, and zombies holding screen doors as defense. Your plants vary depending on the map you're playing. In a day time map you'll be using sunflowers, watermelon catapults, "pea shooters," and wall-nuts (walnut, get it? har har!). During a night time map you'll be using different kinds of mushrooms that all have their own unique attacks.
At the end of each "Map" (as well as each "Level") you get a new plant type to defend your house. At the beginning of each map you have to pick which plants you want to defend yourself with, so as you gain new plants, you'll want to use these and replace older, less useful plants. Asking the player to pick which plants they want to use creates more of a puzzle/strategy feel to it (which the game is anyway) and provides variety. For example: I can choose to go with a mushroom setup or I can work around sunflowers and watermelon catapults. EARLY ACCESS REVIEW
Pros:
Looks nice, graphics are fairly good
Has a more realistic look than most fishing games
Cons:
First and foremost the game has a misplaced focus on locating fish rather than the catching of them.
It can takes hours finding the right spot, time of day, right bait to find what your looking for and when you finally hook one, you can reel it in quickly without much trouble at all. The "fish fight" aspect of the game  is virtually nonexistent.
The game claims to be "multiplayer" however is simply a single player instance with a chat box in the corner.
No customization at all, any gear other than what rod and reel your using doesn't change your appearance at all, in fact you never see more than your own two hands.
In its current state the game seems like little more than a tech demo, the maps are small, and it get repetitive rather quickly.
VERDICT:
I can't recommend the game at this time.
The developers I think are dropping the ball, or what has been the case for many EA titles, the game is just a cash grab. They seem to prioritize how players earn experience over the fixing of major bugs in the game. In the first week of release they adjusted fish spawns and exp rate three times and have again since then. Balance in a game like this is important, however all these changes have been "nerfs" to experience gains to slow player progression. In a normal EA title this would be fine, however this one sells a premium membership in the cash shop that gives 50% bonus to experience.
Early Access or not, if your going to have a cash shop people expect to get what they pay for and not have the game changed in a way that devalues what they purchased. Quite frankly the actions of the developers thus far throws up the   "cash grab" flags in my opinion.

The good old classic Plants vs Zombies! Everyone and their grandmother has probably heard of this game. If you haven't, it's really simple. Use plants to shoot zombies, if a zombie gets to your house it's game over. Play the adventure mode to unlock plants, every single one of them is useful and unique (except for Split Pea, he sucks). There are 5 worlds. Day, Night, Pool, Fog and Roof. Every world has 6(?) unique zombies with special powers. For example:
- Pogo Zombie, Can jump over your plants.
- Snorkel Zombie, Can dive into your pool and dodge every attack.
- Miner Zombie, Can mine to the other side of the lawn and render all your plants useless.
There's also mini-games and an Endless Mode to keep you playing for a longer time.
The special thing about the GOTY edition is... well... nothing really. You can create your zombatar but that's it. The Zombatar you create will replace the face of the Flag Zombie the next time you play.
RATING: 8/10.
PROS:
+ Unique plants and zombies
+ Replayability
+ Fun minigames
+ Quirky humour
+ Sweet soundtrack
CONS:
- The GOTY Version doesn't add much to the game
- The game can be pretty slow at the start
- Split Pea and Cactus were useful for only like 4 levels. They're pretty much the only plants I found to be too gimmicky.

Tactical Intervention is a multiplayer FPS developed by Minh "Gooseman" Le who earlier co-developed counter-strike. This does seem like a good way to make a comeback but Tactical Intervention suffers some major drawbacks.
The game itself seems just like a standard multiplayer FPS. You get a gun wich you then run around and shoot people in the head with and eventually get shot in the head yourself. Seems fairly simple right? But the game got these nice little small details wich varies from using a fire extinguisher to put up a smoke wall to being able to roll away from explosions and thereby prevent taking damage. This is according to myself the only positive point of the entire game.
The gameplay is also one of the worst of modern day FPS games. It's not that it's bad but it's just nothing special.
And don't get me started on the animations. Everyone looks like crabs when they walk around!
And with just around 500 ppl in game at the time this is written? The game has been out for less than a year and the community is alredy dying out.
As a F2P title the game functions as a good example of a Pay 2 Win game (P2W). This means that the people who pay for stuff in the game (be it a more powerful weapon or even dogs) can totally dominate the people who don't. So someone who is far more skilled may get totally rolled over by someone far less skilled just because the far lessed skilled guy has put more money on the table.
PROS
+ Good ideas that later FPS games may improve
+ Better than COD
+ So bad it's funny if you're in the right mood
CONS
- P2W
- Laughable animations
- The community is barely alive
OVERALL SCORE 32/100

You can also restart stages but keep stuff you picked up, allowing you to farm stuff apparently (I noticed this accidentally when I restarted after a screw up). While RE4 had stages technically, it was a much more seamless experience, you only really knew there were different stages because of the save/load screen. Even the interface for selling treasures is a chore. Also it crashed on me a lot (about ten times give or take, in ~16 hours of play), no idea why - maybe because it uses Games for Windows Live? This almost always happened while in the inventory screen between stages though it happened once shortly after launching the game (around the time it checks GfWL account). In any case I don't think it ever occurred during game play, so I never lost real progress - I just had to sell treasures and upgrade weapons again.

This game was *almost* fun to play, with some very good boss fights, but after getting through 3/4 of it, the boring failure iteration loop was eating up far too much of its gameplay. Essentially, if you fail in your platforming, you die instantly. Normally, not a big deal, but Shovel Knight doesn't work in platforming design concepts to make this feel like a good part of the game.
The controls feel unpolished and slow (how many good platformers have a problem with either of those?) After learning the controls over a couple of hours, you don't so much build expertise around the character's movement (as you would in IWBTG, Meatboy, Rogue Legacy), you just learn to avoid certain warts in your character's movement patterns.
The inconsistent difficulty between checkpoints was frequently painful, since dying just before the next checkpoint meant replaying really trivial rooms as punishment. I don't mind an iteration loop of a few minutes, but FOR ALL THAT IS HOLY make those minutes interesting. Don't punish death with tedium. Good games either make the replayed areas difficult and fun to execute (great platformers do this), randomly generate some of their content, or give the player some minor reward for replaying them. Here's a weird suggestion: "be less punishing of failure, you know, like Dark Souls or IWBTG."
All of this stuff about platforming means the RPG elements around attacks, HP and MP upgrades felt tacked on, since they didn't affect platforming in the slightest, even though they were useful for boss fights.
That said, there were some particularly fun and clever parts to this game - the exploration and hidden rooms were well done, and led to a lot of great risk vs reward decisions. The platforming puzzles (how do I get up there?) were great - so long as the happened right after a checkpoint. I really liked the down attack bounce, and the various clever ways the rooms played with it. Unfortunately all of these things would shine so much brighter in a game with more frequent checkpoints, or less punishment around platforming failure.
If you don't mind randomly generated levels, I'd definitely recommend Rogue Legacy over Shovel Knight. It's proof that a tribute to metroidvanias of yore can still incorporate more modern lessons in game design (no tedium, tough is fine if you're fair, controls are super important).
New challenges, new solutions. New stories, new experience.

Edit: I changed my mind. After spending my time playing some other games that attempt this kind of genre, I've realized that this title, and the studio behind it, leave a lot to be desired. From a lack of basic game mechanics (Inability to aim grenades, combine magazines, load cargo, use IR torches, use light and laser simultaneously), to a lack of really basic polish (no hand cycling animations for bolt action rifles, AKs have a bolt hold open for no reason, change of mag types is not visible, people twitch violently and unrealistically when shot, blood is splotchy and weird, faces have 1000 yard stares), to a lack of things to do, ArmA is a title that just needs some work. Sure, there's a myriad of scenarios, and tools to work with, but the game, on its own, feels rather ugly and unfun, and relies on the modding community to be as good as it is.
I'm changing my review because it's not the game that deserves praise, but rather the people who play it, for allowing this game to be popular and playable for so many years. I just wish that Bohemia would make their own games better without relying on unpaid fans to sell their products. For the time being, it just really feels like resourceful people polishing a turd.  It's a gas with the right folks and the right addons, and while I'm appreciative for Bohemia laying the framework for us to utilize, the base game is simply not that good, and I would not purchase this game at all if I could not download mods. Get it when it's on sale, and it'll be a good bang for your buck.

Arma 3 is a military simulation. I personally feel the simulation part is not really a thing much anymore. When I played Arma 2 I experienced large scale combat scenarios where I could just see muzzle flashes. Players barked crazy jargon I had to google and the sounds of mortars/arty terrified me. Dying was horrible because well, respawn times were long on the servers I played on. It was an experience that only Arma could provide.
Then 3 comes out. I join a server and it's Team Deathmatch. That's okay I guess if it's tactial and somewhat resembles real life warfare. Instead I had people screaming not-military type things. Instead of "There is infrantry at grid #####" it was "There is people left, by that...building"
Seems like a small complaint but it ruins it. See I walked into Arma 2 to play DayZ with some friends, hopped into a random server and experienced something that made me fall in love with milsim due to the atmosphere.
Arma 3 lost that the moment I heard voice chat. No one used a compass to help find the enemy. I told my teammates there was an enemy N at ### degrees and the response was "Lol, nerd dont act all cool"
I'm not going to join the military unless I'm drafted or my life takes a dramatic tailspin. I'd like to experience some of the romanticized, seems cool aspects of it. I mean come on, video games are there so we can experience and be things we cant be in real life. Though, the voice chat isn't the only atmosphere breaker.

Imagine if Ducktales and Megaman spawned a child. "Retro" done right for a change. I'm not saying ALL games during the 8-bit era were great (they weren't), but the ones we cherish? They had that magic developers try to capture.
The Important stuff:
----------------------------------
Visuals are 8-bit style sprites, both the characters and the backgrounds. Well animated, movement doesn't look "stiff".
Audio is also 8-bit. Very melodic, excellent chord progression, very catchy.
Controls are solid and very responsive. Attack and jump buttons, use spells with Up + Attack.
Gameplay is straightforward, complete each level by overcoming platforms, enemies with unique patterns and stage hazards. Collect gold, use gold for upgrades (Weapon, Armor, Health, Magic and Spells).
Overall, a very solid title. I'm hoping for a sequel.
Rant Rant Rant:
----------------------------------
Shovel Knight does everything that several other "retro" games fail miserably at. It captures very well what made the 8-bit era memorable. The visual and sound quality to non-gamers was considered "bad". In order to make up for that, games had to be as innovative and enjoyable as possible. Levels had to be challenging and rewarding. Music was composed by experienced and/or talented composers and they only had 4 sound channels to work with, which were also used for in-game sounds.
What you often get with other "retro" titles are uninspired sprite visuals and poor controls (to make it "challenging"). The music is usually decent, but rarely reminiscent of the era the games are based off of.
Do yourself a God damned favor and buy this game.

While one might argue that Shovel Knight doesn't do anything new; what it DOES do is incorporate a bunch of things you already love into a concentrated beam of platformer/RPG goodness. The best way to explain Shovel Knight is in terms of other games, so here's what we've got:
--Super Mario Bros 3 style world map (including random bonus levels and bosses that shuffle around).
--Super Ghouls n' Ghosts style platforming, combat, and level design
--Duck Tales style cane jump (now a shovel jump of course) and treasure collecting
--Dark Souls style experience system
As you platform and shovel-battle your way through each level, you'll want to find and collect as much treasure as you can get your hands on, since treasure is equivalent to XP and can be used to purchase upgrades.
Much like Dark Souls, however, if you die at any time, ALL OF YOUR GOLD will be dropped and you'll be sent back to the nearest checkpoint. You have one opportunity to make it back to your gold and recollect it or you lose it permanently.
An interesting twist that is NOT like Dark Souls is that you can actually DESTROY the checkpoints in the level, which gives you a hefty chunk of treasure/XP, but prevents you from using that checkpoint. (If you die, you'll be sent back a LONG way.)
There are villages on the map where you can spend your treasure to buy HP and MP upgrades. There are also upgrades for your armor and your shovel. You can also purchase various tools and relics (used to cast spells).
The levels in the game start out challenging, but they can get seriously difficult in some places. The first two bosses (the Black Knight and the King Knight) are pretty simple, but once you get to the third boss (the Lich King), the difficulty ramps up quite a lot. The boss battles are well crafted as well. They provide a lot of challenge, but the bosses have patterns and exhibit "tells" for special attacks, allowing you to learn the boss' techniques and develop your skill at them.
While most of the game succeeds at being very challenging without resorting to cheap surprises or death traps, some of the later levels use tactics that will definitely try your patience. In true Dark Souls spirit, prepare to excessively curse and repeatedly protest that you've had about enough of this bu||sh!t only to keep playing anyway. With both Shovel Knight and Dark Souls, it begins with trying to win for fun; and it ends with trying to win because F*CK YOU, MOTHERF*CKING GAME. F*CK YOU RIGHT TO HELL.
Ah, good times.
You can replay levels (including boss fights) as many times as you want for extra money.
Visually, the game appeals to your nostalgia, but the gameplay incorporates many popular conventions from modern games.
It's an RPG platforming adventure, and it's a pretty good time.

5/10 overall
Music: 10/10
The music of this mod is pretty much the only thing they got perfectly valve-like. I didn't find any difference in atmosphere, amount/placement or quality to the 2 original Portal games.
Mapmaking: 3/10
The music is good, but the mapmaking is kinda bad in a lot of parts. I really had to search around a lot, to find out what the devs wanted me to do in a lot of places. There's a lot of places where your instict tells you to go somewhere, which makes it that you won't even see the right way at all.
A friend of mine told me about how you can use light to direct the player. I think the mapmakers of this mod should really think about that technique again. Or maybe Foxcats are prone to walking towards light...
Achievements: 3/10
Also the achievements are a pain, because they are hidden so much, that you'd probably never find all of them in a reasonable time without using either noclip or a guide (which luckily this game has some really great ones, made by both the devs and the community). Some of the achievements don't even appear in the list, until you actually get them, which means that you have to triple check every single piece of wall, ceiling and ground for finding the little holes that the achievements are placed in. Luckily the search is worth it, as some of the achievement events are so funny and out of place that you will probably laugh about them; my favorite one has a lot of color ;)
Story: 5/10
The story of this mod is fitting for the atmosphere and a really nice idea, but does have a lot of logic holes if you think about it a bit. Some stuff doesn't make sense and other things would probably not happen like that. The final part of the story mentions how Portal 2 came to be (still fanfiction, don't forget that), which is a really nice moment and probably the most thought out part of the story.
One thing I dislike is that this mod is advertised as solving the plot hole between Portal 1 and 2, but it actually only tells a story of how Portal 2 might have started, because it doesn't really mention Portal 1's plot. Technically there's now a place for a game between Portal 1 and Stories: Mel and if that ever happens, I really hope that the mapmaking will be improved by a lot.
TL;DR: Story works, but has issues, music fits, mapmaking isn't perfect at all. I recommend this game if you're good at thinking with portals and finding negative possibilty space in games, as those skills will help a lot, when playing through this mod. If you like getting all achievements, this game isn't that fun, because they are hidden very well and some don't appear in the list, which makes them pretty much luck-to-find.

Edit: I changed my mind. After spending my time playing some other games that attempt this kind of genre, I've realized that this title, and the studio behind it, leave a lot to be desired. From a lack of basic game mechanics (Inability to aim grenades, combine magazines, load cargo, use IR torches, use light and laser simultaneously), to a lack of really basic polish (no hand cycling animations for bolt action rifles, AKs have a bolt hold open for no reason, change of mag types is not visible, people twitch violently and unrealistically when shot, blood is splotchy and weird, faces have 1000 yard stares), to a lack of things to do, ArmA is a title that just needs some work. Sure, there's a myriad of scenarios, and tools to work with, but the game, on its own, feels rather ugly and unfun, and relies on the modding community to be as good as it is.
I'm changing my review because it's not the game that deserves praise, but rather the people who play it, for allowing this game to be popular and playable for so many years. I just wish that Bohemia would make their own games better without relying on unpaid fans to sell their products. For the time being, it just really feels like resourceful people polishing a turd.  It's a gas with the right folks and the right addons, and while I'm appreciative for Bohemia laying the framework for us to utilize, the base game is simply not that good, and I would not purchase this game at all if I could not download mods. Get it when it's on sale, and it'll be a good bang for your buck.

Portal Stories: Mel is a mod for Portal 2, but it might just as easily have been full fledged game on its own. The story in the game isn't as rich as one of Valve's stories, but it stays incredibly close to the existing Portal lore. It creates its own little prequel to Portal and Portal 2 and does this in a very believeable, way, tieing itself into the existing story almost seamlessly. The voice talent and musical compositions of Harry Callaghan really bring this game to life like no other Portal mod has ever done before.
Level design is incredibly detailed with well thought out puzzles and two game modes. The original gamemode, now called 'advanced mode', will give any Portal player a run for their... well, money I guess. The puzzles in this gamemode get incredibly complicated as time goes on and require a different level of thinking than the ordinary Portal puzzles. I eventually gave up on them because it became downright frustrating, but if you like a challenge this is absolutely the gamemode for you. For those who just wish to play the game more casually and enjoy the story, the developers introduced a 'story mode' where the puzzles are a little easier to solve, but still challenging enough to keep things interesting.
Overall, by far the best Portal mod I've played to date. Would have paid 10 bucks for this easily, but fact of the matter is that it's completely free. So go get it and go play it if you love Portal.

Shovel Knight fuses many of the elements that makes classic NES games so fun and so great: colorful, endearing graphics, catchy chiptunes, simple mechanics, and meticulous design. The designers liberally borrowed mechanics and design elements from the classics, from Mega Man to Zelda. This game is a nostaliga trip in all the best ways but is also a well-designed, down-right fun game in its own right.
Yacht Club Games clearly took great pains to make classic game mechanics and design accessible to today's more casual audience. Ultimately, this approach is quite successful because Shovel Knight's philosphy on difficulty is use a sliding scale: it's up to the player to deliberately challenge himself by breaking checkpoints, choosing not to use certain upgrades, going for secrets, unlocking achievements, speedrunning, playing New Game+, etc. By default, this game is not easy by any means, but the fact is that Shovel Knight is not nearly as challenging as the original NES classics from which its inspired or other modern retro-style action games like Mega Man 9/10 and Volgarr the Viking.
Shovel Knight, even in its launch release form (which does not yet include all Kickstarter goals like Challenge Mode, Battle Mode, more playable characters, etc.), is content rich with well over a dozen stages including bonus stages, towns, additional bosses, and secrets. Needless to say, the current version of Shovel Knight is very satisfying and feels like a complete experience. Shovel Knight's value proposition will only go up over the coming months.
All fans of NES classics such as Mega Man 2, Zelda II, and Super Mario Bros 3 should get this game. But I also highly recommend this game to people who have yet to experience or really dive into classics like these, as this game is highly accessible and in many ways represents the best that classic game design has to offer.

Every day has been getting harder. Losing the will to go on without my sweet Mary is taking away my ability to perform daily tasks. It's only been 3 days since she passed, but it feels like years. Fishing Planet took everything. It started during the Steam summer sale. "Honey, I added $50 to the Steam Account! What games would you like me to buy?" As if possesed by the will of Satan, my head turned 360 degrees as I said "Fishing Planet." I didn't even know what Fishing Planet was! I've never heard of it before I said it out of impulse in that moment. She told me that the game was free and that we didn't even have to add money to the account. I punched her for talking back to me. We passionately made love as the game downloaded, for we were eager to embark on this gaming experience. 1.2... 1.3... The gigabytes ticked away like a grandfather clock, and when the hour striked, it was finished. We both rushed to our computers to get ready to catch some sweet sweet seafood. The tutorial took a real toll on me; while Mary had no problem passing it, I could not catch a single fish. I'm normally a pretty tame guy, but this drove me to nearly punching a hole in my wall. My wife came over and passed it for me to calm my nerves. I hear a frantic chant from across the room, "Honey, look! We can fish in Missouri!". We lived in Missouri, so that was a pretty cool thing to hear. We traveled to our next destination, but as I spawned into the river, the flashbacks began to haunt me. July 14th, 1973. Me and my father were fishing in the same river as was depicted in the game. My dad said, "Son, there is nothing more valuable in life than patience.", as he could tell I was getting fed up due to my lack of catching anything. "I know dad, it's just a little stressful.", I respond. After a few hours of sitting near the river I start to scream because I haven't caught a single thing all day, while my dad was reaping in bass! This is when I learned that paitience was more than a virtue. My dad wasn't just trying to teach me a lesson, he was protecting the lives of the human race. "This is why you needed to be patient!", screamed my dad as a storm started brewing in the air. Suddenly, the river drained and the daunting hand of Satan tore the riverbed in half, taking my father down with him. It was a tragedy that I will never forgive myself for. As the flashback ended, I realized 6 hours had passed and I had caught nothing. However, my wife was realing in bass like there was no tomorrow! I knew better than to get angry, but something came over me as I started screaming satanic chants into the air. The sky turned black as a meteor struck our house. I was in the living room, but Mary wasn't so fortunate. She was struck directly by the meteor. I couldn't believe I had let this happen again. I lost my father, my wife, and my house. All to Fishing Planet.

ARMA 3 is my favourite first person shooter. You will not be disappointed if you add this to your library. Now I know this has been done before hundreds of times, but I'll be listing the Pros and Cons for this game.
Pros-
This game is fully customisable, you can play in whatever environment and period you want, you can play in 2035  or 1945, it's up to you. You also don't have to do realistic type gameplay; there are COD type game modes available or you could even do role playing games like city life which is pretty much GTA.
Unofficial downloadable  content from the steam workshop or even the internet is incredibly easy to install so now everyone can do it, making realism units even more easy to apply for and create.
The textures in this game are amazing if your PC can handle them.
The Apex DLC is worth its price.
Characters are now fully customisable too, you can edit what they wear down to what's in their vest, backpacks, etc.
Arma 3 is one of the most populated games on steam, meaning you will never get bored looking for a server.
Arma 3 has a very basic form of coding which means you can learn Arma 3 coding. While it isn't much, it still is a start.
You can create your own mods and scenarios now easier than ever with the EDEN editor and Arma 3 tools - you need pretty much no coding skills.
Cons-
Arma 3 can be graphically demanding at points, however you can tone down your settings to accomodate this.
Arma 3 can be very glitchy at times, but as there is still frequent updates, the owners are at least active in trying to combat this.
The advanced flight model doesn't operate as well as people expected and still needs intense work however it is still nice that Bohemia is now looking towards people interested more in the aviation aspects of the game.
All in all, Arma 3 is a great game and gets a 9/10 from me.

This is a surprisingly great add on. The puzzles are excellent and the difficulty level begins very early on. They also benefit greatly from not having the same idiot playtesters that forced the dumbing down of much of Portal 2's puzzles. Some of the earliest puzzles had me stuck way longer than I expected, and still left me with the satisfying "Of course" when I solved them. I spent much of Portal 2 just looking and clicking as everything was obvious once you saw all the pieces.
The level design is really top knotch. A lot of thought went into parts of the level that you only see briefly. Just beautiful animation and great new models and textures.
The voice acting is a little off, but I would say that the fault is really too much unnatural dialogue. I think "less is more" when it comes to talking sidekicks in video games.
I thoroughly recommend this. If you loved Portal 2, but the simplicity of the puzzles annoyed you then this is an excellent addition that gives the same great visuals, a cool story, and much more difficult puzzles.

It's about as far as you can get from Counter-Strike's tense and tactical stand-offs (though maybe that's because of the lack of a 5v5 ranked adversarial mode), but Tactical Intervention still manages to offer satisfying and surprisingly fun action, with a unique blend of old-school mechanics and (for lack of better terminology) New Age multiplayer FPS sensibilities, offering the best of both worlds while steering relatively clear of the excesses of other games on the market...
... except for its in-game economy, which borders on pay-to-win, and doesn't even seem to be doing the developers any favors, monetarily speaking. The starting weapons are decent, make no mistake, but all other weapons which can only be obtained through the in-game store are notoriously overpowered, and other cosmetic gear items provide similarly unbalanced boosts for a variety of stats (truth be told, they don't really seem to do anything either, which is even worse). You're expected to grind matches to obtain points in order to purchase items on a temporary ownership basis, as permanent gear can cost so many points that you'll likely be tempted to pay up with real money (which is probably the intention here).
Still, Tactical Intervention is a game worth trying out, and it does have some value worth offering if you can stick with it. It also has attack dogs, and that makes it worth at least the hard-drive space, in my book.

The graphics are actually faithful to the limitations of old 8-bit consoles, and not just low-resolution pixelart colored dully. The music is phenomenal, and there are a ton of different tracks. Controls are tight, difficulty curve is very nearly perfect, but the game still values your time, so it doesn't feel like an old game, even though it plays very much like an NES classic. The boss fights are varied and fun, and the level design is interesting, and really cleverly teaches new mechanics through play rather than text-dumps.
Replayability is achieved by allowing players to self-impose challenges, and by optional "side-quests" and optional bosses.

Tactical Intervention is a quite intricate take of things on Counter Strike. Created by a co-creator of CS, I was quite pleased to see the changes they had made to it. With some smarts, and patience, one COULD get really good at it, I thought. To an extent, that may have been true. But I can't help but think the devs were a little too greedy with this game, and a bit unfair in other aspects, as well....
First off, the game is a nice take of CS, with great features like rappelling, player VIP escort, drivable cars, breaching charges too! It all seems great, at first. You'll soon find out that rappelling is worse than useless, noob VIPs get themselves killed, thus ending the round, the cars mechanics are absolutely HORRIBLE, and the breaching charges are overpriced. Oh, did I mention that? EVERY perk, attachment, accessory, pretty much anything besides the actual weapons need actual $$$ to use, and most for only a month, as there is no perma unlock for them. I know, crazy, right? But hear me out.
The guns themselves are decent, save for one. They can be permanently unlocked, but it is a pain in the @$$ to do when you only have the default guns. What's wrong with the default guns, you ask? They are significantly lower dmg, accuracy, and mag size. Useless. Good thing is, you can rent guns to get ingame money to payoff your rent and even profit, with the right application of use.
This needs a seperate paragraph of its own. The Super V. Basically the Vector, it outclasses the M4, AK, G36, every other SMG and assault rifle, destroys shotguns and pistols, and snipers aren't even a challange, unless they have 50 meters on you. Even then, its anyone's guess. Accuracy, damage, RPM, this gun has it all. You can use it in a car, on land, in hell, anywhere. It will ruin the poor fool in front. Devs need to fix this, FAST, or this game could quickly degnerate into people relying on other people's sense of goodwill and benevolence.
Honestly though, my take of this game is that it is very good. It has a small community really, so once you meet the right people, (the decent ones with hearts), you will be able to actually play with them, use some strategy, maybe. Strategy in this game, with a closely knit, communicative, strong team will beat almost any opposition out there. Maybe a rehaul in graphics, but that's a minor thing, definitely a change in the whole $$$ grabbing thing, though. Change the way you get the accessories, attachments, aesthetical changes, etc, and maybe TI will get a larger following. That, and a basic autobalance so that it isn't all lvl 40-50s on one team, and like 5 lvl 1-4's on the other. I still reccommend this game, because hey, if you don't give up on it, and you persist, it will quickly grow on you after a while. Then fall off. But let that happen later.

Resident Evil 5 is very much a love it or hate it part of the Resident Evil franchise. There are many reasons for this, most notably starting with Resident Evil 4 and the series departure from pure scare tactics into a more story driven, fight off zombie hordes sort of affair.
I find that this sort of evolution actually makes sense as the games stay contained within the same universe. When zombies, the c-virus, las plagas, etc become common knowledge, it becomes much harder for the characters in that world to become outright scared. This also translates to the players growing up with the games. Whether it was the dogs jumping through windows in Resident Evil 1, the menacing lickers of RE2 or the constant stress of being hunted down by Nemesis in RE3, we've grown up with this series and it's very hard to throw a curve ball at us. We aren't the 10-14 year olds with wild imaginations anymore.
So with Resident Evil 5, it follows the natural course of, we know there are weird creatures afoot, it's down to us to locate the source to try and put an end to it. And I find the story telling and voice acting to be very well done. It can be a bit campy but Resident Evil 5 wasn't going for a "The Last of Us" feel or story narrative.
Now when it comes to gameplay, I actually find it to be somewhat more realistic than many of the shooters and FPS games out there. You are not controlling a platoon of soldiers, you are two trained mercenaries (for all intents and purposes), using strategic fire to subdue your enemies. An argument could be made that you should be able to move and fire at the same time, however in most military skirmishes, soldiers will set themselves up for a shot then move to the next vantage point. Shooting and moving, little own running, at the same time greatly diminishes accuracy and wastes ammo. With this in mind, the enemy AI is designed for this sort of combat. At no time in the game do I feel that because of this style of combat, I am severely limited/hindered as a result. I adapt to the gameplay, learn it's nuances and continue on. I enjoy it!
You might look at my hours count here and think that I might be off base a bit or not enough experience with the game to make a full review such as this. However, I started off the with 360 version of the game, got the PS3 version, and now the PC version. Graphically, the PC version is much more impressive especially with the improved framerates. Not having as many friends on Steam versus PS3 or 360, I tended to play the console versions more often. Which leads to my one complaint towards the game.
Your companion AI can be somewhat infuriating at times compared to playing with a real person and being able to speak your mind in voice chat on how to go about business. While the AI never truly outright fails, their waste of ammo and poor timing of healing items amongst other things can lead to moments of pure frustration, especially at the earlier parts of game and before you complete the game and can start unlocking all sorts of wonderful features (including unlimited ammo leading to your partner never wasting ammo again).
In any case, I love this game, have played it many, many, many times and will undoubtedly come back and play it some more! Thanks for reading my wall of text.
tl;dr- We aren't 10 anymore, scaring within the same universe doesn't work like it did on our younger selves, combat actually makes more sense than people give it credit for, wtf companion AI. Love. Much fun. Such awesome. Wow.

Portal Stories: Mel is a love letter to the Portal series.
It's beautiful, it's heartwrenching, and you can just feel the devotion that each and every member of the development team has put into it. All of the lovely new environments are furnished with graphics that beautifully match the spirit of the games, and the music itself is absolutely wonderful.
Most of all, though, the relationship between Mel (the player character) and Virgil (the personality core) really shows this. Unlike the other betrayals of the series, these two work together with real purpose. They have one another's back, and it honestly feels nice to play a game where you know you can actually trust one of the robots. This is what makes the ending so much more emotional and powerful, and I cannot recommend this game enough.
Dev team: you've done an outstanding job, and your hard work and love that you poured into this project is so tangible. Excellent job, and the best of luck in your future games!

The Third Street Saints return for even more outlandish mayhem!
This time, the missions take wacky to the next level and with a new RPG-like leveling system your character can basically become godlike.
Story: Once again, you are the leader of a gang known as the Third Street Saints. But now, you are tasked with taking down a large organisation simply known as the Syndicate. I won't say too much about the story to avoid spoiling it for people but the plot basically revolves around revenge and oppression. The tone of the story is alot lighter in this game and I feel like the story is better for it, whereas in Saints Row 2, the tone jumped from being serious back to being humourous and this was jarring at times. Story missions are outrageous and fun, placing you in a number of crazy scenarios like providing covering fire with a sniper as you are rappeled down the side of a skyscraper or being inside a TRON-like world with firewalls, anti-viruses and 16-bit creatures.
Graphics: Saints Row 3 takes a departure from 2 in that it's graphics are alot of stylized and cartoony now. This works well with the light tone of the story and looks great artistically. On a good PC on the highest settings, the game looks fantastic and the colours just pop from the screen.
Sound: Each of the characters are voiced very well. The voice actors give alot of personality to the characters and they are quite distinct and unique as a result. One of my favourite characters is Zimos, who is the oldest pimp in Steelport and just sounds ridiculous with his auto-tuned voice. Every time he spoke I chuckled.
Gameplay: The gameplay in Saints Row 3 is a big leap over SR 2. Controlling your character, guns as well as vehicles feels alot smoother now than ever before and is much less frustrating as a result. Gone are the days where the enemies would just ram you with their car, sending you flying off the footpath and inducing rage. The developers have clearly learned from their mistakes with the previous game and have to be commended.
Overall, Saints Row The Third is a very fun sandbox game. There is alot to do in this world and if you are a fan of zany, crude and humourous games, this game is worth a purchase.

Good game, although the poor optimization is really what makes this game a bit offputting to me. Don't get me wrong, I enjoy playing the game and I have played plenty of it. I originally had a GTX 960 in my system, with an i5 4690. After upgrading to a 1070, I've noticed a very small increase in framerate (5 fps at the most). This is due to the 32-bit engine ARMA 3 runs on, meaning it can only really use one core at a time of your processor.
It sounds like Bohemia will soon be releasing a 64-bit version, which should see a significant increase in performance for the majority of players.  If you don't mind playing at 30-40fps on average, this is a great game for you. Even if you're used to 60fps+ gaming (or perhaps 144fps) this game is certainly playable, but the occasional stuttering or graphical hiccup can give you quite a disadvantage in firefights or encounters on Wasteland or King of the Hill.
There's plenty to do, but in my opinion you really shouldn't buy this game if you don't plan on purchasing the Apex expansion as well. Before owning the DLC, I was constantly reminded that the money I gave to Bohemia wasn't adequate enough to be able to snipe someone on Wasteland without having my entire screen fill up with obnoxious watermarks every other minute.
All this being said, this game is a great military simulator, however the game mechanics could be a bit more fluid, and the engine could be much better optimized. I'd highly recommend Bohemia step away from their DLC promotion in-game, or at least make it much more subtle, as covering literally the entire screen with watermarks, or having little pop up windows that cover up your whole crosshair and then some, will be sure to quickly drive away potential long term players - especially those that didn't initially intend to spend the money on a DLC.

Highly recommended for people that has given up all hope in life and does not mind staring at a pointless computer screen for endless hours. Here's for all you good folks out there that has caught a fish, this amazing salmon recipe will help a lot with your future endeavours.
1 (2 pound) salmon fillet
1 teaspoon lemon-pepper seasoning
1 teaspoon onion salt
1 small onion, sliced and separated into rings
6 slices lemon
1/4 cup butter, cut into small chunks
1/3 cup sour cream
1/3 cup mayonnaise
1/4 cup dry white wine
1 tablespoon capers
1 tablespoon finely chopped onion
1 tablespoon caper brine
1 teaspoon lemon juice
1 teaspoon prepared horseradish
3/4 teaspoon dried dill weed
1/4 teaspoon garlic salt
ground black pepper to taste
1. Preheat oven to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C). Line a baking sheet with aluminum foil; grease the foil lightly.
2. Place salmon fillet with skin side down on foil. Season salmon with lemon-pepper and onion salt; top with onion rings                   and lemon slices, dot with butter. Fold foil around salmon and seal tightly.
3. Bake in preheated oven for 20 minutes. Unseal the foil and turn the oven's broiler on. Continue cooking the salmon under the broiler until the flesh flakes easily with a fork, 8 to 12 minutes.
4. While the salmon bakes, stir sour cream, mayonnaise, white wine, capers, chopped onion, caper brine, lemon juice, horseradish, dill weed, garlic salt, and black pepper together in a bowl. Serve with the salmon.

What’s interesting about Amnesia is that it eschews most conventional notions associated with the horror genre and manages to transcend other similar games in delivering an immersive and unparalleled experience. Arbitrary and cheap frights are totally absent. It does Lovecraft in the purest sense; it understands that the imagined far outweighs the known in its psychological punch, which in Amnesia’s case is achieved through stellar environment and audio design. But it is the removal of weapons and consequently combat that introduces a wholly new dynamic and therein lies Amnesia’s brilliance. What the game is capable is elevated to an entirely new level. It is undoubtedly creative, original and works flawlessly alongside Lovecraftian themes hinted at. It is a shining example of what the first-person genre, outside of shooting, can achieve on an experiential level.

In Saints Row: The Third, you play the (male or female) boss of an alleged crime gang named The Saints in the fictional city of Steelport. It is an open-world sandbox action game with RPG elements, essentially a shameless clone of the Grand Theft Auto series. Whereas GTA takes the narrative in a serious dramatic direction, Saints Row goes the opposite way towards the satirical and whimsical; a mix of hilarious over-the-top action, political incorrectness, obligatory zombies, outlandish aliens, and a large dose of ribald humour.
When this game was first released, it received a considerable amount of malign coverage from well-intentioned social media for its use of excessive and gratuitous violence. It was even listed as one of the most violent games of 2013 by website
which had the following to say about the game:
Given this glowing endorsement, gamers worried that this game is nothing more than a simple misogynistic murder simulator can rest easy. Saints Row: Third Third is really a sophisticated equal-opportunity murder simulator with multiple amusing methods to commit non-discriminatory murder and mayhem. There's sure to be something for everyone and fun for all the family.
Although a console port, it is a competent one. In particular, mouse+keyboard works really well without the need for the modding or config file hacking that is endemic to bad console ports. Even for the driving/flying parts of the game, mouse+keyboard controls are responsive and precise. There are lots of vehicles and weapons to unlock, but some of the later unlocks such as Infinite Ammo and Invincibility can make the game too easy. Steelport itself is large and fun to explore. Numerous side-quests, challenges, and opportunities for random violence provide plenty of entertainment in between main campaign missions. Sure the plot is stupid and nonsensical, but at least it doesn't go full-retard like the average Presidential campaign.
Overall, Saints Row: The Third is funny, irreverant, and a great game. Which is fortunate, otherwise it would be called Saints Row: The Turd. An iconoclastic work of art, and a worthy purchase for anarchistic misanthropes everwhere.

Let me preface this review by saying that yes, this game does deviate majorly from the orignal Resident Evil formula. This game is still fun even though it's probably not going to appeal to RE purists. If you are looking for a good third-person shooter that's a bit slower paced than, say, Gears of War, give RE5 a look.
With that out of the way, I'm going to give a rundown of the gameplay. You play as Chris Redfield and you have a partner this time around (AI in singleplayer but Coop is avaiable). She's a new character to the RE world, Shiva is her name. If you've played RE4, Shiva behaves in a somewhat similar fashion as Ashley did except Shiva is armed and she will aid you in fights, collect goodies (you dictate what she picks up), and heal you when you're low on health (provided she has herbs/first aid spray). There's only one storage size, unlike in RE4 where you could purchase larger attache cases. You'll have the same ammount of storage throughout the whole game (both Chris and Shiva have storage so you have some degree of inventory management). You also have a "safe" which can be accessed before you start a mission and between missions. I think that's limited too but it's so large that you'll probably never use all of it.
Guns can be upgraded with the ingame money (I forgot what it's called) that you collect from fallen foes and the environment. There's no more merchant but there's still a store which can be accessed before or between missions. Here you buy guns, first aid spray, etc. and sell treasures found in the game for money. Enemies are very similar to RE4, not really zombies but still kinda mindless guys...I don't want to spoil anything so I'll leave it at that.
There's some puzzles in this game but they're not that hard, certainly not like the original Resident Evil games. Capcom has pretty much taken the way RE4 played, kept that as the base and made some modifications so if you have played the 4th RE, you'll find quite a few parallels between RE4 and 5.
To sum up, this game is a solid third-person shooter that will appeal more to people who haven't played the original RE games (not to say if you have, you won't enjoy it) but will probably leave purists high and dry.

Seeing as how Volition is working on a new game, I think it's time for me to finally take a second look at
. I've reviewed part 4 and
, and I didn't have much of anything pleasant to say about them. In fact, I reviewed The Third around the time of its original release, and even then I wasn't altogether ecstatic about it.
Link to review -
So, after a fairly thorough replay, I've ascertained where The Third succeeds and fails. When
eventually releases, I'm hopeful that Volition will have developed it with their strengths in mind, and not their weaknesses.
is at its best early on. In the beginning of the game, you're in unfamiliar territory, you start out with practically nothing, and everyone has far superior firepower and numbers to overwhelm you with. Exploring the city, discovering rewards, and making small but noticeable upgrades to your firepower and abilities; these are the aspects that are satisfying.
However, as the game progresses, Volition deems it necessary to ratchet up the scale, make the explosions bigger, the body-counts higher, and the Boss (you) the most awesome force of nature. Eventually you're so powerful that nothing harms you, you have unlimited high-tech ordnance that makes everything explode, and the game becomes dramatically less fulfilling as a result. After a certain point, it's all a matter of going through the motions, just so the story can conclude.
But let's rewind and talk about the lowest point of SR3, the intro mission. Saints Row, and by extension, open-world games are at their best when there's as little scripting as possible. SR3's intro mission is just wave after wave of bad guys followed by a rail-shooter, and it's an absolute snore. The mission directly afterwards involves falling out of not one but two planes in order to rescue Shaundi. For whatever reason, Shaundi has to be saved a lot, but that isn't the point. Falling out of planes should be exciting, but instead it becomes an excuse for another rail-shooter section, and a moment where The Boss dodges falling vehicles and storage containers. It's supposed to be exciting, but it isn't, because it's so scripted that it becomes uninteresting.
The first several hours of open-world exploration are great. Players are bound to stumple upon the multitude of "gang operations", which in turn cause numerous gang-members to attack. This part of the game is exciting, because the player has agency. They decide where to go, how to get there, and the situation is different depending on A) the gangs, B) the player's arsenal, C) the location, and D) randomness. As the game progresses, the player takes over Steelport, and all those actual exciting moments dry up.
The introduction of the STAG Army raises the stakes, but in terms of game-design, all it results in is larger explosions and louder noises. One of the strengths of the early game are the Specialists. These unique gang-members attack in ways that are unlike the "guys with guns" that are standard for the genre. STAG doesn't really have anyone that fits the bill, so it's just Police 2.0. Also, by the time the STAG rolls in, the other gangs are all but wiped out, so there are less opportunities for exciting conflicts. To add to this, you're not the lone stranger you were in the beginning, and your gang is on practically every street corner. It's a fine recipe for chaos, but doesn't really make for inspired game-design.
Simply put, The Third needed more variables. If things can go wrong, maybe they should. Situations should be allowed to play out in any number of ways, and players should be forced to contend with a multitude of possibilities. A simple mission could involve robbing a bank, but other rivals are gunning for that same bank. The player could steal an armored truck, but if they crash it into a river, then they have to steal a boat to fish out the cash. Anything is an improvement over standing around with a machinegun, and mowing down thirty or so helicopters.
With all this said, do I still recommend Saints Row: The Third? Yes. It holds up better than its sequel, and the Gentlemen of Steelport mod adds all sorts of fun cheats and extras. At this point, I'm more curious about how
is going to turn out. It has the potential to be a far more creative game than the SR series. It would just be a shame if the open-world design and vision was truncuated or ignored. What could be dynamic and interesting, could also be repetitive and bland. It's all in the execution.

Shovel Knight is a 2D platformer.
You move left, right, up and down ladders, use the jump button to jump and the attack button to attack. Press up and the attack button to use your relic and down while in the air to do a down thrust attack with your shovel to bounce off of enemies and other objects. Those are the basics controls of Shovel Knight. Through playing the game, the player will use these various abilities and more to complete the stages of the game, selected through a world map, collecting gold, relics and songs and battling many enemies, overcoming obstacles and defeating bosses.
About the game
The player chooses a stage through a world map.
There are mini-bosses throughout the stages.
There are encounters (Bonus stages) that can appear on the world map.
There are no tutorials.
Relics are items you can use by consuming magic.
Gold lets you buy all kinds of stuff (Extra health, extra magic, relics, armors, shovel skills, access to mini-games etc.)
You lose some of your gold upon death which you can go back and get. (Disappears upon another death if not collected)
There are checkpoints which the player can choose to destroy for more gold.
Boss fights are really fun.
Beautiful and colorful retro graphics.
Awesome soundtrack.
The NPCs are quirky and fun to ineract with.
Nice little story for a retro inspired game.
Personal experience
Controls are fine with a keyboard. (Not sure if it's only my keyboard, but I sometimes had trouble with quickly changing directions and then jumping)
The fact that there are no tutorials is definitely not a negative point.
Finished the game in 9 hours. (Without collecting every relic or all songs or completed every challenge)
Encountered one bug where one boss got stuck and was easily defeated.
Some boss battles are harder than others, but the more challenging ones are pretty difficult while still being fair.
Stages get progressively harder. For the most part, the stages are fair, even though sometimes an enemy will appear from a breakable block and most likely hit Shovel Knight without the player being able to react. The most frustrating part of the game was when I was stuck trying to get past a one-hit-kill obstacle like lava, pits or spikes. (Spikes are less of a problem since there is an relic that prevents you from dying to them) Some of the chackpoints can be a little hard to reach, but they are usually well placed. Generally, the stages are rewarding, fun to play and filled with secrets. (Treasure chests, songs and relics) The gold management mechanic works well where losing your gold is a good enough motivator for the player to feel the need to get better.
The bosses themselves are all amazing looking and have various personalities. (THE BAZ!)
The general enemies and mini-bosses are all very nice too. (Both mechanically and graphically)
Actually, everything looks beautiful in the game.
The soundtrack is really good.
The ending is nice.
Final thoughts
This is a great game!

Seeing as how Volition is working on a new game, I think it's time for me to finally take a second look at
. I've reviewed part 4 and
, and I didn't have much of anything pleasant to say about them. In fact, I reviewed The Third around the time of its original release, and even then I wasn't altogether ecstatic about it.
Link to review -
So, after a fairly thorough replay, I've ascertained where The Third succeeds and fails. When
eventually releases, I'm hopeful that Volition will have developed it with their strengths in mind, and not their weaknesses.
is at its best early on. In the beginning of the game, you're in unfamiliar territory, you start out with practically nothing, and everyone has far superior firepower and numbers to overwhelm you with. Exploring the city, discovering rewards, and making small but noticeable upgrades to your firepower and abilities; these are the aspects that are satisfying.
However, as the game progresses, Volition deems it necessary to ratchet up the scale, make the explosions bigger, the body-counts higher, and the Boss (you) the most awesome force of nature. Eventually you're so powerful that nothing harms you, you have unlimited high-tech ordnance that makes everything explode, and the game becomes dramatically less fulfilling as a result. After a certain point, it's all a matter of going through the motions, just so the story can conclude.
But let's rewind and talk about the lowest point of SR3, the intro mission. Saints Row, and by extension, open-world games are at their best when there's as little scripting as possible. SR3's intro mission is just wave after wave of bad guys followed by a rail-shooter, and it's an absolute snore. The mission directly afterwards involves falling out of not one but two planes in order to rescue Shaundi. For whatever reason, Shaundi has to be saved a lot, but that isn't the point. Falling out of planes should be exciting, but instead it becomes an excuse for another rail-shooter section, and a moment where The Boss dodges falling vehicles and storage containers. It's supposed to be exciting, but it isn't, because it's so scripted that it becomes uninteresting.
The first several hours of open-world exploration are great. Players are bound to stumple upon the multitude of "gang operations", which in turn cause numerous gang-members to attack. This part of the game is exciting, because the player has agency. They decide where to go, how to get there, and the situation is different depending on A) the gangs, B) the player's arsenal, C) the location, and D) randomness. As the game progresses, the player takes over Steelport, and all those actual exciting moments dry up.
The introduction of the STAG Army raises the stakes, but in terms of game-design, all it results in is larger explosions and louder noises. One of the strengths of the early game are the Specialists. These unique gang-members attack in ways that are unlike the "guys with guns" that are standard for the genre. STAG doesn't really have anyone that fits the bill, so it's just Police 2.0. Also, by the time the STAG rolls in, the other gangs are all but wiped out, so there are less opportunities for exciting conflicts. To add to this, you're not the lone stranger you were in the beginning, and your gang is on practically every street corner. It's a fine recipe for chaos, but doesn't really make for inspired game-design.
Simply put, The Third needed more variables. If things can go wrong, maybe they should. Situations should be allowed to play out in any number of ways, and players should be forced to contend with a multitude of possibilities. A simple mission could involve robbing a bank, but other rivals are gunning for that same bank. The player could steal an armored truck, but if they crash it into a river, then they have to steal a boat to fish out the cash. Anything is an improvement over standing around with a machinegun, and mowing down thirty or so helicopters.
With all this said, do I still recommend Saints Row: The Third? Yes. It holds up better than its sequel, and the Gentlemen of Steelport mod adds all sorts of fun cheats and extras. At this point, I'm more curious about how
is going to turn out. It has the potential to be a far more creative game than the SR series. It would just be a shame if the open-world design and vision was truncuated or ignored. What could be dynamic and interesting, could also be repetitive and bland. It's all in the execution.
