Fell in love with this game very quickly because it's a bit of an oddity. It's a simple retro throwback with all of the charm of the original 2D Action Platformers, but what really won my affection was Shovel Knight's attention to detail and atmosphere.
It plays like colorful, humor-filled poetry.
For example, what really stood out to me is that the game starts with a back drop setting and some short handed exposition about the character you play so we can jump in and get playing. However, The game isn't quite clear about what happened to a lost friend of the Shovel Knight, only that he lost her. At select segments of the game, you dream of her falling and fight to catch her, and this is all done by you, the player. It's beautiful to see a game describe a character's emotional state and motivations through gameplay. I understand and can sympathize with the Shovel Knight's loss because I'm walking in his shoes. Other mediums don't have that potential. And for that matter, a lot of games we play don't deal with the subject of loss as maturely as it's handled here.
Gameplay is tight and varied. The "Shovel Blade" is an excellent weapon and tool for both exploration and combat. The humor is genuine and light-hearted. The color palet and designs are a delicious feast for the eyes. Sometimes I stop and stand just to take in the back drops. The soundtrack is amazing. I've been listening to it for days. And it's all 8-bit too... have you bought this freakin' game yet?

Fell in love with this game very quickly because it's a bit of an oddity. It's a simple retro throwback with all of the charm of the original 2D Action Platformers, but what really won my affection was Shovel Knight's attention to detail and atmosphere.
It plays like colorful, humor-filled poetry.
For example, what really stood out to me is that the game starts with a back drop setting and some short handed exposition about the character you play so we can jump in and get playing. However, The game isn't quite clear about what happened to a lost friend of the Shovel Knight, only that he lost her. At select segments of the game, you dream of her falling and fight to catch her, and this is all done by you, the player. It's beautiful to see a game describe a character's emotional state and motivations through gameplay. I understand and can sympathize with the Shovel Knight's loss because I'm walking in his shoes. Other mediums don't have that potential. And for that matter, a lot of games we play don't deal with the subject of loss as maturely as it's handled here.
Gameplay is tight and varied. The "Shovel Blade" is an excellent weapon and tool for both exploration and combat. The humor is genuine and light-hearted. The color palet and designs are a delicious feast for the eyes. Sometimes I stop and stand just to take in the back drops. The soundtrack is amazing. I've been listening to it for days. And it's all 8-bit too... have you bought this freakin' game yet?

Plants vs Zombies is a lane tower defense game. It's relatively simple but a blast to play. Each level you place down plants in 5 lanes that zombies run down. Your plants kill or block zombies. Some shoot peas that damage them, some are just barriers like walnuts, some might explode like land mines. Different types work better against different types of zombies. You also have to balance resource collection. Each plant requires a certain amount of "sun" currency to buy. During the day sun drops naturally from the sky, but too slowly to be enough, so you must plant sunflowers to get more. At night it's even worse, sunflowers and mushrooms are your only sun generators.
There's also water levels where you must place plants on lilly pads and rooftop levels where you must drop down clay pots for your plants. In all it's easy to understand buy has a surprising amount of strategy and depth.
The visuals are great and the music is fun. There's a ton of great mini games too and upgrades to unlock. There's quite a bit of game here and it's a great value. It can be an awesome 10 min lunch break game or one you sit and play for hours.

Initially, I was going to give Portal Stories: Mel, a rather mixed review. However with the release of story mode, I replayed the game to see what had changed. And I am glad that I did. Many of the complaints I had with the original version of the game have been rectified with story modes addition, namely the removal of filler in the test chambers, which unnecessarily complicated the puzzle and lengthened the amount of time each test chamber took to complete. The unnecessary length of time that it took to complete each test chamber bloated out the story so much, it became difficult for me to remember what Mel, you as the player, goal was. While the "original" version of the game is playable under "advanced mode", I highly recommend that you play story mode first.
Set prior to Portal 2, Portal Stories: Mel is an unofficial mod that takes place during Aperture Science's glory. You play as Mel, selected to become a test subject for Aperture. However complications arise, and soon you must explore the ruins of a now defunct Aperture Science. Guiding you is Virgil, a personality core who's voice sounds uncomfortably like PewDiePie. Virgil is often annoying at times, mainly because of the games rather average dialogue. In both Portal and Portal 2, GLaDOS, Wheatley and Cave Johnson were absolute triumphs in voice-acting and personality. Being one of the few voices you hear in those games, it was going to be hard for Virgil to stand toe-to-toe in quality, humor and dialogue. Virgil's character isn't "badly" written, its just he sounds out of place in the Portal franchise, where both the voice acting, dialogue and humor were absolutely essential to making a great character.
The difficulty in Portal Stories: Mel is also worth mentioning as not being for a Portal beginner. The previous two Portal games were excellent in teaching you game mechanics (listen to the developer commentary, it's seriously amazing how they did it). Portal Stories: Mel throws you in the thick of it and assumes that you have already mastered all of the games techniques. While this is in no means a bad thing in that the game doesn't hold your hand, it's worth noting the spike in difficulty levels between Mel and both Portal games. Played on story mode, Mel would take on around 5-7 hours to complete for the average Portal player. Advanced mode is a whole new beast, and will widely vary depending on player's persistence.
One thing the game nailed was soundtrack. Portal and Portal 2 have excellent soundtracks, and it would have been hard for Portal Stories: Mel, to stand in comparison with them. Fortunately, the soundtrack is one of the games highlights. Suitably "portal-esque" in sound and atmosphere, the music is fantastically written and is worth the download to this already free mod.
If you wish for more Portal, Portal Stories: Mel is worth a shot. While the game cannot hold a light to the franchise's voice acting, humor and in particular level design, at the end of the day it's a free mod so you have almost nothing to lose but your own time playing the game. As long as you don't try to extensively compare the game is it's amazing predecessors like I did, Portal Stories: Mel is a well made mod, and shows the power the modding community has to games and that sometimes, we get a mod that some may call worthy of an expansion or standalone title.

Plants vs Zombies (PvZ) is a one dimensional tower defense game.  Zombies move from right to left while you plant plants to defend against the invasion.
PvZ puts the casual in casual gaming.  It really reminds me of broccoli.
The good:
- Mildly interesting and entertaining like broccoli
The bad:
- Highly repetitive.  Like broccoli, this game needs more variation.  For instance more plants that improve other plants' abilities or retard them - or other interesting ways to improve your plants' abilities.
The ugly:
- Nothing mysterious or puzzling about this game - like broccoli it is really simple and straight forward - no thinking required.  It is really a test of how fast you can click.
Buy if you have a few hours to waste on an airport.

In the deluge of indie games trying as hard as they can to be "retro" or "challenging" it's easy to become jaded. It feels as though every game rips off Cave Story's asthetic, or they feel the need to cram in stupid physics or RNG sections.
Shovel Knight isn't one of those games.
The controls are very tight for an indie platformer, Shovel Knight has a limited attack range and the levels are designed around this and his ability to dig up terrain blocks. The music is fantastic, it's Kaufman and Matsumae, you cannot improve on that. Even my most hated level had a theme I find stuck in my head from my repeated failures.
The only thing that truly seperates this game from its predecessors is a lack of a life system, where they've instead opted for a Demon's/Dark Souls-esque system where you only drop your money which has to be recovered. And in typical Souls fashion, the levels are easy if you take it slow but fiendish if you try to rush, especially if you want to be cool and go for those final achievements.
If you find the money and have any fondness for 2D platformers, then you should definitely pick this game up.

I am really liking this game so far and I'm really glad I found it. Probably the one of the best fishing sims I've played. You can do most things you can in real life like adjusting drag, jerking your rod to get free from snagging some weeds, choosing where and what time to fish, etc. I'm not gonna lie, it'll take you awhile to level up and you'll probably be catching a lot of bluegills when you first start because certain fish needs a certain bait and time of day to get. Not to mention where you cast on the body of water and how high or low you set your bobber/leader can also make a difference. Took me some time to get to level 3 so I can get the casting spoons for bass but when I got them, it was worth it. There's also an in-game chatbox where other players can chat with one another. I found this useful. The majority of the community is just great in this game. I did however, run into a few people arguing on chat about irrelevant topics and a player who told everyone that they suck and he is the best fisherman on the server but most of the people are willingly able to help each other out if a player needs help or tips on how to do things. The game kinda tends to be a bit laggy at some times but not a lot. Anyways, with that being said, this game is still a great and relaxing simulator. It's free, why not try it out? :)

I'll be very honest with it. Out of all the horror games I have played so far, this is the only TRUE survival horror. Amnesia is the kind of games that put all other games in perspective. The first thing that hits you after playing this is the realization that there hasn't been any game so true to the horror genre in its more pure form since the first Silent Hill.
As I say all the time, developer Frictional Games might just be the freshest, most interesting group of minds to grace gaming in a good while. Reading about their thoughts and ideas in their blog is the kind of experience that brings back the hope in gaming.
And it's not just words: Watching the progression made from Penumbra: Overture to Penumbra: Black Plague and then to Amnesia is akin to watching a firmly, steadily ascending curve of game design.
Finally, the success in  sales and reviews that Amnesia achieved (along with that of Minecraft) sends out a strong message to other indie developers about being true to your ideas and never compromising.

It's strange how the direction to Resident Evil has changed so dramatically. From what amounts to open world exploration, with the need to gather keys, and clues, to uncover more passages; to an outright liner level design, with no doubling-back, and actual individule stages. It's just very strange, more than anything! As well--though Resident Evil. . .3, or was it zero? handled partners well, in this version it removes all the tension and fear, because you're very alert AI companion is by your side virtually at all times, and in fact I just stopped looking for enemies myself because I knew my partner would see them before I often would.
It should be called. .something else; a different series, with different characters; because that's what it feels like. It could be successful if that's what it was, but what's here does not really feel like an actual Resident Evil game, and that's really the very worse thing about it!
I don't know what the project leads were thinking, but perhaps they were actually turned into zombies during production. Especially the later levels feel, just not well thought out in basic ways. Like, there's these just knee-high walls preventing you from travelling across the path, and you simply can not cross them, even though any human--or zombie--could just step over those walls! It was really my greatest memory of the game, after the first level; just standing there, saying to my character: "Leon, please, just. . . just step over that wall. . .Leon, Leon, please. . . please. . .you're a super special-ops trained officer; you've travelled across the world, fighting monsters! Look, I can see the path on the other side of it; there's even a treasure chest there! Just. . just please step over this tiny wall!!!" . . . . .It's not even a  hard puzzle to get around them, it's just that no human would ever have trouble walking from one side of that room to the other; even if they had a broken leg! Ugh!!

A game that feels like one out of the old generation of games, but brings a lot of life to the genre. On top of fantastic gameplay with nice feeling controls, I am perhaps most impressed by the vivid world of Shovel Knight. There are some truly novel concepts (Troupple King?!) and a lot of characters who bring life to the world. The skills all have a place but never feel overpowered, and much to my delight, the developers did not make each one tailored to wreck a specific boss in the fashion of Mega Man. One aspect that I loved is that the game was tough, but seldom unfair. At one point, I died 20 times without making any progress, simply because I was making mistakes. However, in this span, I was frustrated but never felt like quitting the game.
Whether you are a veteran of the genre or are looking to dive into the genre with a newer title, Shovel Knight will provide a ton of fun and a good challenge. It isn't just a great throwback to the old days, it's a game that would shine in any era.

While I am no dedicated fan of the Resident Evil series, nor an everyday follower, I hear many cite Resident Evil 5 as the beginning of what they felt was a decline. Having only foggy childhood memories of Resident Evil 2 on my old Nintendo 64 and a close friend's dedication to the series holding me back, I can still say I understand why.
It is no secret that I am one for action games with good tempo and flow; the countless hours I've invested into Payday, E.Y.E., and Killing Floor speak volumes. I am no stranger to horror; I've played the far ends of the spectrum in Amnesia and Penumbra, Dead Space and STALKER. Even as restrained as I can be, I can say wholeheartedly that Resident Evil 5 struck none of the high notes that any of those titles - for all the hours and playthroughs they've offered me - have achieved.
While undoubtedly far in advance of the fixed camera perspective I recall from Resident Evil 2, Resident Evil 5's combat hit me as clunky, backwards, and bizarrely slow. Clunky, where the player is rooted to the ground while firing and is most often required to use slow-firing manual and semiautomatic weapons. Backwards, where headshots are passively discouraged by the early introduction of particular reactions to headshots. Bizarrely slow, where mentioned focus on pistols and pump-action shotguns combines with a dawdling enemy pace that would make some of my slowest games in strategy titles seem like they were taking place at superluminal velocity.
Storywise, I doubt I have ever cringed as much as I have through the course of watching Resident Evil 5's plot. It is easily the most unashamedly cheesy and melodramatic game I have ever played, bereft of humor and serious to a fault. In some cases, I saw plot elements coming from miles away. In others, I could feel the word "why" trying to beat its way out of my skull. Particularly, a character is introduced early on with all the subtlety and rationality in design as a tank skydiving into a ballpit. As the plot continued to thicken, I could feel my "immersion" - had I even pretended to carry any - shrivel further and further.
Bogging down gameplay and storytelling yet more are the absurdly numerous and absurdly lengthy quick-time events that sometimes boggled the mind as to why they even existed. Events such as the player characters running down hallways became, at some points, interactive cutscenes, rather than allowing player control and offering meaningful challenges over button mashing contests and keyboard (or controller) attention checks. While I do not deny that Dead Space - oft-compared and of similar genre definition - featured many of its own quick-time events, I feel much more confident in their role and value than I do Resident Evil 5's.
The game is not without its strengths, of course - I don't deal in absolutes. Balance, both in supply hurdles and enemies, is well laid-out. Graphical quality is astonishing for an early 2009 game. Voice acting, though given material I find questionable to follow, is done well. High marks are also to be given for its stability, though it should be known that I and a close friend encountered a gamebreaking, though eventually resolved bug at the very end of the game. Multiplayer features offer some replayability, but unfortunately play to one of the game's weak suits - its combat - outside of regular cooperative play.

Shovel Knight is a game designed to be a throwback to the NES era of videogames. It takes inspiration from many classic games such as Super Mario Bros. 3, The Legend of Zelda, DuckTales, Metroid, Mega Man, and the list goes on. You take on the role as Shovel Knight whose beloved friend, Shield Knight, has been taken away and it is your job to pass through the multiple levels and save her.
There are multiple stages in this game and each of them have a different element to them which differentiates one from the rest. The levels have some difficulty to them but a set amount of checkpoints allow the game to feel less "rage-inducing." The checkpoints may also be ignored or "broken" in order to achieve more jewels or treasure, the curreny in the game, which may be used to purchase new armor, items, health upgrades, magic upgrades, or shovel upgrades. Each of the bosses at the end of the level are unique so the game does not get tedious or feel boring at any point. There are also collectibles in the form of "Music Sheets" which are in hidden locations throughout the game and can be collected for money, providing an incentive.
The best part of the game is the fact that it is extremely replayable because of its brilliant concept and level design. The score is also amazing and very true in achieving that "NES" feel to the game. Any fans of classic games will appreciate this game and anyone who enjoys having fun will enjoy it as well. It definitely provides some challenge on the first playthrough and there is also a New Game + Mode for the daring. Overall, Shovel Knight is just a blast to play through and just shows the power of KickStarter.

As the industry grows and creating games becomes more feasible for small time development teams amazing games spawn from nostalgia and peoples love for their past favorite games. Shovel Knight perfectly encapsulates the community wanting their retro game feel, while still maintaining a modern experience in flow and glitch-free gameplay. Pulling from the experiences of Mario 3, Zelda II, Megaman, Duck Tales, and other retros games Shovel Knight mixes these all in a pot and gives us something we couldn't experience on a NES by expanding on colors and gameplay that the system would not have allowed at the time. That's what makes Shovel Knight appeal to so many of us.
The game itself is fantastic. The action platforming and game design makes you feel like you are playing a Castlevania Megaman love child. Each zone has its own theme (a castle for king knight, a graveyard for spectar knight etc.) drawing from the best part of Megaman; its uniqueness. And the stage has hidden areas and challenge rooms giving you the exploratory feel of a Castlevania game. Your trek to the boss is challenging, but not frustrating and the game allows you to make things more difficult for yourself by rewarding you for destroying checkpoints. Defeating a stage always feels like a true accomplishment because the boss battles are hard and long fought. Once completed you are back to the overworld where you may be met with random encounters, challenging areas to test your skill, or fun banter with merchants and towns people. Combine that with masterful music and beautiful artstyle and you find almost no issue in the game.
The only issues one can bring up are sadly the game is too short, and the difficult cap may be high for those new to platformers. I myself had a hard time in many areas and I adore games like this. A lot of trail and error is involved, but with deligence any player should be able to finish the game. On the issue of the game being to short. I do not necessarily think that is a bad thing. A game as good as this is bound to leave a player wanting more and wanting more is what all games should leave you feeling. I do not hamper on Shovel Knight for being to short because it is my own selfishness that wants 20 more bosses and stages, endless music, and new and greater challenges.
Overall Shovel Knight is an easy 10/10 and I have taken my nostalgia goggles off even for this score. I may seem biased, but even if I didn't have history with the aforementioned games Shovel Knight would still be a fantastic piece on its own. For those new to platformers and this style Shovel Knight will be a refreshing challenge and a wonderful gameplay adventure. For lovers of the old platformers this is the game we have been waiting for; all your favorites wrapped up in a new intersting experience that will both satisfy your thirst for nostalgia and leave you begging for more.

RE5 is a great game spoiled by atrocious controls. I mean the worst ever. These are the main problems: You can’t move while reloading, aiming, or shooting; instead you become rooted to the spot and therefore hopelessly vulnerable to attack. When aiming the sight is often (although, oddly, not always) wrenched away from the point already centred so you have to find your target again. And you can’t jump or crouch unless prompted. What the hell is that all about? Also the AI is pretty poor. Sheva gets in the way more often than not. The UI looks like something out of the 90s and is clunky to say the least. And you can’t access the inventory during gameplay (although I understand the reasoning behind this it is frustrating at times). So what is there to like? Well it looks amazing. The graphics are among the best I’ve ever seen, with particularly impressive character models and animations. And, controls aside, the gameplay is enjoyable, with a good selection of environments, some pretty tough bosses, and a range of simple but enjoyable puzzles to solve. Ammo is often scarce so you have to be more thoughtful about your approach to the combat than in many games. Overall it’s a top-flight game marred only but it’s poorly designed controls and interface. Sadly these are so bad I can only give it 3 out of 5, which is a real shame.

Honestly, I was skeptical at first having bought into dovetail games fishing and just plain disliking that, but this game was a pleasant suprise. I'm an avid fisherman and haven't been out much this year because I'm a full time college student (summer classes too...). This game has scratched that itch and will continue to do so every winter when I just want to be out bass fishing.
It's early access, so I assume things will only improve from here on out, but it's a solid game. The graphics are awesome, fighting with a fish seems awesome (except when you yank a small fish out of the water and it flies around you...but it's a laugh at least), and the sheer number of items is impressive. I personally dislike that it's the type of game that deals with in game purchases and such, but the game is totally playable without spending a dime. Getting started until you reach level 3-4 is a bit of a grind, but after then is when the game truly becomes fun. The community is great, I get into discussions about all sorts of things and we help each other with game tips. All in all, it's a great experience and it's a relaxing break from your regular day to day.
I definitely recommend this game to any fishing fan.

Shovel Knight performs like a platformer, but it exudes a nostalgic homage to the Megaman and Castlevania NES games that made 2D side-scrolling action-adventures popular. Think of it as the spiritual successor to these games, while altogether aware of the current generation of gamers' appeals.
The graphics are crisp, the music is on-point (albeit you must have at least a modicum of interest in chiptunes), the story is both amusing and exciting, and most importantly, the gameplay is smooth and decisive.
Shovel Knight doesn't just echo a sense of the brilliance behind sidescrollers; it masters that sense of intrigue and pushes on to complete perfection.
This game is not only a work of art - it's also a hell of a good time. Support these guys, and buy this game. Even if you don't like games like this, I assure you that Shovel Knight will win you over with its charm.

You take the best bits from Megaman (8 boss themed stages, ridiculously catchy 8bit tunes) and you mix it with some Mario style overhead level selecting (including extra areas and extra boss encounters) and top it off with some lite RPG leveling mechanics, and you got an amazing homage to the 8bit era. The platforming is engaging, with treacherous enemy placement and a down attack mechanic that boosts your height. The combat is simplistic, but with a regular stream of new relic abilities, ensures an ever expanding arsenal and mobility enhancements. There's a few too many insta-death areas which will increase your frustration level, but this is classic gaming where pattern recognition and memorization are the name of the game. Plus it has a very forgiving checkpoint system, about 5 per stage, which is about 4 more than you got back in the day. Not only does it look the part, but this is old school gaming at its best.

Resident Evil 4 massively broke the formula. Whilst there were some complaints from the diehards, the overwhelming census was that the franchise's break away from fixed camera was for the best. Whilst their recent titles Code Veronica and Resident Evil 0 were decent enough, but not amazing, RE4 found audiences every bit as awe struck by the game as they were when they first stepped foot in Spenser Manor in 1996. The franchise looked onward to a bright new future that whilst certainly would leave its survival horror roots behind, would immerse it's audience in a detailed 3D world with tight new gunplay as they fought back overwhelming hordes of
Spaniards.
Alas, the dream was too good to be true. RE5 was merely a mediocre third person shooter with nothing more than an arbitrary RE universe story featuring some familiar faces. The fantastic difficulty balance and pacing of the battles seen in its predecessor  were absent, and the distinctly Japanese over the top story and set pieces were replaced with Western feeling low key blandness. Whilst some areas such as the swampy island area offered enjoyable large scale battles, much of the game was spent trudging down corridors spraying a continual stream of bullets.
The biggest upside to this title is that coop mode plays very well, and overcoming a difficult spot with teamwork on the harder difficulties feels very rewarding. Also, it means you won't have to put up with the immersion breaking ai ineptitude of Sheva.
Spear-chucking Mud Men out of Ten
***Fun Stuff for RE Fans***
Check out where the series really got it's root's from by playing Sweet Home on the NES (or at least an English rom on an emulator...). It's a survival horror RPG in which a team of characters explore a haunted mansion (which is refereed to as a 'House of Residing Evil'!). You have limited inventory space, one character has a permanent lock pick, one has a permanent lighter, and the only way to heal if to carry the limited number of inventory hogging healing items you find. Also, doors open slowly in first person. Any of that sound familiar to veterans of the series? Its a far better, and far scarier experience than RE5!

Why do people still use umbrellas in modern society? The question is a deceptively simple one, for reasons upon which I will elaborate.  Firstly, people use umbrellas for the purpose of remaining dry, or not wet. Specifically when their surrounding area is being rained on, pelted with wetness as it were.  But whence this desire for retaining dryness when one's environment is wet, whence this human urge to ostracize one's self from the natural cycle, or rather...  To ostracize nature from ones own life.  Is the clue not in the question? Is it not the same with modern man's wish to spend his life in cities, homo urbanus.  Removed from the tumult of the organic world.  And yet, what is this world, and what is rain?  Rain wets, providing plants and animals with nutriment, filling up their cells with cytoplasm, and their veins with blood to transport nutrients, allowing them to stay alive.  Rain wets, providing the ground with moisture, moisture which seeps down through the sedimentary layers of soil, and without which no repositories of drinkable water would be present for the urban human to hydrate himself.  Urban man is desiccated, but relies upon this natural cycle to replenish him, yet he pretends that this ancient arrangement is beneath him, as when he removes his domicile from the wet ground, as when he removes his body from the rain, the umbrella is a symbol of man shunning nature, of woman shielding herself from the life giving sky.  Rain wets, and it erodes the cracking ground creating landslides, waterfalls, floods.  It reforms the terrain, allowing new flora and fauna to make their inroads on the surface of our world.  Yet from this, modern man and woman shield themselves.  Why?  Why to keep their clothes dry, to keep their electronic items secure. For you see rain wets and kills technology, and that is the bane of homo, so called sapiens.  What sapience is there in erecting the edifice of your life and society on a foundation that is enemy to the water, who's anathematized cloud and air and sea and sky, for water is in all those things.  And then, what is an umbrella?  An umbrella is an illusion, a self delusion that you can keep the wet out of your life, that though you breathe and eat and walk on things infused with it, you can control the dominion of water over your existence. My experience with this game has been... dicey.
I've enjoyed my experience so far, i really do. However, to get better at the game, for me, at least, is really difficult.
Put simply, R6Siege is CS:GO on steroids; a map and objective based twitch shooter, this time with unique operators with their own loadouts and their unique gadgets. It's easy to pick up, yet hard to master.
There lies the crux of the matter; matchmaking (at least in casual) is non-existent, and there's no way to go around maps excepting the terrorist hunt mode which is vastly different from pvp. Getting matched with players with multiple times your experience means that with their mastery of the operators and the map, there is very little you can do against them. People will shoot you from impossible angles, you will lose aim-for-aim, you will be dumbfounded at how people will spot you from 5 pixels of your helmet peeking behind cover.
My only hope is that with Operation Health, the game heads in the right direction and put in place some much needed matchmaking system.
Post-Operation Health update: There is very little difference between the start of Operation Health and after it. The pervasive issues such as ping spikes and long loading is still there, matchmaking in casual is still non-existent, ranked is still in beta; perhaps the only notable changes i saw change were the hitbox updates and what, being able to browse the shop and operators while waiting for a match.
And now they're delaying game updates and holding back releases.
tl;dr hellish new player experience, high skill floor while at the same time being really difficult to master. Do not approach if you're not planning to go all the way with the game and invest mighty amounts of time in it.

Portal Stories: Mel is a Portal 2 mod so completely epic and well polished that it should be considered as an actual game in itself. It boasts new characters with custom dialogue and visuals, features an awesome original soundtrack (available as free DLC), and contains its own Steam Achievments. But best of all, it has a well-conceived story set some time after the events of the original Portal, and directly leading up to the opening of Portal 2. The new storyline adds even more depth to the history behind Aperture Science Laboratories without conflicting with the details of the official plot.
Possibly the greatest strength of this ambitious project is that it features something that the official games don't; Difficulty Settings. Portal 2's puzzles build upon the difficulty of the original title, and Portal Stories: Mel takes it a step further, but offers players the option of "Story Mode", or "Advanced Mode". New players should consider playing "Story Mode" first and moving on to "Advanced Mode" once they're ready for some serious aneurysms and cerebral hemorrhaging. Portal offered us "Challenge Chambers", Portal 2 gave us the "Cooperative Testing Initiative", but only Portal Stories: Mel allows us to choose how difficult the standard experience is. It may not be Portal 3, but it might as well be. I highly recommend this game to anyone who loved the official titles.

Play as the Shovel Knight as you make your way through diverse levels to face off against the knights of The Order of No Quarter.  An evil enchantress is up to no good, and you must stop her!  Along the way, you'll collect subweapons and magic, upgrade your health and mana, purchase upgrades to your shovel and armor to give you new abilities, and occasionally run into enemies and other events on the field between levels, just to spice things up a bit.  And.. of course, collect treasure!
This game looks generic at first glance, but it's full of depth and drenched in personality.  Every level has unique 'gimmicks' and every boss battle is different from the last.  There are sub stages, mini games, and events that appear on the map at certain times, just to keep things even more spiced up.  This game is full of secrets to find.  Every NPC has dialog, many have events associated with them, and you'll find surprises everywhere (such as a really cool boss living right inside one of the main town areas!)

It takes some inspiration from games like Megaman, Castlevania, and Ducktales.. but does enough new stuff of its own to not just be lackluster copy or retro homage, or just another mediocre indie platformer.. It holds up just fine on its own.  Seriously.  It can be a little hard at times, but it's not unfair.  Challenging, but not frustrating.
Bottom line, GET IT.  If the price seems a little steep for you.. Well, first of all, it's worth it.  But if you just can't drop that much dough, at least wishlist it and wait for a sale.  This game is worth playing, and the developers are worth supporting.  This is truly an example of a kickstarter dream gone RIGHT.
(note that at the time of writing, I'm roughly about halfway through the levels.  I'll be completing this game soon because I love it.. and I'll probably go back to find all of the collectable music pages that I've probably missed, as well.)

Have Ubisoft actually made a genuinly awesome game? Well yes, yes they have.
The tale of Siege is an intriguing one. It went from having a horrid release to being an incredibly popular and dare I say, one of the best FPS multiplayer games to be released to this date. The constant development and support keeps the game fresh and changes up the meta every few months. The shoddy business model of Ubisoft's previous titles is gone for good. When a new DLC comes out, all of the content in it is available to everyone for free, albeit with season pass owners getting it a week prior to everyone else. The map is free on day one and can be played by everyone. The new operators can be purchased with in-game credits and while the price is certainly a little high, I wouldn't say it's too high. Realistically, it'll probably take you a few days of successful gameplay to earn enough to purchase one.
And while we're on the topic of operators, in my personal opinion, this is the reason you should buy the game. So many different characters to choose from and almost all of them (with only a couple of exceptions) are well balanced and fit into the meta very nicely. Nothing beats the feeling of when you've gotten exceptionally good with your main. I will live and die by Caveira. The gunplay is fantastic, the matches are intense and the community is definitely better than most FPS games, but there are also the black sheep, of course.
This game is an experience you need to have.

Resident Evil 5 is an action-adventure third-person shooter video game developed and published by Capcom. It is the seventh installment in the Resident Evil series, originally released on September 2009 for Microsoft Windows.
The plot revolves around Chris Redfield and Sheva Alomar's investigation of a terrorist threat in Kijuju, a fictional region in Africa. Prior knowledge of previous Resident Evil games is not required to enjoy this game. I myself have only played RE1 and RE2 back on the PS1 and missed out on the rest of the series until RE5, and I still enjoyed the story. For players who have played thru the whole series however, i'm sure they'll feel right at home with this one.
RE5 breaks away from the original dark feel of the original series, and focuses alot more on action rather then horror. (Although the story is still horror based). Fans of the original RE dark survival horror feel may not appreciate this change in direction however.
The main selling point is it's ingenious use of 2 players co-op mode which works extremely well. Level designs felt like they're made especially for co-op and the intense boss fights can make the game really fun and engaging. Alot of puzzles are also catered very much for co-operative play.
Graphically, the environments and lighting are very good looking, especially the skin textures of the characters. Sound effects are crisp and sharp, and i enjoyed the english voice-over work. Every character sounds pretty good and fits their role well. The game also features alot of extra modes and unlockables which greatly enhances replayability.
Downsides, the controls feel clunky. For example, you cannot run and shoot at the same time. Do not play this game expecting it to be a FPS. Its better to slow down and make your shots count. Quick Time Events (QTEs) are very annoying, and is especially aggravating when they appear during boss fights or even cutscenes.
Some QTE key combinations are also just plain sadistic. I mean i'm ok when you need players to press A+D, but who the heck thought it would be ok to put F+V as a combination? In general, the QTEs are excessive and just plain rediculous.
Overall Rating: 8.0 / 10

Resident Evil 5 is an action-adventure third-person shooter video game developed and published by Capcom. It is the seventh installment in the Resident Evil series, originally released on September 2009 for Microsoft Windows.
The plot revolves around Chris Redfield and Sheva Alomar's investigation of a terrorist threat in Kijuju, a fictional region in Africa. Prior knowledge of previous Resident Evil games is not required to enjoy this game. I myself have only played RE1 and RE2 back on the PS1 and missed out on the rest of the series until RE5, and I still enjoyed the story. For players who have played thru the whole series however, i'm sure they'll feel right at home with this one.
RE5 breaks away from the original dark feel of the original series, and focuses alot more on action rather then horror. (Although the story is still horror based). Fans of the original RE dark survival horror feel may not appreciate this change in direction however.
The main selling point is it's ingenious use of 2 players co-op mode which works extremely well. Level designs felt like they're made especially for co-op and the intense boss fights can make the game really fun and engaging. Alot of puzzles are also catered very much for co-operative play.
Graphically, the environments and lighting are very good looking, especially the skin textures of the characters. Sound effects are crisp and sharp, and i enjoyed the english voice-over work. Every character sounds pretty good and fits their role well. The game also features alot of extra modes and unlockables which greatly enhances replayability.
Downsides, the controls feel clunky. For example, you cannot run and shoot at the same time. Do not play this game expecting it to be a FPS. Its better to slow down and make your shots count. Quick Time Events (QTEs) are very annoying, and is especially aggravating when they appear during boss fights or even cutscenes.
Some QTE key combinations are also just plain sadistic. I mean i'm ok when you need players to press A+D, but who the heck thought it would be ok to put F+V as a combination? In general, the QTEs are excessive and just plain rediculous.
Overall Rating: 8.0 / 10
An excellent co-op game. If you don't mind its more action oriented take on the RE series, and sometimes excessive and badly designed QTEs during gameplay, it is a definite must buy.

Plants vs. Zombies is a twist on the traditional Tower Defence genre, being narritive driven and intuitive, but also easy to learn with nuances to master, so players of all skill ranges can enjoy it, from your mum to the elite pro's of Starcraft.
Serious time:
You play as a humble homeowner, who owns five lawnmowers for some reason, who happened to buy a house behind a cemetery, where the titular zombies pour forth. Now you, with your neighbour Crazy Dave (or you can just call him Crazy Dave) and all the seeds you could grab from the garden centre must stop the zombies from entering your house and EATING YOUR BRAINS!
There's a variety of plants to choose from which you earn as you progress through the game, and there's a vast plethora of Zombies to see and get eaten by, from regulars to those who look like Micheal Jackson. Gameplay's simple: Get some sunlight, plant some...plants, and kill some MOTHER, ♥♥♥♥ING, ZOMBIES!
It's genuinely funny. Along with an artstyle so adorable it's probably illegal, just looking through the Suburban Almanac (a book that contains info on all the plants and zombies you've seen so far), there's certainly enough giggles in there alone, and that's not even mentioning the shenanigans Crazy Dave gets up too, when he's not flogging you stuff from the back of his car (spoilers!).
I suppose the only real failing of PvZ is that it's designed for casual play, so isn't particularly difficult, both a blessing and curse. After a while, it does get a bit 'samey', even with new plants and zombies to plant and kill respectively. Eventually you'll get a routine going for each level, so it can become a bit monotunous at times.
8/10 - Simple gameplay, nice artstyle.

Good things, but not a good game in overall. If you look for realism, it may be what you want, but not if you want a good game inmersion. Arma III is far better than Arma II, with good graphics, good plot, good ambientation and great realism.. but it still has bad phisics, bad AI, bad inmersion, and again really bad controls. This experience is only based in the Campaign.
These are the personal reasons, why I ended not liking this game:
-Poor phisics make it unrealistic and really hard to aim at the enemy. Enemy will do lots of turns, crouches, and random things supported by a bad AI. It takes you out of the game experience that the plot brought.
-Vehicle controls such cars or trucks is really painfull, aswell as other nonsense vehicles you have to learn to drive reading the manual just for using them couple of minutes.
-Body or weapon controls are catastrophic. You will never feel comfortable beeing your character. They are unnatural and in the end in stress your character won't do what you want him to do. You will stand up from cover in the middle of the battle by error, or not find the correct way to give a concrete order, couch, or simply aim with the visor.
-Envoirmental intereaction with the caracter is pretty bad. Your body will get stuck when couching, won't be able to aim correctly because something hit the rear of your gun, or just because of reasons. So realistic, but they forget we don't feel what our character is feeling and in the end, it's just really anoying.
-There are millions of different orders, formations, and things you will never really use despite you like such tactial stuff. And some basics like telling "get down" to your patrol are not there. Anyway, in the end, your men won't do what you ordered them to do. They wont move to exactly to that spot you saw, they will just get close to it. Even if it means the wrong side of a wall. Also, you may end seeing your men dying when you say "open fire" and they just do nothing and smile at the enemy.
-The enemies will also get 3 hits in average to die. If you hit them once, they will keep running covered in blood like you hit them with a paintball. Also it doesn't matter if you hit them in the face. They have 3 lives.
-And finally, as my personal top "no go", the gun won't aim where you aim. Seriously. First it moves when you are tired, and that's ok. But even if you manage to aim the aimcross due to the movement, it will shoot randomly arround the designated point. Good luck with the stealth shots.

Hello everyone of Steam and probably the internet, this will be a review on the indie game called "Shovel Knight" developed and published by Yacht Club Games. Just imagine ideas from some of your favorite NES games such as Duck Tales, Castlevania, Mega Man, and Legend of Zelda 2: The Adventure of Link (and probably more) just put into one fantastic 8-bit game. That is what this game is in short words.
Ok, now for the good things about this. This game plays like a melee version of Mega Man, with a bounce and attack system of DT and LoZ. It has the classic 8-bit style of the NES, which some might be "Ewwww this game sucks because look at the graphics." Just ignore those people because this is near the beginning of the real start of the video gaming era and was a great one. The music is epic too, it has the sounds like it was an NES game and it is just awesome. I would love to see more to this game soon, it is such a great experience for me since I love classic old games.
Now for the bad. On some low end PCs, you can't play as well, but that should not be a problem for others due to the advancements in technology since when my PC was made. The one problem with some of the ideas borrowed is mainly one that I found, which is that, like in Castlevania, you get knocked back, and hopefully, not into a hole and die. Otherwise, that is all I have to complain about this game.
After hours of watching and playing this game and examining it I came to a conclusive result. For the final result of this game, I will give it a 9.5/10. It is not a perfect game, but damn is it good. I would love to see great games like these more often, instead of stuff like the new Call of Duty, which is just a slightly altered game engine, and a multiplayer focused point and click game. I know people ask for a different formula, but when people do it, it sucks, but because they failed in some aspect of it and because the majority now is so stupid to have a change for once. So overall, this game is great, everyone should go get it if they enjoy games like Mega Man, cause it will be worth the money to you and the developers.

Originally, I was going to put a funny review like "♥♥♥♥ catfish" or "more like Bluegill Planet LOL", but I guess I might as well make something serious once a while, right?
The game has a memory leak thing going on, make sure to turn of anti-aliasing or else you might experience severe FPS drops (I'm talking like dropping down to 5 FPS) after about 1 hour of play.
The game is incredibly slow at first because until you hit level 3, all you can do is cast bait and wait for something to bite. And without actually knowing anything about fishing, that's going to be Bluegills. Or Pumpkinseed. Very rarely. So what do you do? You... actually figure out how to fish. Either do that by asking people in the chat (because we all love answering 10 times a day how to catch a bass or catfish), or by reading the absolutely marvelous Steam guides. You could also actually read up on how to catch this thing IRL, because this simulator is incredibly realistic in the sense that they implemented real-life fishing tactics to work ingame. That's pretty sick.
Once you hit 3, you probably want to grab yourself a Spinning Rod and, well, spin. That's a much needed change of pace I found, since instead of waiting for something you bite you reel in the lure... and then you wait for something to bite. I don't know what people expect, this is a fishing simulator. Pretty much all you do is wait for something to bite. It's incredibly engaging if you like exploring areas, figuring out cool fishing spots, and eventually collecting all the different sorts of fish that are in the game. I would like to mention, I've played for like 30 hours now and I haven't even seen half of what the game has to offer. That is, of course, in part because of the relatively slow leveling system, but also because the game actually has a substantial amount of content for something so recently released. For a free to play Early Access game, it's actually amazing of how much content this game has compared to some other games on Steam.
It should be mentioned that ANYTHING in the game can be obtained with ingame money. You do not need to spend a single cent on this game. Sure, yes, of course, it speeds things up, but not even by a significant amount. Fishing isn't "easier" by buying things. In fact, reeling in a big fish is completely skill-based, and even if you spent a hundred bucks it won't be any easier. That's because the most powerful equipment in the game is purchased by achievement coins. And, as you guessed, you get those coins by doing achievements or logging in 5 days in a row. You can only buy regular money with real money, and that's stuff you usually get plenty of ingame. Personally, the only really overpriced thing in the game in my opinion are licenses for new areas. And that's only because I want to save up for permanent licenses. Licenses to catch certain fish are cheap for a day, and probably worth investing in if you play the game often, I just really hate buying timed stuff because I feel forced to play something instead of doing it on my own.
All in all, this is an incredibly solid fishing experience, it's addicting if you like collecting stuff and not a whole lot of fun unless you like fishing. But give it a try, it's free. Maybe you're like me, and you didn't even know you have a passion for fishing.

I was pretty skeptical about this game prior to purchase. A lot of the reviews were great, yet some pointed out that this game isnt optomized very well. I have always been a fan of millitary shooters, but I wasnt sure that the realism would do enough to ensure that I would stick around with the game. However, to my extreme delight this game has turned out to be amazing. Not only is the gameplay super engaging, but it is super easy to learn as long as you are willing to stick around to understand some basic controls.
The gameplay itself is a little stiff, its definetly not your average Call of Duty game where the aiming is flawless. Instead, you trade that familiar fluidity in for some mechanics that demand a slow pace and intense concentration in order to suceed. The most fun that I have had in the game so far is using the in-game editor and setting up scenarios to test out my aim on non-sentient NPC's. The whole game is just a lot of fun to learn.
Finally, I want to address the concerns over the optomization:
Right now my gaming companion is an alienware 15 R2 laptop with a gtx 965m card. I was very unsure that I would be able to run this game on a laptop - yet im pleased to say that I can get a solid 60fps on 1080p with settings at very high. My recomendation if you are experiencing problems would be to lower post-process effects in the third tabs in the menu.

I think some people just don't want to play this game for some reason. My brother, for instance, refuses to play it. Partially my fault, however. I described the game as a first-person, squad-on-squad tactical shooter from the co-creator of "Counter-Strike". So, I can see why my brother would refuse to play this thinking it was a Counter-Strike rip-off.
THE GOOD: Having played both this game and Counter-Strike I can say with great certainty that each has their own charms, but this game is by far the better value, being that it is free. The controls are tight and responsive, adding more features to the Counter-Strike control scheme without making the controls clunky and confusing. The graphics are a few notches above Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, judging from what I saw. (My computer is 5 or so years old and doesn't have a lot of memory dedicated to graphical RAM. I run the game on the lowest graphical settings and it still looks great). The game plays differently than Counter-Strike. The addition of sprinting, leaning, and blind firing make this game feel more like an actual high stakes firefight. My favorite aspect of the game, the one that made me fall in love with Tactical Intervention are the chase missions. While the game CAN be like Counter-Strike from time to time (Slow, methodical, a game of tactics, cunning, and wits), the chase missions show a completely different side to the formula. They're fast, high-octane, highway shootouts that allow players to revel in violence and destruction when slow and methodical isn't cutting it for them.
THE BAD: There's not much worth mentioning as far as bad goes.  My biggest complaint is about a problem that all Counter-Strike clones suffer from. The game can live up to its claims and be tactical if the conditions are right (i.e. everyone has a mic and communicates between teammates), but most of the time, the game devolves to a Call of Duty-esque shoot em up. And since the match ends when an entire team is wiped out, this makes the pacing jarringly switch back and forth. Aiming from a moving car is really difficult. That's not to say that I expected it to be as easy as aiming while standing, but between the high speed, quick turns, and occasional lag, I find it very difficult to hit anything besides the sides of parked cars. Second, the weapon shop uses micropayments. They're a pet peeve of mine, though I don't hold it against the game. A free-to-play online game has to bring in money somehow. But the option to buy guns for span of five or so days really bothers me. I can't think of any game where I would buy a weapon for a limited period of time just to have it taken away when time's up. , (and this isn't even a legitimate complaint. It's more like a request for the developers) the game would be so much better with controller support. Like most of us, I grew up playing consoles and controllers are the one thing that (most) PC games lack. I've gotten used to keyboard and mouse controls, but I still feel that games like this one would benefit greatly from controller support.
Overall, I was impressed with Tactical Intervention. For a free game, it is worth every bit as much as Counter-Strike. The gameplay is the right blend of old and new, and all the new things don't feel forced or out of place, even if a few of them aren't as useful as you would hope. The micropayments annoy me, but I don't hold it against the game. The game captures the essence of a firefight more completely than other games, but still can't compete with tactical shooters with a greater emphasis on tactics like XCOM or the original Syndicate. The game is worth getting, for sure.

Shovel Knight is nothing short of a masterpiece, an homage to our childhoods that tugs on the strings of nostalgia just enough to make you smile but not so much as to make this child of the 8 and 16-bit eras roll my eyes. Make no mistake; this is not some lazy ROM-hack like the new Mega Man games. No Shovel Knight is not some blatant attempt at very cheaply pandering a product tied to an IP with a large fanbase. It is a love letter, a REAL love letter, to those who enjoyed any of the games from which Shovel Knight blends its expertly combined gameplay aspects.
Shovel Knight, while built using a modern framework (complete with a native widescreen aspect ratio, sprites far too large and complex for an NES to properly render, highly detailed beautiful scrolling background layers, and camera shake effects simultaneously on the X & Y axes) is an amalgamation of some of the most classic game concepts of the 8-bit era. Pogo-stick-esque jumping borrowed from Duck Tales (or the downward stab from The Legend of Zelda 2 : Link's Adventure if you prefer), an overworld map that works like the one from Super Mario Bros. 3 (complete with random encounters in between levels similar to the wandering Hammer Bros. on the maps of SMB3) the explorable towns filled with many interesting NPCs of Bionic Commando, secondary items and abilities structured similarly from the original Castlevania games, Megaman style boss-fights and level designs, RPG-like loot that can be used to upgrade abilities, and buy special optional pieces of equipment, and, of course, delightfully infectious chiptune music courtesy of a composer who is arguably the king of the genre, Jake Kaufman, aka "virt."
And yet, Shovel Knight is something more than just a "retro" game. Besides its classic mechanics it offers some new ones such as the ability to risk the loss of various checkpoints throughout a level by breaking it for hidden loot stored inside. And as you play, you will discover that Shovel Knight tells a story using its mechanics that is more mature than most games executed in this style. It explores themes such as one feeling helpless to protect or save ones they care about, and the emotional struggle that entails.
All in all, I cannot recommend it enough. It is a pure joy to play, and though not too long, I found myself only being pulled away after realizing how long I had been sitting and playing during a single session.

There are a few things I would like to suggest to the developers.
1.  Allow gear sorting based upon desired fish.  As someone who has 0 knowledge of fishing other than you find some water, use a stick with a rope and attach something pointy to the end of that rope, knowing what sort of things I need for certain fish in the shop would be invaluable.  I've seen the suggestions in the description of items and that helps, along with chatting with people while in-game, but allowing sorting in-shop would have been very helpful.
2.  Allow sorting by acceptable gear.  As, again, someone with no knowledge about what the difference between a caster and telescoping rod are as well as what should go with them, an option in the shop to sort by gear that will work with specific equipment (I.E. a sorting when looking at rods as to what reels, hooks, lures, etc will work with that rod) would be incredible and very useful.
3.  Tool-tips on equipment in your inventory.  I think it would be very useful to be able to hover my mouse over items I have equipped, such as the rod, and get the item descriptions.  This way you don't have to take them off your angler and into the inventory to read the description and then re-equip.  Rods look similar and being able to tell which I put on via tool-tips as well as reels, etc would be appreciated!
The only other real comments I have are most likely goingt be addressed via expansions and DLC later on (boats, new fish species, larger areas in which to pick fishing spots).
To that end, I say bravo and thank you for getting this simulator off on the right foot!  :)

A solid co-op TBS that gets a lot of blind hate from Resident Evil purists, and more deservingly, from those that say it's a reskinned and lesser version of Resident Evil 4.
Despite that, I found it thoroughly enjoyable, playing through the game multiple times, and accruing more than 100 hours. This is thanks in large part to: Impressive visuals, a fantastic porting job (game runs silky smooth even on average hardware), addictive and responsive shootan/melee mechanics, enjoyable co-op, large weapon variety and customisation and one of the greatest bossfights ever (7 minute Wesker <3)
It is brought down somewhat with cutscene QTEs, mandatory on-rails shooting segments, hamfisted cover system in the last quarter of the game and not having nearly enough Wesker.
Mercenaries mode is also balls to the wall awesome, plenty of unlockable levels and characters (and you get to play as Weskerfu :3c)

Have Ubisoft actually made a genuinly awesome game? Well yes, yes they have.
The tale of Siege is an intriguing one. It went from having a horrid release to being an incredibly popular and dare I say, one of the best FPS multiplayer games to be released to this date. The constant development and support keeps the game fresh and changes up the meta every few months. The shoddy business model of Ubisoft's previous titles is gone for good. When a new DLC comes out, all of the content in it is available to everyone for free, albeit with season pass owners getting it a week prior to everyone else. The map is free on day one and can be played by everyone. The new operators can be purchased with in-game credits and while the price is certainly a little high, I wouldn't say it's too high. Realistically, it'll probably take you a few days of successful gameplay to earn enough to purchase one.
And while we're on the topic of operators, in my personal opinion, this is the reason you should buy the game. So many different characters to choose from and almost all of them (with only a couple of exceptions) are well balanced and fit into the meta very nicely. Nothing beats the feeling of when you've gotten exceptionally good with your main. I will live and die by Caveira. The gunplay is fantastic, the matches are intense and the community is definitely better than most FPS games, but there are also the black sheep, of course.
This game is an experience you need to have.

If you like your escapist ultraviolence-and-raunchy-humor games with tongue planted firmly in cheek, then this is definitely a game you should check out.  From running around with a three-foot purple dong on a stick to bludgeon enemies with, to blasting enemies with drone-based high-explosive ordinance, from riding around in everything from a Prius-analog to a Lambo clone, to screaming through the clouds in a laser-equipped VTOL aircraft, you can cause enough mayhem to satisfy even the most jaded individual.

A beautifully designed and built mod, taking the player back through the decrepit Aperture facilities before the events of Portal 2. Familiar concepts are explored in new ways, giving a tighter focus and fresh spin on what may seem like simple puzzles but in actuality challenge the player in new ways.
For those out of touch with Portal, I would highly recommend playing through Portal 2 first as that will serve as a tutorial for Portal Stories. Concepts are not re-explained and the player is expected to understand and approach the puzzles with the same mindset they would have having just completed Portal 2.
If you are looking for some brain-teasers this game will offer you that and more, the puzzle design is the standout feature for me. The puzzles are never cheap, and the solutions lie in logic rather than execution giving the player that sense of satisfaction of discovering a soltuion, rather than the frustration of not being able to execute it correctly.
However, the difficulty can perhaps be a turn-off for some. This game is hard. No two ways about it. The puzzles can almost feel relentless in their difficulty as you approach the end of the game, but the solutions are always deceptivly simple and the sense of satisfaction upon completion is very rewarding.
The characters and voice-acting seem like they have been written and performed by Valve themselves, and fortunately never feel forced. There was always a worry the humour would fall flat but there were some genuinley funny dialogue moments and the return of Cave Johnson was a nice throwback during the game opening.
All in all, Prism Studios have developed an excellent addition to the Portal series, and given that the game is free - What are you waiting for? Highly Recommend.

Why do people still use umbrellas in modern society? The question is a deceptively simple one, for reasons upon which I will elaborate.  Firstly, people use umbrellas for the purpose of remaining dry, or not wet. Specifically when their surrounding area is being rained on, pelted with wetness as it were.  But whence this desire for retaining dryness when one's environment is wet, whence this human urge to ostracize one's self from the natural cycle, or rather...  To ostracize nature from ones own life.  Is the clue not in the question? Is it not the same with modern man's wish to spend his life in cities, homo urbanus.  Removed from the tumult of the organic world.  And yet, what is this world, and what is rain?  Rain wets, providing plants and animals with nutriment, filling up their cells with cytoplasm, and their veins with blood to transport nutrients, allowing them to stay alive.  Rain wets, providing the ground with moisture, moisture which seeps down through the sedimentary layers of soil, and without which no repositories of drinkable water would be present for the urban human to hydrate himself.  Urban man is desiccated, but relies upon this natural cycle to replenish him, yet he pretends that this ancient arrangement is beneath him, as when he removes his domicile from the wet ground, as when he removes his body from the rain, the umbrella is a symbol of man shunning nature, of woman shielding herself from the life giving sky.  Rain wets, and it erodes the cracking ground creating landslides, waterfalls, floods.  It reforms the terrain, allowing new flora and fauna to make their inroads on the surface of our world.  Yet from this, modern man and woman shield themselves.  Why?  Why to keep their clothes dry, to keep their electronic items secure. For you see rain wets and kills technology, and that is the bane of homo, so called sapiens.  What sapience is there in erecting the edifice of your life and society on a foundation that is enemy to the water, who's anathematized cloud and air and sea and sky, for water is in all those things.  And then, what is an umbrella?  An umbrella is an illusion, a self delusion that you can keep the wet out of your life, that though you breathe and eat and walk on things infused with it, you can control the dominion of water over your existence.  What could be more intolerably vein than the child wishing to control his parent, except the child believing that he can and is.  It is the delusion of created over creator, of art over artificer. But is that truly so mad?  What is the artist if not the channel for the divine?  The whisper of muses in the song of demons.  Where inlies the purpose of the artist if not in artistry? Who's essence is its product, the work of art, and water is the artist, animal creation the art and human civilization the crowning jewel, the final stroke of the paintbrush.  Why do people use umbrellas in modern society?  Because; they are life.

My experience with this game has been... dicey.
I've enjoyed my experience so far, i really do. However, to get better at the game, for me, at least, is really difficult.
Put simply, R6Siege is CS:GO on steroids; a map and objective based twitch shooter, this time with unique operators with their own loadouts and their unique gadgets. It's easy to pick up, yet hard to master.
There lies the crux of the matter; matchmaking (at least in casual) is non-existent, and there's no way to go around maps excepting the terrorist hunt mode which is vastly different from pvp. Getting matched with players with multiple times your experience means that with their mastery of the operators and the map, there is very little you can do against them. People will shoot you from impossible angles, you will lose aim-for-aim, you will be dumbfounded at how people will spot you from 5 pixels of your helmet peeking behind cover.
My only hope is that with Operation Health, the game heads in the right direction and put in place some much needed matchmaking system.
Post-Operation Health update: There is very little difference between the start of Operation Health and after it. The pervasive issues such as ping spikes and long loading is still there, matchmaking in casual is still non-existent, ranked is still in beta; perhaps the only notable changes i saw change were the hitbox updates and what, being able to browse the shop and operators while waiting for a match.
And now they're delaying game updates and holding back releases.
tl;dr hellish new player experience, high skill floor while at the same time being really difficult to master. Do not approach if you're not planning to go all the way with the game and invest mighty amounts of time in it.

WOW. This was a great game. There was great writing, incredible level design, and some fun voice acting. When I initially started up the game, I was a little jaded about the voices—hearing someone besides J.K. Simmons trying to do Cave Johnson was disappointing to say the least. It felt like the designers were trying to imitate Portal 1 and 2. But as I went through the game and found more and more challenging levels, I began to appreciate what the team who made this had put together. They made their own game. Your companion in the game is endearing and interesting, and the writers did a great job of fitting this story into the Portal universe. I left the game feeling very satisfied. I just have a few pieces of advice for anyone wishing to play:
1. This is a mod, and it is meant for experienced Portal players. If you loved playing Portal 1 and 2 and were able to get through both games without much trouble when it comes to puzzle solutions (as in, you didn't have to look up a walkthrough for more than two or three test chambers), you should do okay here.
2. When you start the game, take what you get at face value. Remember, this is essentially a different game and should be treated as such. You'll be disappointed if you expect to see familiar faces (or familiar test solutions, for that matter).
3. There are some patterns I noticed that led me to solutions during the maps. The designers have had some innovative ideas about ways to use the map elements. So here are my tips (I'm trying to be helpful while simultaneously being sufficiently vague so as not to ruin any challenges for you):
a. You'll find yourself thinking, "If this was co-op, I could do this. I just need another set of portals." I spent a lot of time frustrated thinking that. Well, you don't have another set, and you CAN solve each puzzle with the two portals you have. I went through the whole game, and I needed to use a walkthrough on two maps, but it is possible. The level designers did not make mistakes. Nothing is broken.
b. If you get stuck, think about where you are placing your portals. I got stuck on a particularly difficult map, and the whole problem was that I wasn't thinking about the fact that there was a specific place on the floor/wall that my portal needed to go (I know this sounds basic, but this really was a problem at a few points). That leads me to...
c. You'll find that many elements of each map are multipurposed, your portals included. You need to think outside the box. One thing that helped me was thinking about each thing differently. For instance, later in Portal 2, you had to put repulsion gel on a cube instead of on the floor or wall, which made the cube break out of a glass enclosure. Think about everything each action you take really does, and use what you learn to solve the puzzles.
d. The map designers made things difficult, but their focus wasn't on convoluted solutions. For instance, I spent a good five minutes trying to figure out a way to stack some cubes so I could use them as stairs. That was not the way to get through the map.

First things first: THIS GAME DESERVES YOUR MONEY! Don't wait and buy it when it is on sale, that would be doing a disservice to not only Yacht Club Games and Shovel Knight, but also yourself (This may or may nit be true).
Now with that out of the way, let's start with my review.
Story:
Shovel Knight puts you in the shoes of the titular character as he travels throughout the land to stop "The Order of No Quarter" and "The Enchantress" with shovel in hand. That is really all that is needed of the plot, since the game is an homage of games past which also lacked in the plot department. This isn't a bad thing, since it has enough of a plot to give you an excuse for the adventure at hand.
Graphics:
Shovel Knight looks beautiful! Fantastic pixel art is on display for the whole journey, with each area having a distinct visual flavour to it. You'll travel to all sorts of fantastical locales, ranging from an ancient underground city to an airship in the skies.
Each member of "The Order of No Quarter" also look fantastic, each having an interesting design to them.
Sound:
For the most part (read: 98% of the game), Shovel Knight has a wonderful chiptune soundtrack, each delightful tune is easy on the ears and you can find yourself humming along to each one. The sound effects are also excellent. They sound great, but never overpower the fantastic music. There was only ever one tune in the whole game I did not like, mainly because it sounded rather generic for where you are in the game.
Gameplay:
The only thing I can say about the controls in Shovel Knight is that they are sublime! Everytime you die, you can tell it was your fault for messing up a jump or taking a hit, not the game being cheap. Each time you die, you lose a portion of you gold, but it will float in bags until you collect them or die again, so you have a chance ro regain you lost gold. By the end of the intro stage, you'll have the basic controls mastered, and the game doesn't even tell you how to do any of the moves so you have to learn to do them on your own. The only thing the game tells you how to do is how to use your current relic, which is classic Catlevania controls (Up+Attack).
Each level is wonderfully handcrafted so that you face a specific set of challenges in each stage. I only got stumped once on where to go in one of the stages because where I had to go looked like a bottomless pit. Each boss fight is unique in how they fight, and there are more bosses than just "The Order of No Quarter" and "The Enchantress".
And unlike a game like Mega Man where you will tend to gravitate to one or two weapons, all the Relics in Shovel Knight are useful in some way or another. One of the first relics you can get is the Fishing Rod, which lets you see sparkling areas above bottomless pits which means you can get something worth while by dropping the fishing line and catching something there. Using the Fishing Rod is also required to get some of the secrets in the game, and there are a lot of secrets.
Each stage is littered with secret areas, be they hidden alcoves or entirely hdden rooms, all of them found with only your wit and some with visual indications (each visual indication is unique to each stage as well). Within these secrets are a plethora of different challenges and rewards, ranging from chests with some bonus gold to new relics. The ones that contain relics have some sort of challenge you have to do in order to familiarize yourself with how the new relic works and to get out safely with all gold intact.
There are two towns in the game, each with NPCs that you can talk to for some cute dialogue to merchants that will sell you various items. Standard town stuff. The world map works just like Super Mario Bros. 3, so it is pretty self explanitory.
Conclusion:
Shovel Knight is perfect in every way. Great controls great soundtrack, great graphics, and is a perfect homage to the games of yesteryear. With only one tiny blemish to speak of in my honest opinion.
So my final verdict for Shovel Knight is to buy it without delay!
