Resident Evil 4 is where the series changed. I'd say that change was for the better as... well, it's the first Resident Evil game I actually enjoyed completing. The others I lacked motivation due to how clunky everything was. That being said, Resident Evil 5 is 1 step forward and two steps back. The atache case from RE4 is gone, which I think is fine as you shouldn't need more than 9 slots. The problem rises when you realize, herbs don't stack, eggs take up a whole slot, and you can't temporarily pick up items. On top of this you actually have to use a slot for armor and the stun baton. Why? The knife doesn't take up a slot. Armor is armor. This is bad game design. Sounds like a bad game? Don't worry it has its moments, let me finish the negative first. Partner AI requires lots of manipulation in order to be bareable to deal with. I had no problem due to my playstyle but many people hate how it works. It's not entirely broken, but it should be a lot more functional seeing as how when your partner dies, it counts as you dying. The bosses are also kind of a joke seeing as how they don't really... feel unique from each other. Giant monsters, big whoop. The exception however is the boss in 5-3. That is actually a fairly interesting fight that I found quite enjoyable to play through.
Now for the good. The game feels well paced, despite the irritating abundance of quick time events, you get warnings of when they'll happen and if you screw up even once all you need to do to get passed it the next time is just mash the button as this isn't an action command situation where you must time it perfectly and only press it once. The game is very forgiving compared to Resident Evil 4 in that you rarely run out of ammo, if you ever don't feel confident in your ability, just go back to a previous chapter and play through it to pick up some ammo/money. 4-1 is especially good for farming. Don't want to play with the AI, get a friend to join your game, problem solved, so long as they don't suck. The game really starts to shine when the two of you can communicate and actively work together to achieve a goal.
I can't recommend playing this game on any difficulty higher than normal, as past that, all that changes is the amount of health your enemies have and how much damage they do. I like a challenge but I don't care for tedium. For the sake of completion I fully intend to beat the game on professional and unlock everything but I don't expect to enjoy it.
The game has treasures which, for someone like me who enjoys getting collectibles, is nice. You actually have to look around a bit to get most of the important treasures so exploration feels rewarding. There's also the BSAA emblems scattered through the game which are require for some special features in the game, costumes. Don't care about that, you don't have to do it.
Overall while I have quite a few gripes with the game I found it to be an enjoyable experience. I only had it for about a week and already sank nearly 40 hours into. The controls (keyboard and mouse) are extremely tight and I never felt as if I was killed due to anything but my own stupidity.
8/10, would recommend purchasing when its on sale. I actually grabbed it for 5 bucks but even for 10 you can't really go wrong. Would I say full price? No. Hell, if it wasn't for the superior controls I'd actually suggest getting the console version and all the DLC as the DLC (aside from costumes) is actually pretty damn good.

- Summarized Review.
This game is purely story driven, there is no combat. It's horrifying and wonderful all at the same time, I strongly recommend it.
- Full Review.
Many would assume the lack of any form of combat would force the gameplay to quickly become stale however the fear of being caught if you don't continue to move forward and the horrifying realization that every time you open a door you may be face to face with a horrifying demon and find yourself defenseless creates for a very unique sense of hopelessness not often found in gaming. To pile onto the already uneasy feeling that you may not be able to find your way out of this nightmare if you're in the dark for too long your character (Daniel) will begin to loose his mind inclining you to constantly light candles and use your lantern; however your resources are limited so if you don't take each action into consideration you'll quickly find yourself running through damp corridors running for your life from a foe you can hardly see.
The graphics in this game are impressive for an independent developer but the audio work far surpasses that even of a AAA title; large events like rocks smashing through a roof to collapse a passage will send ground shaking rumbles through your room but it's the attention to detail in the minor moments like a bone chilling scream echoing down a hallway as you walk by that really stand out, there is a clear love and dedication in the consideration of sound when it comes to Amnesia the Dark Descent.
Overall I was highly impressed by the game and thoroughly enjoyed my play through, this game clocks in at around 5 to 8 hours of game play depending on how fast you move through it and in my opinion is worth more then the regular price; if you can get it on sale go for it but if you can't don't worry about it because it will be worth it anyways!

WOW. This was a great game. There was great writing, incredible level design, and some fun voice acting. When I initially started up the game, I was a little jaded about the voices—hearing someone besides J.K. Simmons trying to do Cave Johnson was disappointing to say the least. It felt like the designers were trying to imitate Portal 1 and 2. But as I went through the game and found more and more challenging levels, I began to appreciate what the team who made this had put together. They made their own game. Your companion in the game is endearing and interesting, and the writers did a great job of fitting this story into the Portal universe. I left the game feeling very satisfied. I just have a few pieces of advice for anyone wishing to play:
1. This is a mod, and it is meant for experienced Portal players. If you loved playing Portal 1 and 2 and were able to get through both games without much trouble when it comes to puzzle solutions (as in, you didn't have to look up a walkthrough for more than two or three test chambers), you should do okay here.
2. When you start the game, take what you get at face value. Remember, this is essentially a different game and should be treated as such. You'll be disappointed if you expect to see familiar faces (or familiar test solutions, for that matter).
3. There are some patterns I noticed that led me to solutions during the maps. The designers have had some innovative ideas about ways to use the map elements. So here are my tips (I'm trying to be helpful while simultaneously being sufficiently vague so as not to ruin any challenges for you):
a. You'll find yourself thinking, "If this was co-op, I could do this. I just need another set of portals." I spent a lot of time frustrated thinking that. Well, you don't have another set, and you CAN solve each puzzle with the two portals you have. I went through the whole game, and I needed to use a walkthrough on two maps, but it is possible. The level designers did not make mistakes. Nothing is broken.
b. If you get stuck, think about where you are placing your portals. I got stuck on a particularly difficult map, and the whole problem was that I wasn't thinking about the fact that there was a specific place on the floor/wall that my portal needed to go (I know this sounds basic, but this really was a problem at a few points). That leads me to...
c. You'll find that many elements of each map are multipurposed, your portals included. You need to think outside the box. One thing that helped me was thinking about each thing differently. For instance, later in Portal 2, you had to put repulsion gel on a cube instead of on the floor or wall, which made the cube break out of a glass enclosure. Think about everything each action you take really does, and use what you learn to solve the puzzles.
d. The map designers made things difficult, but their focus wasn't on convoluted solutions. For instance, I spent a good five minutes trying to figure out a way to stack some cubes so I could use them as stairs. That was not the way to get through the map.
Good luck. You can do it! Think with portals!

as you can see, i have played this game for almost a thousand hours! i think now is the time to finally make my review.
my relationship with this game is somewhat a love/hate relationship. the game itself (concept, gameplay, tactical FPS) is magnificent. but it still remains to have serious problems that the developers seem to completely ignore till this day.
overall i do not recomend this game although i had my fairshare of fun. but what you go through makes the fun factor not worth it. below is some pros and cons:
Pros:
1. nice concept of defenders and attackers with cool and balanced exclusive operator gadgets and abilities.
2. decently tactical yet easy to master.
3. good graphics
4. regular updates, DLC's and operators/weapons + maps
5. insanly addictive given the level of online FPS competitivness.
6. fun and satisfying online experience specially with friends.
Cons: (here is where the pros become irrelavent)
1. No middle east servers (average ping is between 160 to 300) if your from ME, which is extremly high and makes the game fraustrating.
2. this game is so effected by ping. not like BF or COD etc. R6S is literaly a ping battle rather than competitive FPS when your ping is high.
3. matchmaking is a mess
4. 2 PCs or more cant play the game from same network unless a private match. which is not fair and extremly disapointing.
5. charecter movement is not smooth and certian animations are buggy, like jumping, reinforcing walls or barricading doors which can only be executed if the screen shows you the "Vault, barricade and reinforce" option and sometimes it doesnt appear and you lose the match because of it.
6. random bugs and crashes observed on multiple machines
7. very weak online support from Ubisoft, i assume their busy with DLC and other new content of which many are pointless.
8. critical technical errors such as losing profile, deleting loadouts, not loging in etc.
9. no single player mode except for the situations which is part of the tutorial.
conclusion:
R6S in principle is an amazing game. but the developers limited the potential of this game big time. i can no longer play this game with my brother and friends from the same network. i always enter with higher ping which gives the enemy an unfair advantage 90% of the times. as good as this game is, i cant recomend it at all. keep your money and buy a working game instead that you can enjoy with your freinds without all the fraustration and disapointments.

Shovel knight has a certain charm to it that a lot of recent retro platformers have been missing that rises it to the top over others. Instead of feeling like a tribut to old school platformers, this is almost the exact lightning that struck with the NES platformers of yesteryear. That's not all it's got going for it though, although it does go a long way with it's charm and presentation alone.
The real genius here, however, is the level design. Taking a leaf out of the mega man booklet, Shovel knight excels when it comes to a difficult but fair structure. It's pretty easy to go through all these levels without dying at all, but it's equally easy to mess up and lose all of your loot, sobbing all the way. If you are a fan of mega man, i strongly recommend this title.
There are tonnes, and i mean tonnes of little touches that make this game stand out. I won't spoil them here, but let me tell you that if there's one word i'd use to describe this game, it's definitely 'character'. This game is oozing with it and you shouldn't waste any time checking it out.

If you ask any Resident Evil fan their opinion on the latest installment of their beloved franchise, they will likely tell you how far it has fallen from its roots. Some would consider the first Resident Evil game a pioneer of the survival horror genre. With scarce resources and a daunting atmosphere, the game made every encounter felt tense and nerve wracking. Resident Evil 5, released in 2009 and a good 13 years after the first game, took this formula and turned it upside down. Maybe the creators felt that the series needed to evolve. Perhaps they wanted to cater to a wider audience. Regardless of intent, this significant change was poorly received. But contrary to what the most hardcore “fans” have to say, Resident Evil 5 is far from a bad game.
The thing that struck me immediately as most impressive about Resident Evil 5 was its game engine, one internally developed by Capcom themselves. It is extremely optimized and capable of rendering impressive visuals at playable frame rates even on low-end systems. Unfortunately, Capcom never capitalizes on its engine’s abilities. Instead, players are treated with boring brown scenery after brown scenery. It would have been a pleasant surprise to see the engine render something other than foliage and sand so that the audience may witness its potential in full.
If you came into Resident Evil 5 expecting a thought-provoking plot driven by ethical dilemmas and life-changing lessons, you really should first reevaluate what you think narrative focused games are before looking elsewhere. Resident Evil 5 doesn’t aim to be a social commentary (and if it is, it probably does so unintentionally). It doesn’t aim to make its players question their morality. It just tells a simple story of two agents trying to stop the outbreak of a virus and honestly, that’s all it really needs, since the main driving force behind this game is its solid gameplay.
Resident Evil 5 can be played solo or with a friend. Prior to release, this was a very controversial inclusion as the community argued that co-op would diminish any sense of horror. While this argument is valid even today, having a partner to play with actually enhances the game’s enjoyment by allowing two players to share the experience of being overwhelmed by zombies. Even if you do prefer to play alone, the game forcefully pairs you with an unresponsive A.I. partner, so ultimately co-op is still the lesser of two evils.
The aforementioned major addition aside, Resident Evil 5 feels and plays very much like its predecessor bar the horror aspect. The controls are extremely responsive and every bullet fired or punch thrown has an “umph” to it. If you’ve never played the previous installments, you might be disappointed to find that the characters cannot shoot and move simultaneously. While unrealistic (and occasionally frustrating), this limitation does make a rather laid back game slightly more intense during fights against overwhelming odds. Staying true to its heritage, Resident Evil 5 also retains an inventory system that encourages players to be strategic with their supplies. With only nine available slots, players must give careful thought to how diverse of an arsenal, how much ammo, and how many herbs (essentially potions) he or she should carry.
Resident Evil 5 gets a lot of things right and had it not carried the burden of following its predecessors, I suspect it would have been wholeheartedly accepted by the gaming community. As long as you keep your expectations at bay, I can guarantee you that there is much fun to be had, especially when playing with a friend.
Grade: 4/5

Prism Studios’ Portal Stories: Mel is a free standalone mod for Portal 2, which is my favorite game of all time, which leaves it with quite the expectation from me. So did Prism succeed in recreating the Portal experience?
Well did they? Yes and no, while their puzzles are most definitely Portal-like just harder (I’ll came back to this soon), however it almost completely lacks in the humor that was a staple in the first two games, I count maybe 3 times I laughed at something funny the characters said compared to the innumerable amounts of time I laughed in Portal 2. That isn’t to say that the writing is bad, it is quite good just not Portal good if that makes sense.
The voice-acting is something I have to criticize since, it’s not that good, Virgil’s is okay but Cave Johnson’s was just awful and AEGIS nothing to really complain about in the voice-acting department but it doesn’t really come across as having any sort of personality whatsoever.
Now the story, the story is entirely okay, nothing fantastic but nothing cringe worthy either I enjoyed the story but as I said the writing is lacking humor wise. Now you play as Mel a Olympian who was in some unspecified sport during the Nuremberg Olympics in 1940. The game begins in 1952 but the majority of the game takes place quite some time later sometime before Portal 2 (which takes place an unspecified amount of time after the original). The story feels like fanfiction, but the best kind of fanfiction wherein it instead of glorifying the existing characters it choses to make a story with a little relevance to the canon but has all new characters and in this case barely mentions anything to do with the two main games.
And now we come to the biggest problem with the mod but I’ll bring this into contrast, in my review of the first Portal I argued that the games biggest flaw was that it was too easy and that I would like to see some harder puzzles, most of the puzzles in this mod goes way too far to the other side of the spectrum. Mean that it is too hard, now there are plenty of good puzzles too, the ones in the beginning of Chapter 4 were fantastic and some in the beginning of Chapter 3 as well and then there were the odd very good puzzle with well balanced difficulty. Most of the puzzles however had way too contrived solutions, like one of the earliest chambers in Chapter 3. So I will say this, if you already found Portal 2 to be too hard for you then you should NOT play this. I’ve seen other reviewers say that this could have been made by Valve, and well that isn’t true, Valve knows (for the most part) what difficulty balance, Prism (for the most part) doesn’t.
Now the final boss I have to criticize as well, not for how they choose to do it because that I had no problem with but rather it was something that I picked up on rather early is that the feature which allows you to hold on to object like cubes works rather badly, I don’t know why that is, but you have a tendency to lose “grip” of the object without doing anything which was the only reason I barely defeated the final boss, since it uses the usual Portal boss in that you have a limited time to defeat him and when I beat him he was just about to start counting down from 5.
And if there is one final little thing I have to say the it would be that the game is very bad a directing you to where you should go when you are outside of Testing Track and sometimes even inside them.
Overall though Portal Stories Mel is one of the best mods I have ever played through, the only I can think of being better is Interesting NPCs for Skyrim, and it is free which I would say leaves no harm on you trying it out just be aware that there are issues with it. I hope those of you who play it have an enjoyable time with it, ciao.

Ah, yes, back to the world of Saints Row; where people had to pay for their absurdly damage-resistant cars by not having locks on the doors, racism and sexism don't exist but being a psychotic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ makes you nigh-invincible, some resources are seemingly infinite (like cars and police) but 'difficulty' is read as 'sending in even MORE kamikaze vehicles at the player with enemy troops that apply damage the same way a fire hose applies water'. It's a world of tradeoffs, really.
Anyway, Saints Row: The Third is Saints Row 2 again, but with more wacky humor as well as 4 or 5 problems of varying degrees of annoyance. They are as follows:
My character in Saints Row 2 was supposed to look exactly like me, but ended up looking like a cross between me and any skinny white punk. I was initially frustrated with this, but I grew to love my character because he developed a personality and agenda all his own, while still being mine. He had funny dialogue lines, a penchant for suits and classical music, and a proclivity for martial arts. When I started this game, I wanted to create the exact same guy, so I copied all the numbers over from the character editor from SR2 into SR3 (well, to the best of my ability; the character editor has been changed, and clothing options have been reduced dramatically). And you know what? He came out looking like someone else entirely! Well, actually, he looked kinda like my SR2 character had gotten a bit older, so if that's what Volition was going for, then nice job.(At least he wasn't changed as much as Shaundi.)
Stilwater has been replaced with Steelport, which is like Stilwater but with less diversity in the different neighborhoods, and its Rust-Belt♥♥♥♥♥fancy-modern-city-but-really-gray-and-desaturated aesthetic replaced with...nothing. Steelport has no personality whatsoever, except to be slightly wackier.
The story of SR3 is a mess compared to that of its predecessor. In Saints Row 2, there were three concurrent storylines that you could complete in any order, or do at any time, to defeat the three gangs bothering you. At the end of each storyline, the psychotic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that had been taunting you since the beginning of that storyline was killed in a horrific yet cathartic way, and you got all his stuff. After you did all three, you went on to kill the head psychotic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who had been taunting you. It was a great structure for a good story. In Saints Row: The Third, there are also three gangs, but you kill the boss of the one that killed your friend Johnny Gat (spoiler alert for something that happens within the first twenty minutes of the game) AT THE END OF THE FIRST ACT, and only then are you allowed to go after the other two. In addition, the gone are the memorable gang archetypes of punk rednecks, Rastafarians, and ninjas, and gone are the interesting characters that went with them. None of the three new gangs are that memorable, and the only halfway-interesting boss is Killbane, and that's because he reminds you of Maero from SR2. However, some redemption is gained with the Saints themselves. Like SR2, this game has way better characters than it has any right to or need of, and it's wonderful to see Gat, Shaundi, Pierce, and the Boss interacting again. In addition, there are new characters to bolster the ranks, including Kinzie, Viola, Angel, Zimos, and my personal favorite, Oleg. Also, story missions are now activated by your phone instead of going to a certain place, so there's less excuse to avoid them and screw around, which can be annoying. Overall, the story is only worth it for the Saints' character moments, and the occasional funny thing that happens elsewhere in the plot.
This one takes some explanation. In Saints Row 2, side activities and just random screwing around earned Respect, which was required to do story missions. In addition, side missions gave you certain upgrades when you did them enough. Story and side missions both also gave money, which was used to buy clothes, guns, and other stuff. In Saints Row: The Third, side activities and screwing around still give you Respect and money, but story missions give Respect as well. Respect is essentially an XP bar: once filled, you gain access to new upgrades, which you buy with money. This has the overall effect of making the upgrade system more boring, as well as making the game harder to break, since you can't do all six really hard Snatch missions right away and get the infinite ammo dual SMGs right off the bat. Also, it has the same problem as Arkham City where your character is learning things from the upgrade system that they already knew, like how to hold two guns at once or fall any distance without dying.
Speaking of fall damage, it scales ridiculously in this game. "You fell 20 feet? DEAD!"
Overall, Saints Row: The Third has a lot more wacky humor than Saints Row 2, but it balances this by having less content and depth. I don't need to tell you why the latter is a bad thing, but the increase in wacky humor isn't all good, either. It makes the game kind of atonal at times, as you find a clone lab making 10-foot-tall damage sponges with flame throwers, but then that mission ends and you go back to kicking people out of their cars and shooting police. In SR2, the crazy stuff was special because it was thinly spread; here, it's often enough to not be special, but not often enough to tip the game into nonstop craziness. Still, it passed the important test of making me laugh most of the time, and it's an important step towards what I understand Saints Row IV to be.
Overall, this game is still good, and funny as hell. It's Saints Row 2 with some deficiencies, but Saints Row 2 is such a high point that dropping it down a few notches doesn't mean all that much.
P. S. It also made me realize that Just Cause 3 needs a massive city map. I'd play that for days on end.
P.P.S. They took all the good songs off the radio and replaced them with far fewer good ones. Those new good ones are good, though. I didn't realize I wanted Handel's Messiah playing during my car rampage until I had it.

This fishing simulator is great. Truly free to play, realistic, and has a great community.
Once you grind to level 3 the experience really begins as you can start to fish bass which is a great start on your way to trout in Colorado. Many of the new players say it is hard to level up and get money. I would agree, until level 3 I was struggling to break even but once you read the wiki and just ask for general advice in the chat then you realize how easy it is to make money and gain xp.
The community that plays this sim is fantastic. Especially once you level up and move on from the starter state and get to the places where the true players really are. Everyone is always more than happy to give you assistance or advice if you ask and as long as you are just as willing to give out advice yourself you can easily become respected within the community. The devs are great as well, they are active on the forums and are always busting their butts to try and sort out issues and help new and seasoned players alike.
Since this sim is in early access there are some bugs here and there but overall for me personally it's not too bad, only twice have I become concerned about losing my catch for the day which really isn't a big deal depending on what you are fishing. My one and only complaint is the major lack of tutorials and descriptions about what goes with what in the store. When I first started I was baffled by the amount of different things you could buy and wasted quite a bit of credits trying to figure things out, but again, read the wiki and ask in the chat and it is quickly sorted out and you are busy hauling in that fish.
I would absolutely reccomend this to anyone who enjoys fishing and is willing to take the time and learn the tricks of the trade.  Just remember three things: It's still in development, read the wiki, and upgrade your gear as it becomes available.

As a startup game designer myself, this is the kind of quality game that I hope to create some day. Something that obviously has months and months of care and hard work put into it, regardless of how simple the game is. Shovel Knight is in short, a joyful walk down NEStolgia days with inspiring tight gameplay, beautiful and admiring pixel art, and an abundance of incredibly polished chiptune music. I was a kickstarter backer since it was announced, and I was very worried with the few delays they made, but the final product has proven to be 100% worth the price of admission.
You play as an adventurer Shovel Knight, our pogosticking protagonist who's searching for his long lost companion Shield Knight. Both of them were exploring the mysterious Tower of Fate, when the dark magic of a cursed amulet cast them out and sealed the tower. When Shovel Knight awoke, Shield Knight was no where to be found, but instead The Enchantress has risen to power and spreads evil across the land. Now Shovel Knight must quest out on a search for his long lost companion. Also in his way are several other cleverly themed knights in an ensemble known as "The Order of No Quarter", each with their own unique character and fighting specialties.
The gameplay itself is a side-scrolling mixture between NES classics like Mega Man, Super Mario 3, Castlevania, and DuckTales. It also happens to take some modernization from newer games. For example: there are no lives per se, but instead when you die, three money bags spring where you bit the dust, and you must recover them to save from losing any gold a la the notoriously difficult Souls series. Along your journey you can spend gold you collect to upgrade your shovel to perform new attacks, or purchase different armors that all have different effects. You can also buy relics from a traveling salesman which allow you to shoot fireballs, dash in mid air, and go invincible for a short period of time among several other abilities.
The art is very impressive for that 8-bit pixel look that so many developers are caught on lately (myself included). The animations are very characteristic and help bring the game to life with ease. The game can almost guarantee a giggle the first time you see Shovel Knight dig through a treasure chest. Speaking of the giggles, the dialog is extremely humorous and doesn't allow the game to take itself too seriously. It tries for the casual joke or two at the expense of actual game knowledge, which helps make the game feel more alive and interesting. These two components help seal the game and bring it to life. However, there are a couple reused assets for enemies. For example different mage enemies, and rat like enemies are made different only by their color palettes. A small nitpick to an otherwise gorgeous and endearing world.
Finally, the music is possibly my favorite thing about the whole game. Jake Kaufman(Shovel Knight's composer and OCRemix veteran code-named "virt") is bound to have put himself on the map with this soundtrack, and with the help of Manami Matsumae(Mega Man composer) it's really no surprise. Each tune is specifically designed to run on actual NES hardware and helps secure that classic retro feel to the game. Thus, the music in this game not only shines, it radiates light in every way. Every level has it's own distinct composition, while each boss has a remixed version of that same song. It's instantly catchy chiptunes will have you hook, line, and sinker throughout all of the almost 50 compositions. Jake has also been kind enough to offer the entire soundtrack, as well as a second full arrangement album from various artists, each for a "you name it" price tag on his BandCamp page.
Shovel Knight is an astounding achievement that just plain works. Every person attached to this project put their heart and soul into the game, and it shows in every way. Rarely do I say that an independent video game has a shot at making it to Game of the Year status, but Shovel Knight easily digs its way to the top of the list. A must-have gem in any Steam, 3DS, or Wii U library. (9/10)

Saint's Row the Third has everything that was awesome about Saint's Row II except going several steps further. This game takes place two years after the events of the last game where the Saint's have successfully taken over the city of Stillwater and have generated celebrity status in the same sense as Mickey & Mallory Knox from Natural Born Killers. The boss of the gang decides to pull off a publicity stunt by robbing a bank with the aid of Shandi & Johnny. As it turns out, the bank tellers were informed about the heist and start open firing on the Saint's and before any of the Saint's realize what was going on they landed in jail only to get bailed out by the guy who tipped off the bank. Phillipe Loren the kingpin is the man responsible for the incident and is the top notch leader of an organization called the Syndicate. The kingpin offers the boss a deal in which the boss quickly denies and after a series of mayhem and tradegy the boss and the Saint's have a new goal which is to take over a new city called Steelport. The game has tons of improvements on content and gameplay a like. The animation is more flexible, the option to upgrade your skills is much easier, & the navigation system is more direct. Most of the weapons are either brought back or excluded from the last game. Certain side missions were nixed in favor of the new ones. There is no option to drink, eat, or smoke as your health regenerates on its own. Some new vehicles are introduced while fan favorite vehicles might be missed here. The customization option is slightly different from the option in the last game, you can't choose two colors for hair and certain articles of clothing are in sets instead of seperated items. However with the addition of multiple color skin tones and newer outfits this issue is immediately overlooked as I was able to customize my character to resemble the boss I played as in Saint's Row 2. And as noted with the previous game, it is populated with various side missions and additional DLC that gives you the freedom to choose which missions to start first either the main missions or the extra missions. Any sand box genre gamer will be pleased with this game and any one who enjoyed Saint's Row 2 will love this sequel even more. It's a third person shooter at it's best.

As a startup game designer myself, this is the kind of quality game that I hope to create some day. Something that obviously has months and months of care and hard work put into it, regardless of how simple the game is. Shovel Knight is in short, a joyful walk down NEStolgia days with inspiring tight gameplay, beautiful and admiring pixel art, and an abundance of incredibly polished chiptune music. I was a kickstarter backer since it was announced, and I was very worried with the few delays they made, but the final product has proven to be 100% worth the price of admission.
You play as an adventurer Shovel Knight, our pogosticking protagonist who's searching for his long lost companion Shield Knight. Both of them were exploring the mysterious Tower of Fate, when the dark magic of a cursed amulet cast them out and sealed the tower. When Shovel Knight awoke, Shield Knight was no where to be found, but instead The Enchantress has risen to power and spreads evil across the land. Now Shovel Knight must quest out on a search for his long lost companion. Also in his way are several other cleverly themed knights in an ensemble known as "The Order of No Quarter", each with their own unique character and fighting specialties.
The gameplay itself is a side-scrolling mixture between NES classics like Mega Man, Super Mario 3, Castlevania, and DuckTales. It also happens to take some modernization from newer games. For example: there are no lives per se, but instead when you die, three money bags spring where you bit the dust, and you must recover them to save from losing any gold a la the notoriously difficult Souls series. Along your journey you can spend gold you collect to upgrade your shovel to perform new attacks, or purchase different armors that all have different effects. You can also buy relics from a traveling salesman which allow you to shoot fireballs, dash in mid air, and go invincible for a short period of time among several other abilities.
The art is very impressive for that 8-bit pixel look that so many developers are caught on lately (myself included). The animations are very characteristic and help bring the game to life with ease. The game can almost guarantee a giggle the first time you see Shovel Knight dig through a treasure chest. Speaking of the giggles, the dialog is extremely humorous and doesn't allow the game to take itself too seriously. It tries for the casual joke or two at the expense of actual game knowledge, which helps make the game feel more alive and interesting. These two components help seal the game and bring it to life. However, there are a couple reused assets for enemies. For example different mage enemies, and rat like enemies are made different only by their color palettes. A small nitpick to an otherwise gorgeous and endearing world.
Finally, the music is possibly my favorite thing about the whole game. Jake Kaufman(Shovel Knight's composer and OCRemix veteran code-named "virt") is bound to have put himself on the map with this soundtrack, and with the help of Manami Matsumae(Mega Man composer) it's really no surprise. Each tune is specifically designed to run on actual NES hardware and helps secure that classic retro feel to the game. Thus, the music in this game not only shines, it radiates light in every way. Every level has it's own distinct composition, while each boss has a remixed version of that same song. It's instantly catchy chiptunes will have you hook, line, and sinker throughout all of the almost 50 compositions. Jake has also been kind enough to offer the entire soundtrack, as well as a second full arrangement album from various artists, each for a "you name it" price tag on his BandCamp page.
Shovel Knight is an astounding achievement that just plain works. Every person attached to this project put their heart and soul into the game, and it shows in every way. Rarely do I say that an independent video game has a shot at making it to Game of the Year status, but Shovel Knight easily digs its way to the top of the list. A must-have gem in any Steam, 3DS, or Wii U library. (9/10)

Pros:
+Realism is there. Fishing rod mechanics, dynamic waters, surreal environments, and overall decent fishing physics.

+Bugs aren't game-breaking, from what I can tell.

Neutrals:
=You have to make an account to play. That's common in free games.
=There's almost too many options, but I think it makes the game more exciting and immersive.
=It's hard to tell if what you're doing works sometimes, or if it's programmed to work.
=No gamepad support.
=Cannot see other players fishing with you.
Cons:
-A decent rig is needed for this game. Framerate is bad, but doesn't make the game unplayable.
-Menus can be very confusing. It took me ten minutes before realizing that the "Join" button registers my account.
-So far I've only been fishing by a shore, or fishing in a boat. I wish to be able to go into the waters and see the fish.
----------

There are a few things I don't completely like about this game. Particularly the difficulty level and the character of some of the puzzles. Call me a wuss, but even as a veteran of Portal and of puzzle games back to the dawn of home- and personal computing, I like my riddles to be solveable without  walkthrough or (ancient history) hint books. Also, the story is no match for either Portal or Portal 2.
That said, one has to take into account that this is 1. A fan project and 2. FREE!
While that can also be said for the absolutely brilliant Portal (1), considering that it was kind of a gift-with-purchase in the Orange Box, this does in no way diminish the worth and value of Mel. It's not only excellent value for free (dividing by zero has that property), but it even would be great value at, say, $10. I've had hours of fun, lots of entertainment, only a moderate amount of frustration (blame my problem-solving deficits for it) and will certainly play through it again in a couple of years.
All I have to say about this game (except for the above and the things I left out) is: A heartfelt THANK YOU to those who have provided it! Well done indeed!!

What happens when you take a semi-serious open world game and let the developers let it go in any direction they want? You get the third entry of Saints Row. Create your full avatar with an advanced character creator and run around the city with rocket launchers. Perhaps murdering people in a game show is more your cup of tea? Let's keep this short....I love horror games.  Or, survival horror...or, whatever you want to call them.  Some of these shock you with sudden scares that dissipate in a cloud of blood and grotesque body parts as you fight to stay alive.  The best of these lure you in with atmosphere and story, until, before you realize it, you are completely terrified.  In that dark room, with your controller/keyboard, do you continue to play and ignore the dark space behind your computer chair or do you exit to Windows, turn on the lights and watch more Family Guy?  This isn't a game so much as an experience...completely immersive, technically impressive, unforgettable.  It's a classic, so experience it while it's fresh so you can say, "Yeah, I played Amnesia."  Afterward, watch all the Family Guy you want, you deserve it.

Why do people still use umbrellas in modern society? The question is a deceptively simple one, for reasons upon which I will elaborate.  Firstly, people use umbrellas for the purpose of remaining dry, or not wet. Specifically when their surrounding area is being rained on, pelted with wetness as it were.  But whence this desire for retaining dryness when one's environment is wet, whence this human urge to ostracize one's self from the natural cycle, or rather...  To ostracize nature from ones own life.  Is the clue not in the question? Is it not the same with modern man's wish to spend his life in cities, homo urbanus.  Removed from the tumult of the organic world.  And yet, what is this world, and what is rain?  Rain wets, providing plants and animals with nutriment, filling up their cells with cytoplasm, and their veins with blood to transport nutrients, allowing them to stay alive.  Rain wets, providing the ground with moisture, moisture which seeps down through the sedimentary layers of soil, and without which no repositories of drinkable water would be present for the urban human to hydrate himself.  Urban man is desiccated, but relies upon this natural cycle to replenish him, yet he pretends that this ancient arrangement is beneath him, as when he removes his domicile from the wet ground, as when he removes his body from the rain, the umbrella is a symbol of man shunning nature, of woman shielding herself from the life giving sky.  Rain wets, and it erodes the cracking ground creating landslides, waterfalls, floods.  It reforms the terrain, allowing new flora and fauna to make their inroads on the surface of our world.  Yet from this, modern man and woman shield themselves.  Why?  Why to keep their clothes dry, to keep their electronic items secure. For you see rain wets and kills technology, and that is the bane of homo, so called sapiens.  What sapience is there in erecting the edifice of your life and society on a foundation that is enemy to the water, who's anathematized cloud and air and sea and sky, for water is in all those things.  And then, what is an umbrella?  An umbrella is an illusion, a self delusion that you can keep the wet out of your life, that though you breathe and eat and walk on things infused with it, you can control the dominion of water over your existence.  What could be more intolerably vein than the child wishing to control his parent, except the child believing that he can and is.  It is the delusion of created over creator, of art over artificer. But is that truly so mad?  What is the artist if not the channel for the divine?  The whisper of muses in the song of demons.  Where inlies the purpose of the artist if not in artistry? Who's essence is its product, the work of art, and water is the artist, animal creation the art and human civilization the crowning jewel, the final stroke of the paintbrush.  Why do people use umbrellas in modern society?  Because; they are life.

My experience with this game has been... dicey.
I've enjoyed my experience so far, i really do. However, to get better at the game, for me, at least, is really difficult.
Put simply, R6Siege is CS:GO on steroids; a map and objective based twitch shooter, this time with unique operators with their own loadouts and their unique gadgets. It's easy to pick up, yet hard to master.
There lies the crux of the matter; matchmaking (at least in casual) is non-existent, and there's no way to go around maps excepting the terrorist hunt mode which is vastly different from pvp. Getting matched with players with multiple times your experience means that with their mastery of the operators and the map, there is very little you can do against them. People will shoot you from impossible angles, you will lose aim-for-aim, you will be dumbfounded at how people will spot you from 5 pixels of your helmet peeking behind cover.
My only hope is that with Operation Health, the game heads in the right direction and put in place some much needed matchmaking system.
Post-Operation Health update: There is very little difference between the start of Operation Health and after it. The pervasive issues such as ping spikes and long loading is still there, matchmaking in casual is still non-existent, ranked is still in beta; perhaps the only notable changes i saw change were the hitbox updates and what, being able to browse the shop and operators while waiting for a match.
And now they're delaying game updates and holding back releases.
tl;dr hellish new player experience, high skill floor while at the same time being really difficult to master. Do not approach if you're not planning to go all the way with the game and invest mighty amounts of time in it.

There's one thing you have to be aware of when starting playing this mod. The levels are different. I felt exactly the same way when I am solving integrals on university. The tricks you have to master are simple in their nature, but it's nearly impossible to figure them out yourself in a reasonable time. Some of the levels require some unconventional solutions, like throwing a cube into another cube in my case (though I am more than sure that this wasn't supposed to be the "correct" solution).
Story-wise, the mod is excellent. It blends nicely into the Portal universe, and could be easily declared canon. Also the visual design, soundtrack and voice-acting are all marvellous, you'll feel like you're playing the original Portal 2.
The weakest part of this mod is what makes Portal what it is. Levels. As mentioned above, most of the levels required me to figure out the most impossible solutions, and sometimes it felt like exploiting the Portal game mechanism to a way it originally wasn't meant to be played. The hard-to-figure-out tricks are somewhat acceptable, but what's unacceptable for me is making a solution of a level dependent on placing a portal on a surface you see either from only a very small spot in the level, or surface you see for a very short period of time whilst flying/falling, making it extremely difficult to hit with the portal gun.
I can recommend this game for the art, the visuals, the music, the story and the voice acting. But the very core of Portal as a game - the levels/puzzles - is not executed well. That's why you see the red thumbs down over there. And I feel bad for smashing that "No" button, because it's obvious that so much work was invested into this mod. But a mod which doesn't execute the core of the original game well will never be good, no matter how beautiful the art behind it is.
So, to sum up:
Pros: The art - visual design of the levels, soundtrack, voiceacting, story.
Cons: Levels executed the wrong way. (oh the nostalgia of integrals on math lessons), one or two times you'll find yourself shouting at the developers "You damn trolls!"
It's unlikely you'll pass this game yourself unless you're a genius. But with the little help from a walkthrough video on YouTube, you'll be fine. I admit, I had to look it up three times.

Before Shovel Knight was once a proposed product, I never actually helped kickstart a project before. This was the first game that made me feel confident enough to help invest in the project when it was still very early in development.
Many months passed, and now it's finally out. How does the finished game hold up? Astonishingly well, actually. It successfully delivers on the promise of a true old-school, NES-style game with mechanics borrowed from classics such as Mega Man, Ducktales and Zelda II. There's even a bit of Super Mario Bros 3 style overworld map and patroling enemies thrown in for good measure. Also makes the rare accomplishment of emulating the look and feel of a real NES game, whereas most modern-made retro games only manage to capture the look and feel on some level, but not quite all there.
Only critique I can give is that sometimes you might find yourself letting go of your left/right direction while trying to hit down for the downthrust attack, but the most recent update rectifies this by allowing you to remap the down key to another button, if you so wish.
I can say with confidence that I am proud to have been one of the thousands of backers that helped get this project off the ground. Absolutely fantastic game, and one that I will likely be finding myself revisiting time and time again.

In its attempt to turn the series into a cinematic direction following Resident Evil 4 and refreshing its gameplay with the introduction of co-op mechanics, Resident Evil 5 lost its horror feel along the way. If you play it with a friend, however, you're in for a lot of fun.
The story of the game is rather simple and is presented with a slightly over-the-top direction giving it a stronger action movie feel. The graphics are sharp and detailed, an example of superb texture work and optimisations, despite the game's palette being somewhat monotonous. The gameplay turned from being scary into being fun, especially with a friend, and its variety keeps the game from becoming boring. Collectibles, various difficulty modes, unlockables, bonuses and extras add to its replayability.
If you're a horror fan looking for new thrills, look elsewhere. But if it's the cinematic zombie-slaying entertainment you're after, you will surely find it in this game.

This mod would totally stand up as an official paid DLC or even a standalone game. It has tons of content, with really hard yet very rewarding puzzles. You're forced to think outside of the box, working with the mechanics already introduced in Portal 2 in new fresh ways.
And as if a collection of great new puzzles weren't enough, Mel provides full experience, with ton of new models and resources, complete story arc, awesome new characters and much more. Story is very well written and voice acting is on par with any AAA game titles. Harry Callaghan's Cave Johnson voice was basically indistinguishable from the original, I honestly thought they got J.K. Simmons to read the part.
I was stunned when I saw, how few people have worked on this huge project, all in their spare time. If you own Portal 2, there is no excuse not to play this. And if you don't, well this essentially doubles the value you get for buying it.

Note this game isn't some yearly AAA game published by some huge corporation. It's a unique game and it's both a blessing and a curse.
Positive aspects include it having a highly customable gameplay because it comes with an editor. With this "mission" editor you can pretty much make cool scenarios without knowing how to script. Of course the game has a campaign and "showcase" missions and those are actually pretty high quality but my point is that you don't have to play what the devs have made for you. Modding for Arma 3 is sometimes complicated but easy enough. Could be better in some aspects.
Negative aspects are that besides single player missions and tutorials there isn't much official content so you have to find your own. Server browser is quite confusing so you have to use some website to find good servers. Arma 3 does have offical servers too and these can actually be pretty fun. It's just that Arma 3 doesn't have any weapon unlocks or anything like Call of Duty or Battlefield. If you want something to grind you have to find a right server.
So buy this game if you enjoy more sandbox experience. If you just want to jump into action and shoot people then buy something like Squad or Red Orchestra. Or any old Battlefield 2 mod. Arma 3 is for those who want to make their own gameplay.

However, the final boss fight, as well as ending sequence are superb and have a good chance to 'touch teh feels'. What's more, it manages to fit fairly well into the existing canon, although this mod actually isn't canon.
- The graphical quality is absolutely superb. Great care is taken to each and every detail. There are also a smattering of jokes hidden here and there in the environment.
- The music is all original, and while differing slightly in tone from the music from Portal 2, is still in very much the same vein.
- I am told there are several easter eggs, as well as an entirely new character. So far I've only found one minor one, and I was looking for them the whole time. They must be very well hidden.
Overall this mod is definitely a 9/10. The only cons could be a potential brain-haemorrhage from trying to solve a few of the puzzles, as well as some slightly stilted voice acting from the lead character.
So download it and play it! NOW!

The quality and polish of this game is just fantastic. We'll probably never get an official Portal 3 but this is the next best thing. The story, level design, custom textures, score, voice acting etc. are all top notch.
The only bug I found through the entire game was that anytime I activated a button, the audio and video would get glitchy for a second, this was consistent and reproducible through most of the game but it was only a minor distraction in an otherwise remarkably enjoyable experience.
As others here have noted, most of the puzzles are very difficult. Whether this is a pro or con is going to be a matter of personal preference. Mevious has a really good walkthrough on Youtube that I used a few times when I got stuck. Personally, I would have liked slightly easier puzzles or maybe just a few more hints.
Overall the game is just great, it pulls you into the story and makes you feel like you're in Aperture. It's a fun, stressful, exciting and satisfying experience. Subjectively, I'd say better than Portal 1 and not quite as good as Portal 2, but pretty close. Probably even worth a second playthrough in a few months.

Have Ubisoft actually made a genuinly awesome game? Well yes, yes they have.
The tale of Siege is an intriguing one. It went from having a horrid release to being an incredibly popular and dare I say, one of the best FPS multiplayer games to be released to this date. The constant development and support keeps the game fresh and changes up the meta every few months. The shoddy business model of Ubisoft's previous titles is gone for good. When a new DLC comes out, all of the content in it is available to everyone for free, albeit with season pass owners getting it a week prior to everyone else. The map is free on day one and can be played by everyone. The new operators can be purchased with in-game credits and while the price is certainly a little high, I wouldn't say it's too high. Realistically, it'll probably take you a few days of successful gameplay to earn enough to purchase one.
And while we're on the topic of operators, in my personal opinion, this is the reason you should buy the game. So many different characters to choose from and almost all of them (with only a couple of exceptions) are well balanced and fit into the meta very nicely. Nothing beats the feeling of when you've gotten exceptionally good with your main. I will live and die by Caveira. The gunplay is fantastic, the matches are intense and the community is definitely better than most FPS games, but there are also the black sheep, of course.
This game is an experience you need to have.

If you get Shovel Knight, don't expect to stop the game at the end of your first quest. NG+ has a great challenge to it with double damage to you, no health pickups (save for your own chalice), and half as many checkpoints as before. It'll make boss battles very difficult, but never frustratingly enough that it feels impossible.
The lack of a lives system (instead of losing lives, you lose a portion of the treasure you've obtained) also improves this feeling. You can recover the money you lost from each death if you get back to that point without dying. This element never makes the death feel painfully brutal like the games it is inspired by, but keeps death with enough meaning that you still desire to get back to the point you failed to pass.
All in all, the game proved itself to be a real joy to play and well worth your time and the $15 cost. I cannot wait to see what Yacht Club has in store for the game's further developments and their future projects.

Wow, can you see the "not P2W" part? Well, now its all that it is about. When you start fresh you will have really hard time to break through the mechanics without boosting with $ to get at least medicore experience, and if you have invested some time and already have some background you still have to pour cash in it or leave. ---------Review written in 2015-------------
Fishing planet is the ultimate relax experience. Moreover, despite being F2P is not by any means P2W and not repulsive in graphic/simple stupid gameplay terms.
In fact, graphic is nice and close to imitate realistic pond and everything you can find around it- logs, plants, boats etc. Audio is calm and minimalistic. Besides intro music (which is great) there are only sound effects which is actually a great decision as it fulfills the calm and silent atmosphere of fishing contemplation. Birds, water and mosquitos are the perfect background to sit back and chill out.
As for gamplay it is really more complex than throw and tow. You get yourself into two main ways of fishing- spinning and angling. Spinning is where you go for the fighters and predators. You must master several techniques of spinning as different predators respond differently to given bait and its movement.
When you get tired of fighting you can take out your angler and do some peaceful casting for some less fierce fish. There you have to know what given fish likes to eat the most, where they hide and at which depths.
There is a lot to learn and fishing blind and random will result in small blue basses. When you do your research and come prepared, you will get comparable results with big largemouth basses and heavy catfish as there is very little randomness in this game. If you know what you are doing you will get results making it very high commitment-high reward game. It will never make you feel you lost your time, even when you pour many hours into it.
I covered barely some of the aspects of the first fishing place, there are more really challenging lakes as well as more types of fish to catch. Although being still in early access, game provides countless hours of fun and relax and there is lots of competitive stuff planned for the future.
Moreover its free, so you can try it out with no money loss. Although when you try it, you will feel that the devs deserved some monetary gratitude for their tremendous work that is far superior to good ol' Trophy Bass series in every aspect.

Video games are a very subjective experience, much more than any other medium of art and entertainment. In a peculiar way, Amnesia is both for and against this sentiment in that it has an uncanny way of emotionally stirring the player but also makes the player react in the same way as others. The brilliant rigging of in-game events, design of the audio and the overall presentation of the game creates an unforgettable experience - unforgettable because it is possibly the most frightening & terrifying game to ever be developed. And that is not at all a bad thing; the game is extremely immersive because of how gripping and tense the game world becomes as a result of its ingenious design. It can be so immersive in fact that it can cause players to shut down the game because the discomfort and horror composed by the game world can be too emotionally heavy & distressing. This is what video games should be, a direct and interactive emotional experience, and Amnesia executes this flawlessly.

- Cube reseting buttons. Awesome, when you screw up and you need to get the cube back to you. Too bad, when game, without warning, expects you to use this button to solve a puzzle.

Amnesia isn't a game that's easily described to someone who hasn't played it. The story moves along at a snail's pace, the enemies are few and far between, and the game's action sequences often involve you running from danger rather than combatting it head-on.
What the game does have is excellent atmosphere and legimately scary enemies. In some of the more difficult sections, my heart rate noticeably increased and my breathing became shorter and faster. I was drawn into this game and for a time I became the protagonist, deathly afraid of whatever was around the next corner and occasionaly unsure if the enemy was real or part of Daniel's imagination.
Amnesia starts off slow, but it gets better and saves the best until the very end. I can genuinely say I enjoyed the hell out of this game, even if I was terrified while playing it. Amnesia does horror right in all the right ways. If you want to experience a simultaneously beautiful and horrifying game, you can't go wrong with Amnesia.

I usually post steam reviews in portuguese, but since I wrote this for another website, here it goes:
You play as shovel knight, and your goal is to reach the enchantress and save your old partner, shield knight. In order to do so, shovel knight must defeat eight members of "The order of no Quarter".
Shovel Knight is very much inspired by our beloved classics. Mario, Zelda, megaman, castlevania, it's very easy to see how shovel knight has been inspired by all of these games, but all in the best way possible. The best thing shovel knight inherited from those games is the marvelous level design. The tutorial level is wonderfully done, teaching you the basic mechanics without the need of a message or even a button display. Even in later stages, the game will never put you in a dangerous situation without teaching you first, something that megaman in particular was always known for.
The overworld map looks a lot like the Mario Bros 3 map (there are even wandering enemies with special fights or stages), and you can usually choose the next stage from 2 or 3 avaiable, and visit the villages, where you can buy upgrades, relics and equipment with the gold you got on the levels. Relics basically works like spells, but there are also chalices that can hold liquids which will grant you one time effects (like the bottles in zelda). You can also upgrade your shovel, but there are only three upgrades. One of them makes sparks come out of your shovel while you're at full health (zelda again). There are some different armors too, but I felt like just one of them was really useful, so in terms of upgrades the game could do better.
Shovel Knight is great, and as far as I'm concerned it deserves the praise it's been getting. Combining the best elements from classics, with great boss fight and some beautiful animations, it's pretty easy to recommend this game whether you enjoyed the classics that inspired it or not.

Shovel Knight is everything a lover of platformers should want. From the moment you boot up the game,  you are greeted with the fantastic soundtrack that Yacht Club games has delivered to us. In a mere moment, you're set to dig through the first stage with a wonderful retro style, and great gameplay.
Shovel Knight has you swinging your shovel to defeat enemies, or using it like a pogo stick to do the same, or as a tool for platforming. Stages can be a challenge, but it never feels like it is too much of a challenge. Between upgrades you can purchase and the relics the game has scattered about, you have no shortage of tools to get out of a bad situation besides your spade. The bosses also pose an interesting challenge, each with their own style of digging your grave.
While the story is lacking for the most part, the story isn't the focus. The gameplay is, and it sure is solid. If you aren't sure about purchasing this game, but you love platformers, don't give it another thought. Get it, and dig in.

This is a solid co-op title, and plays like a more action-heavy Resident Evil 4. It's not particularly scary - in fact, I don't even remember any jump scares, much less the feelings of dread from the first few RE games. But that's not a turn-off, just a warning: don't get into this if you're expecting an atmospheric, unnerving crawl through the Spencer Mansion. RE5 should definitely be played with a friend, the AI is passable but far from solid. My biggest gripe (apart from the nonsense story) is all the Quick Time Events (QTEs) that show up during cutscenes. They can become unreasonable, especially if you're playing over a network with any lag. A controller is pretty much necessary.
Overall recommendation: you could do a lot worse with co-op titles. Bring a controller.

A retraux masterpiece that everyone and anyone should play, given the slightest chance and interest.

Saints Row the Third is a good game with some bugs, but still a good game,  it's also very similar to Grand Theft Auto. But lets get into the pros, and the cons
Pros
- The game is very fun, I would get side tracked alot, playing the fun, and new activities, or finding the collectibles, or just killing everything I see, or again taking over the city, and getting money to upgraded my guns, the game again is very fun, just like Saints Row 2.
- The story is good in my opinion, I mean it might have some chessy moments, but the story does have some epic moments, and with new, and awesome characters, and a sad moment, but I loved some missions, and hated some, the story again is very good, but can have some ridiculous moments.
- The gameplay is very fun, I love the new guns, and the freedom, and theres a new choice system which I very much kind of like. The AI is good, and playing activities are really fun, also theres this new upgrade system, where you spent money to get upgrades to your character, but otherwise the gameplay isn't sometime boring, but fun, also the car handling is pretty ok.
Cons
- The city is very boring, theres really nothing to do, after you're done, there isn't really any new, or interesting places to explore, the game just gets boring, and you see the same skin model everytime, the city is so boring, and bland,  compared to Saints Row 2
- The choice system really doesn't matter, I mean come on, I didn't really care that much about the choice system, it really didn't affect the game that much, until the last mission.
- I really disliked that a lot of THE MAIN MISSIONS, WERE ACTIVTIES, I MEAN COME ON, YOU GUYS COULDN'T COME UP WITH SOME NEW IDEAS FOR THOSE MISSIONS, and I just really disliked that
Conclusion
In the end, Saints Row the Third is a fun game, with bugs, and a good story, and a good, and fun gameplay. My final rating is 7.5/10

Counter Strike has been a part of our lives and we all love it... until now. Welcome to the review of an amazing, and one of the best, spinoffs in gaming history: Tactical Intervention!
Graphics: 8/10
Made on the Source Engine, it makes the game look a lot like Left 4 Dead 2. The game's graphics are somewhat outdated, but don't let the graphics bog you down. The only thing that is bad about the graphics is that it makes this game look more cartoony than it would've if it were Unreal Technology graphics.
Gameplay: 9.5/10
Gameplay is just flat-out amazing. Tactical Intervention is virtual and you can do pretty much anything. The developers even took the time to program a roll mechanic, which in my opinion is the best thing a game could have. Especially a First Person Shooter. Tactical Intervention also has a huge variety of guns, and for that, I put a special little tab of that in this review. This game has wonderful mechanics. You can grab hostages, lean, roll, pick up extinguishers and smoke up an area, kick things, etc. This game is an overall work of art in this area. However, one thing wrong with this game is that you cannot aim down your sights. That bogs us all down if we are all into modern day FPS's, however, that is one minor thing and it shouldn't stand in your way.
Sound: 8/10
The gunshots sound pretty realistic. Footsteps are soft and immersive, juggling of equipment, very interesting ambiance (hope I spelled that right :P), and very immersive enviroment. Only problems: the switching does not sound realistic, the gunshots sound "pretty" realistic (so it would be nice if they improved it just a wee bit), the menu sounds are a little annoying.
Gun Selection/Variety: 8.5/10
Tactical Intervention has a realistic "Gun Store". You can either rent a gun for 1-7 days, or you can buy it for permanant (for a lot more money, or GP). Tactical Intervention also has a HUGE selection of guns, coming from the AK-47, all the way down to the SPAS-12 and probably even more I haven't seen. Now now, it isn't like Borderlands II where you can't get the same gun twice... but it feels like it!
Server Security: 9/10
I have been playing Tactical Intervention for a while now, and so far I have come across very few hackers (like, 1). This proves either people friggin love the game too much to hack, this game has VAC Security on it, or the people just don't have hacks compatible for Tactical Intervention. (DO NOT MAKE ANY!!!)
Overall: An amazing 9.25/10!!!
This is probably the biggest score I have ever given to a game in my opinion. The game truly out-ran CS:GO, in my opinion. It is basicly the same thing, however it is way better... and FREE! So, if you don't have this game, stop reading this review, go back to the store, and get the game. It is free, however I would've gladly paid $10, $20 on it. This is a really fun game and I highly suggest supporting the developers, so they can import new stuff into this amazing port. Tactical Intervention, everyone! This is the MP Game of the Year!!!!

I have played many games in the era of NES. Megaman. Metroid. Rygar. Ducktales. Castlevania. Super Mario Bros. Legend of Zelda.
All of these games. These challenging, challenging games, and its here in 2014, where I find a game that absolutely trumps each and everyone one of my NES favorites. It has the level design, the aesthetic, the music, the artstyle, and most of all: The challenge.
This game is by far, one of the most fun, and sometimes the most challenging, of all the 8-Bit Classic Platformer type games that I have ever played. This game takes all of my feelings for Mario Bros. 3, Ducktales, Castlevania, Megaman, and just, combines it into one sweet package.
-When you play, the system that acts as your "lives" so to speak, is replaced with instead "loot". In stages, you collect gold, treasure, gems, and jewels from either chests, mounds of dirt in the ground that you dig up, or secret parts of the wall where you'd have to hit as if Castlevania in search for chicken. When you do die, however, your total loot will be decreased by a good chunk, and three bags of loot will fly up into the air awaiting for you to recollect them when you return from the checkpoint.
-Speaking of chicken, you do have a lifebar like Castlevania and Megaman, which you are able to fill up by finding either random apples or carrots strewn about the stage, or finding a platter of chicken/turkey in the walls. However, those platters don't always contain chicken.
-Jump and Attack. With Jump, you basically jump. You can attack while jumping, so theres that out of the way. With attack, you are able to either slash the air, or dig piles of dirt and rock laid around the stages to collect treasure and gems. At some points, you are able to slash at certain blocks in the walls, and collect more bountiful treasure, that which acts as your lives. When jumping, if you hold the down button, your shovel will point to the ground like Scrooge McDucks cane, and you can jump off of, and deal damage to enemies, or jump off of blocks of dirt and sand. If you like old-school 8-bit games, you absolutely must get this one.  A love-letter to all of the NES greats, incorporating elements of Mega Man, Super Mario Bros. 3, Zelda 2: Adventure of Link, Castlevania, and more, it is truly amazing.
Gameplay is solid, with none of the floaty response that plagued actual games from the NES era.  Earlier stages start off easier and get progressively more difficult as they go along, but at no point does the game hold your hand.  There are relics to find that give extra abilities, or you can choose not to collect them to give an added challenge.  Your life and magic meters can be likewise extended or not based on your preference.  And the same even goes for weapon and armor upgrades.
All of the usual suspects can be found in the stage design: Fire stage?  Check!  Ice stage?  Check!  Water stage, clockwork stage, and multiple-form bosses?  Check, check and check!  And the music!  Oh boy the music.  You'll be humming a lot of the tunes long after you've quit for the night.  I highly recommend picking up the soundtrack, available at a choose-your-own-cost.
Get the game.  Get it now.  And love it.

Amnesia - The Dark Descent is the kind of survival horror game that must be done right. By that, I mean not playing it surrounded with natural and/or artificial light and plenty of people around who may or may not have played this before. This is the kind of title that asks for you to be alone in the dark with stereo headphones on. This is how you properly set the gamma the first time you play the game. You have to properly set the mood in order for you to get the best possible horror experience out of Amnesia - The Dark Descent.
Overall: Amnesia the Dark Descent is an enjoyable title with a refreshing twist on the survival horror genre. But as stated the re-playability is limited but is at least worth the 20 bucks just so as long you enjoy this type of experience. Other than that: Good job Frictional Game!

I recommend this game if you like platformers. In spite of the hype about how good it is, simply because it's a throwback to retro games - the game is overall very average in difficulty and it was only deep enough mechanics wise to get me through the first 3/4ths of the game.
The issue specifically was that if you just did a couple quick runs of older levels, you'd acquire all the gold you need for any of the interesting gear. It is great though that they allowed you to run the levels again just in case you were something like 200 gold short of something. The re-runs simply award too much, making them worthwhile to farm. You could argue I ruined my own experience by farming, but I found this out from being in the very situation aforementioned. Gold then later becomes utterly useless, which was disappointing because the suspense of death is nearly lost then.
Despite all that, the graphics style is pleasant, reminding me of Kirby Superstar and Sonic. I enjoyed the movement/mechanics, the knight behaving like Link in Super Smash Brothers Melee (if he had a pogo shovel.) I'm not an 80's kid so I don't really have a bigger arsenal of experience with retro games to compare it to.
The music, I'll be honest - I expected better. However, I allowed myself to be hyped about this game; so there's that. The tunes actually are quite catchy and some deliciously solemn (
.)
The story was predictable, but I didn't really buy the game for the story so I'm not disappointed. Characters were predictable as well, but less so than the story - and their mechanics were fairly interesting and fairly unique (I am inexperienced, though.)
The best parts of the game were really the goofy/silly dialogue and the gameplay (not story, music, etc.) Despite me saying it was average difficulty, there was some brutal and frustrating parts for myself - but I fully expected to be frustrated going into this game.
If I were to give it a rating, it would be 8/10 overall. Got a good 10 hours out of it. Took me 12 to beat it.

Amnesia takes most after the penultimate episode of Penumbra (lol), after they'd cut out most of the tedium from their games, but before it turned into a surreal platformer. The game progresses by a find-item-here, use-item-there mechanic that would be annoying, but when immersed in the atmospheric castles and dungeons this complaint is mitigated. Danger (i.e. enemies) are leveraged sparingly and terrifyingly; at points I actually had to quit playing because it was so stressful.
At the beginning of the game you're exhorted not to "play to win," but to just immerse yourself. This is difficult for me, perhaps the most anal retentive gamer who ever lived. But Amnesia managed to make me forget myself a few times. Total time played was about seven hours, and I accidently cut the bad guy's speech short in the final battle because I panicked and struck prematurely, perhaps robbing me of a more satisfying conclusion. The game is good, and Frictional deserves your money.

There are plenty of things wrong with this game, but somehow it seems well worthy of a recommendation.
The BAD:
* The controls are clearly designed with joypads in mind, which means your crack soldier will have little difficulty popping heads off the zombie waves, but will probably come a cropper walking around bends, and spend a lot of time stuck in the corner of the room.
* Some of the cutscenes require the player to jab some key combo to avoid being decapitated/disemboweled. A nice interlude, but it does get a bit tedious watching your character run down a hole the 11th time in a row.
* The final boss fight goes well over the melodrama quota for any title. Just die already!
The GOOD:
* Two-player co-op is awesomely good fun. The levels are well-designed for the most part, and have plenty of moments when players really have to rely on one another. Reviving/rescuing your comrade is also nicely tuned.
* There's a DX9 version which runs well on aging hardware. Woohoo!

Amnesia takes most after the penultimate episode of Penumbra (lol), after they'd cut out most of the tedium from their games, but before it turned into a surreal platformer. The game progresses by a find-item-here, use-item-there mechanic that would be annoying, but when immersed in the atmospheric castles and dungeons this complaint is mitigated. Danger (i.e. enemies) are leveraged sparingly and terrifyingly; at points I actually had to quit playing because it was so stressful.
At the beginning of the game you're exhorted not to "play to win," but to just immerse yourself. This is difficult for me, perhaps the most anal retentive gamer who ever lived. But Amnesia managed to make me forget myself a few times. Total time played was about seven hours, and I accidently cut the bad guy's speech short in the final battle because I panicked and struck prematurely, perhaps robbing me of a more satisfying conclusion. The game is good, and Frictional deserves your money.
