There are so many good and so many bad things, which can be said about this game and this review, can be really long, but no one will read it, so it is waste of time for me to write it in details. All I will say is:
1.	I have bought CS:GO a week before I have installed TI and so far, I have accumulated 125 hours on TI, I am level 23 and I have bought quite few items (already have spend about 260,000GP) and I have accumulated just 6 hours on CS:GO and those are actually, because I have started to play CS:GO now/recently.
2.	I am a real world, skill/tactics based, FPS fan and TI had it all and more than any other FPS, I have ever played, but all the romance disappeared after I started to notice some serious unbalance in the game and after a while it is not anymore that much about skills, than just, what gadgets/items you have equipped. From that point on, it will start to become more and more a rat race to gain more GP and buy better armor, shoes, gloves etc, because it will highly influence your success rate, mind you I am not talking about the weapons…. and it begins to feel more like a RPG game than a skill game.  When you win or lose, you know and the rest of the players know (even, if some of them do not admit it), that most of the time you win or lose, because of the better gadgets/items you or they have equipped and the skill factor and the satisfaction of winning are pathetic, if you have to be honest to yourself.
3.	I do understand, that the game is F2P and the developers need to make money, but if I buy some DLC, I will become even more overpowered and it will be more like shooting fish in a barrel, than a fair challenge and satisfaction for all the players. What can I say about Shovel Knight that hasn't been said before? Awesome music? Pays homage to classics of the NES era? A damn fine platformer I was happy to have backed on Kickstarter? All true, but it doesn't take much digging to find that this game is a much grander treasure than that.
Within moments of starting to play, I was smiling and trying to contain my sheer glee. If somebody were to take the finest ingredients from Mega Man, Super Mario Bros 3, Zelda 2 and Castlevania, wrap it up into a deliciously nostalgic package and pump it full of love, you still wouldn't quite get Shovel Knight. The game doesn't hide its influences, but it's much more than just some cheap indie retro attempt to play on nostalgia.
This isn't like Mega Man 2. This is like how you
MM2 being. Those happy memories were a younger you ignored the flaws of the game, those that tend to sting a little when visiting games from those era without the nostalgia goggles.
Shovel Knight, even without those old-timey goodness, still stands up proudly on its own merits, featuring fun gameplay, excellent level design, a stunning NES-accurate soundtrack and simplistic but charming characters.
is how you do platformers, people. I've not felt this kind of sheer joy in any platformer (save maybe Rayman Origins) in a very long time.
There's exploration, secrets, plenty of challenges, optional levels, tigh controls, pleasant aesthetics and it just feels...right.
I don't care that I've just beaten that level, I want to play it again with the new relic I have, find those music sheets I missed and then when I've found every secret...I want to play it again.
I'll admit, for all my hyping about it (and I do feel the hype was justified, now that I've beaten it once), it carries some issues. A few achievements/feats seem buggy, there are some delays with localisation and Mac/Linux ports, plus not all features are available yet (Kickstarter stretch goals to be added in free updates later).
While I personally like how they've handled dying (go back to a checkpoint and lose some gold than can be recovered, checkpoints can be sacrificed for more gold if you're feeling confident), with a difficulty I'd describe as "challenging in places but forgiving and never frustrating", fans of the games Shovel Knight is styled after may find even the New Game+ too easy.
The final issue is that, well, there's just not enough of it. I played rather slowly, exploring, talking to NPCs and while I didn't accomplish every feat I could or find every single music sheet, and clocked in about 6 hours. Others seem to do about 5 or less and someone trying to accomplish just the main story could beat the game in less than 2 hours (like most NES games, minus the same level of difficulty).
That being said...there's still plenty of replay value, more features are on the way and based on the quality, I'd rather have this short and sweet delight than have the experience ruined by unneccesasy padding. And besides maybe when Portal first game out, I can't think of many games where I thought "I wish there was more of this...but it works best that there's not."
So, is SHOVEL KNIGHT for you?
If you have any love for the classic platformers of the '80s, yes. If you have any love for platformers in general, yes. If you just want one heck of a great chiptune soundtrack, then yes. Unlike other "retro" platformers, it doesn't just take the appearance of the old school, but takes the basic soul of those classics, reinvigorates it and sprinkles in just enough advancement from the modern day to make a brilliant experience.
Whether it's on PC, Wii U or 3DS, play this with a big smile on your face and prepare to meet Justice! SHOVEL JUSTICE!

Without giving too much of the story away, you play as the eponymous Mel who has signed herself up for some SCIENCE. Needless to say, things go wrong. After stumbling around for a bit you find a ye olde portal device and get to work flinging yourself everywhere. Eventually, you meet up with a personality core that wants to help you escape. The two of you set off for freedom, but nothing is ever that easy...
Be warned: even if you dream about portals the puzzles in this game won't be a walk in the park. The game starts out 'difficult' and ramps it up from there. My playtime is indicitive of one playthrough. A couple of the puzzles left me stumped; I had to come back later with a fresh perspective to nail them. If other mods or custom maps seem too easy for you, try Portal Stories: Mel.

I'm going to try to not offend anyone in this review, but I think it is important to address the people who are saying it is too difficult…
I understand that people have different intelligence levels, however I believe that people who aren't completing certain puzzles in this game are just looking at the puzzle too laterally, maybe.
I completed this game without the help of any guides or walkthroughs, and I'm the type of person who has to look up walkthroughs for stupid point-and-click flash "escape" games….
This game isn't more difficult or complex than Portal 2, in my opinion. It is different, and forces the player to think out of the box a little more than Portal 2. In my case, I got really stuck on a good 3-4 puzzles in Portal Stories: Mel and it took me walking away for a day and coming back to it, or just retracing my steps, or finding a pad that I can use my portal gun on that I hadn't noticed before. This game takes more attention to detail and more patience, but is much more rewarding  once you complete a puzzle.
I am not a genius, but I loved the difficulty level of this game, and thought it fair and perfectly challenging. I will say that one of the levels was particularly difficult, and could possibly be labeled  as "unfair," but even that I feel had a clear solution once you thought out of the box.
At the end of the day, this is my breakdown:
HIGHLY RECOMMENDED
Pros:
-Beautiful
-Looks, sounds and feels exactly like Portal 2
-Challenging in a great way
-Free as heck
-Few bugs/glitches
-Good amount of gameplay
Cons:
-What I hated most was the beginning, which took you between loading screen after loading screen for very little exposition and story development and bored the heck out of me.
-I didn't care for Virgil. I just didn't think he was funny, and sometimes I muted the game because I thought he got annoying. I wouldn't recommend doing that because he does give you direction and hints at times.
-There were times I clipped through something I thought I could jump on and died. That was a surprise and a bit of a bummer.
-There was this one major glitch where I would die and the screen would go black and freeze
-There was a glitch in which I had full WASD control, but no control of my mouse. I would force suit and restart the game and it would do it again…the final solution was I had to reload a save from earlier in the game, and just not die at that specific spot.
So obviously the cons are negligible and the pros are awesome, so if you like Portal, puzzles, and/or free games, try this one out!

So i played this for roughly for half an hour and here are my first impressions of the game.
It's still an early access game so i won't be too rough on it since it's not completed yet, but as a person who has been fishing for his entire life this game unfortunately does not quite deliver. First of all, it doesn't have the multiplayer co-op mode mentioned in the store page, you can chat with your friend while you fish but you can't see their model which is a huge bummer. Second, there are a metric TON of customization options for both your rod and your baits. But most of them are XP locked and are kept as "end game content". Meaning that you have to fish for the boring small fishes for hours on end before you can get to the real interesting stuff, this was why i stopped playing after the half hour point.
Now, although i sound negative there is a massive potential in this game. If they can add the before mentioned multiplayer mode and give us a little bit more options at the beginning of the game this could be a THE fishing simulator experience you are looking for. Right now it just needs more work, however i'm very keen on seeing what they can come up with next.
TLDR;
+ Great graphics. (For a fishing simulator.)
+ Leaderboards, this is always a nice plus for a game like this.
+ Rather pleasing music and ambient lake sound effects.
+ Quite a lot of different options when it comes to the actual fishing, reeling speed, weight customization, etc.
+ XP System in a game like this is a fantastic idea, although it could be handled better.
+ Business model seems to be really fair, almost all the rods that are on the market can be bought with ingame currency.
+ Ton of rod/equipment customization, you can choose practically everything you want to take with you...
- ...If you are high enough at level to do so.
- Very limited map space, although kinda understandable.
- No co-op unlike the store page says.
- Only one musical soundtrack in the menus, gets repetetive really fast.
- Fishies gnaw way too often, makes the fishing feel rather artificial and randomized.
- Can't really adjust on how far to throw your reel, or then i'm just missing it.
- Some button placements are a bit off, and it doesn't look like you could rebind them.
- Disable HUD button doesn't work.
- Striking the fish is pretty difficult sometimes, more of a reflex game than actual fishing. It's not like a pike can really escape a hook once it's bitten it so deep that the whole floater sinks underwater.

There are a lot of video games. Many try to capture a retro style to win over a nostalgic crowd, or try to pull a more unique art style to grab people's attentions. Others tell deep stories that hook you in, make you feel invested, like you have to get to the end. Few try to sell on quality gameplay alone, something that's genuinely fun to play.
Few games do all three. Games like Dark Souls, Shadow of the Colossus, Bastion, Transistor, Earthbound... And now, Shovel Knight.
From start to finish, Shovel Knight is a fantastic game. In the first level, it teaches you how to play subtly without throwing it out at you in a text box, much like Megaman X had done years ago. The controls are simple, each move shown to you as you accomplish it on your own without heavy handed guidance. Even the ability to identify an alternate path or a hidden wall is subtly placed into the world, so you always know what to look for. And everything is used throughout the game from then on, in new, creative ways each time, through platforming and combat.
There's more to my mentioning of Megaman. Shovel Knight uses the original color palette of NES... The very limited number of color choices presented is clear in the still vivid scenery. It stays true to its nostalgic feel. Each world is unique in more than just appearance as well. The variation of enemies is absolutely beautiful, new types of critters appearing in every single stage. Even Rats, re-used throughout the game, are fought completely differently each time. From little Helicopter Rats to ones that outright explode when killed.
And finally, the story. The prologue is simple, a tale of fallen heroes... Many more than you'd think at first. But Shovel Knight gets up, and goes to fight the good fight. The story builds up further in short conversations with enemies. It deepens as you fight your rival more and more, until you learn something about him that changes everything. But most importantly, this game is about saving Shield Knight... And when Shovel Knight dreams, there's only one thing he dreams of.
Buy Shovel Knight. Don't wait for a sale. Play it.

I'm going to try to not offend anyone in this review, but I think it is important to address the people who are saying it is too difficult…
I understand that people have different intelligence levels, however I believe that people who aren't completing certain puzzles in this game are just looking at the puzzle too laterally, maybe.
I completed this game without the help of any guides or walkthroughs, and I'm the type of person who has to look up walkthroughs for stupid point-and-click flash "escape" games….
This game isn't more difficult or complex than Portal 2, in my opinion. It is different, and forces the player to think out of the box a little more than Portal 2. In my case, I got really stuck on a good 3-4 puzzles in Portal Stories: Mel and it took me walking away for a day and coming back to it, or just retracing my steps, or finding a pad that I can use my portal gun on that I hadn't noticed before. This game takes more attention to detail and more patience, but is much more rewarding  once you complete a puzzle.
I am not a genius, but I loved the difficulty level of this game, and thought it fair and perfectly challenging. I will say that one of the levels was particularly difficult, and could possibly be labeled  as "unfair," but even that I feel had a clear solution once you thought out of the box.
At the end of the day, this is my breakdown:
HIGHLY RECOMMENDED
Pros:
-Beautiful
-Looks, sounds and feels exactly like Portal 2
-Challenging in a great way
-Free as heck
-Few bugs/glitches
-Good amount of gameplay
Cons:
-What I hated most was the beginning, which took you between loading screen after loading screen for very little exposition and story development and bored the heck out of me.
-I didn't care for Virgil. I just didn't think he was funny, and sometimes I muted the game because I thought he got annoying. I wouldn't recommend doing that because he does give you direction and hints at times.
-There were times I clipped through something I thought I could jump on and died. That was a surprise and a bit of a bummer.
-There was this one major glitch where I would die and the screen would go black and freeze
-There was a glitch in which I had full WASD control, but no control of my mouse. I would force suit and restart the game and it would do it again…the final solution was I had to reload a save from earlier in the game, and just not die at that specific spot.
So obviously the cons are negligible and the pros are awesome, so if you like Portal, puzzles, and/or free games, try this one out!

Portal Stories: Mel is a game great for those who want more to the Aperture Science story. If you want story, soundtracks and visuals, you got it. If you want gameplay, well, I hope you frequented the Portal 2 Workshop beforehand or there is a good chance you'll be hitting the spanish-subtitled walkthrough.
Pros:
-An entertaining story that fits well within the Portal 2 universe.
-Fun references to other Portal games and even Half-Life
-Fully voiced.
-Amazing music which fits Portal 2 while still having a style of its own. (Not to mention it's availible for free download.)
-New assets fit Valve's art style like a glove.
-Great effects are used throughout the game.
-A great ending with a tragic twist. (Befitting of the story it expands upon.)
-The main antagonist sounds like the Axiom from Wall-E.
Cons:
-The aforementioned great story does have the occasional hiccup.
-The intro takes too long to do very little. (Not sure if meant to be foreshadowing the puzzles.)
-There is no learning curve or clues for the harder puzzles, which tend to call upon techniques from community chambers they didn't even create and even knowlege of the game engine itself. (You'll even be rummaging through the final boss chamber looking for where the story continues.)
-Some of the more complex chambers have holes in them, making it easy to BS your way through the level
-Level pacing ceases to exist after the second chapter.
-(Cue Buzz meme.) Invisible walls, invisible walls everywhere!
-The final chapter is a 'different enough' rehash of Portal 2's mid game.
-The game goes from a puzzle game to an unchallenging platform shooter for the climax. (Which Valve themselves said was a bad idea in their Portal commentary.)
-The ending sequence starts too early. (There were more opportunities for interaction/exploration before Bink Video plays the rest of the game for you.)
Final Verdict: Portal Stories: Mel is like Portal: Prelude but with a way better story, real voice acting, and is hard by choice rather than extreme error. Would I reccomend this game? Definitely.

SR3 is always going to have a special place in my heart--partially because the entire SR series got me through a very difficult time in my life, and partially because there aren't a lot of other games I can say will let me drive around in a hot dog costume with my naked co-op partner while a tiger's mauling me in the back seat. An iconic moment in our friendship.
If you're new to the series and debating where to start: SR2 has a better story and more solid writing, SR3's gameplay is a lot more flexible and fun and the graphics are nicer--especially on PC, since the SR2 PC port is...bad--and SR4 is basically SR3 after it jumped the shark and added a few new gameplay mechanics. So it really depends on what's important to you! I'd say that as long as you can play it on another platform, SR2 would be your best bet to start with, since then you get to see the series grow over the next three games. But if you're only able to play on PC, you can start with SR3, fall in love with riding a carriage pulled by a mostly naked man with a ballgag and a golden microphone he speaks through via a hole in his throat, then work back to SR2 and enjoy the good aspects of that game while ignoring the PC port's flaws.

Amnesia: The Dark Descent redefines the idea of "survival horror." You have no guns, no weapons, no way to fight back against the monstrosities that roam the halls of Castle Ican'trememberthename. You play Daniel (or is it David?), an amnesiac fellow who writes letters to himself and tries to convince himself to do things that a normal man shouldn't want to.
The whole game takes place within the crumbling walls of a single Castle, though the environments change as you plunge further into the game due to Daniel's bleeding sanity. If you stay in the dark for too long, inanimate objects begin to breathe, Daniel hallucinates bugs crawling all over him, and he might even fall over, unable to take another step until he finds light.
If you're into atmosphere and immersion and being terrified by the idea of opening doors, try Amnesia out -- you won't be disappointed.

Imulation isn't the defining aspect of Arma 3. It's scale.
The enormity of the map is the foundation for the experiences that distinguish Bohemia Interactive's flagship franchise. It's what makes radios, topographical maps, binoculars, and compasses practical equipment in an FPS. It's what allows for kilometer-long headshots and coordinated convoy raids. It's what makes using your eyes to spot hints of enemies muzzle flashes, tracers, and gunsmoke.
Arma 3 represents an aesthetic overhaul of the series. Unbelievable dynamic lighting, a volumetric cloud system, genuine vehicle physics, 3D weapon optics, ragdoll, noticeably improved weapon audio, and other grainy, eye-level details await scrutiny inside Arma 3's macro elegance. The best improvement is the merciful cutting of Arma 2's rigid, Tin-Man-without-oil combat animations, which makes infantry combat more responsive in your hands.
A half-year in paid pre-release has given Arma 3 time to gestate, but the final build is far from being a comprehensive reinvention of the series, and some long-standing blemishes that arise from its nature as a gargantuan simulation linger. Even on high-end hardware, the framerate dips under the spectacle of some multiplayer missions. Friendly AI units, though marginally better-behaved, still depend on the player to be their brains, an issue that's circumvented by playing Arma the way God intended it cooperatively.

Amnesia: The Dark Descent redefines the idea of "survival horror." You have no guns, no weapons, no way to fight back against the monstrosities that roam the halls of Castle Ican'trememberthename. You play Daniel (or is it David?), an amnesiac fellow who writes letters to himself and tries to convince himself to do things that a normal man shouldn't want to.
The whole game takes place within the crumbling walls of a single Castle, though the environments change as you plunge further into the game due to Daniel's bleeding sanity. If you stay in the dark for too long, inanimate objects begin to breathe, Daniel hallucinates bugs crawling all over him, and he might even fall over, unable to take another step until he finds light.
If you're into atmosphere and immersion and being terrified by the idea of opening doors, try Amnesia out -- you won't be disappointed.

Portal Stories: Mel has a lot of things going for it; a great story, good voice actors, suprisingly pretty visual design, and an amazing soundtrack that is also available for free. Unfortunately, one major flaw hangs over most of the experience: the puzzles are way too hard. If you think I'm just an idiot, I implore you, read some more reviews. I'm not the only one saying this. The first chapter is probably the best puzzle-wise, with challenging but rewarding puzzles. After that, they start to get incredibly difficult. For some people, they love a really difficult challenge, which is part of the reason I'm reccommending this. For me, it became demoralizing. By the end of the third chapter, I was dreading having to solve another insanely difficult puzzle, and pretty soon after I just started using noclip for half the puzzles. The point when it hit me that the puzzles were really getting too difficult was when I had to look up a walkthrough, and after seeing the solution to the puzzle I was on I said to myslef "I could never have figured that out." Usually when I look up a walkthrough for a puzzle game I go "Oooooohhhhh... That makes sense. I'm dumb," or "Wow am I stupid, that was so obvious." This is the first time that thi has ever happened to me, and it makes me sad to see something that obviously had so much love and hard work put into it fall short because of something like this. It is free, so you should give it a go, but you should just focus on the story rather than the gameplay.

Shovel Knight, where to even begin? Such an amazing nostalgia trip for those of us who remember what it was like being a child growing up in the late 80's / early 90's. Some new age gamers might not "get it". The game is as casual or difficult as you want it to be depending on the items you collect throughout the journey, so it's definitely a game that can be played by everyone.
There is checkpoint system implemented in the stages so it's casual but after the tutorial stage you are given the option to destroy the checkpoints you come in contact with, for hardcore gamers this is a Godsend. If anyone remembers games where dying at a boss meant repeating the entire level over again, this is for you. Honestly I don't remember any NES game that did this, most games had checkpoint systems implemented and I feel it's a bit of a misnomer and hyperbole...
The music is created by the incredibly talented Jake Kaufman of Contra 4, Double Dragon Neon and Mighty Switch Force fame just to mention a few. It's definitly no slouch in terms of catchy tunes so it'll keep you thinking about the game long after you've shelved it.
It borrows game play elements from games like Mega Man, Zelda II, Ducktales and Super Mario Bros. 3 just to give an example of what to expect. There is a small upgrade system implemented but it doesn't take control over the game entirely. You still have to earn most of your upgrades through good old fashioned game play and I thought it was a fine balance. It'll give you an edge in the early game to buy out shops but aftewards you will have to rely on some skill which could proove frustrating to some gamers not used to those sorts of elements.
I found the game fair in difficulty, none of the stages are "easy" but none of them are overly frustrating either. I noticed the game never ramped in difficulty too much, it kind of goes up a notch with each new wave of bosses and seems to level off from there. With some replayable factors such as New Game+, it will keep you coming back to try again. The only way to get good at games like this is to keep playing and memorize them, it will become more enjoyable if you plug in the hours.
The one big peeve I have about the game is the sloppy level design, I found it a bit erratic at times and too random. The one big flaw with this game is the way it flows and that could proove to be an issue for speed running. Get this game if you even remotely like Portal or Portal 2.
It is an awesome production made by people who not only love the Portal games, but understand what made them such gems. The test chambers(puzzles) in this game are some of the finest I have seen and equally match the quality of the original games.
The test chambers in the game, however, are much harder than those found in Portal 1 or 2. This is not necessarily a bad thing, but be warned: This game does not hold your hand and difficult puzzles appear quite early in the game. It is assumed you have played both Portal and Portal 2 and they utilize not only the skills you learned in those games, but innovate in ways that require you to think in new ways. Everything, however, does makes sense and the puzzles have logical solutions. I played and beat the entire game and I only found one solution that I considered "cheap". It involved using the laser bridges to lift a box off a switch, something I did not know could happen. That is minor nitpicking, though. The vast majority of the puzzles are mind-bending, logical, and extremely satisfying to play. I spent 45 minutes solving one with my wife and even though we made minimal progress, we both agreed that we enjoyed puzzling through the particular chamber we were on.
The final puzzle, a timed battle similar to the one in Portal 1, is a total pain an is an unfortunate mark against the game. You are required to use the turrets to shoot things and placing turrets is actually quite difficult. They tip over too easy, self-destruct, and you can hardly control your rage when you are trying to do the right thing and can not.
Anyway, overall, this game deserves huge marks. Valve should hire the individuals that made this game to devise a genuine Portal 3, though this game almost serves as Portal 3 already. It's puzzles are top notch, it's story is quite captivating, the voice acting is excellent, and the overall production values are amazing.
Anyone who likes Portal even a little should get this game and enjoy it to the fullest.

I'm not exagerating when I say that this is one of the best games I have played in a long time. From beginning to end I felt as if I had been transported back in time for another shot at some of my childhood gaming feels. The graphics, sounds, music... it is all there to help make Shovel Knight your perfect adventuring experience.
I played through 90% of the game in one siting because I was so enthralled with the gameplay. Though it is a short game, this was a wise choice to retain the charm and character of the game from start to finish, never over-staying its welcome. Shovel Knight is the true ofspring of the old school Megaman and the newer Dark Souls games. With a number of different relics to pick up, armour and weapon to upgrade, and secrets waiting in every corner of every level, there is a lot to do.
Even having finished the game, I've already started my new game+ and am still enjoying it. What is a real treat, having played it so soon after its release (but having been a kickstarter backer), was that very little in the way of story or gameplay was ruined for me before playing it. Even now as I play new game+, I wonder what other secrets await me upon collecting all that there is to collect, and going everywhere there is to go.
I would highly recommend this game. I expect to enjoy this game for many more hours to come and I hope you choose to as well in the name of SHOVEL JUSTICE!!!

Bought this game because it was on sale, is a battle royale, and has a decently big player base. My hope was to find a game that, although I didn't expect to be as good as PUBG, would fill in as a nice alternative at times. As a PUBG fan I tried to go in as unbiased as I could. However comparing it to PUBG from time to time was impossible. From launching off the plane. To running towards the circle. The overall feel and concept made it feel like "Well I should only waste my time playing one of these games."
Positives:
- The game runs well on my set up ~100 fps. 480 rx 8gb, 16 gb ddr4, Ryzen 1600x. About as well as you can hope for a game of such graphics.
-  I liked the cosmetics of weapons and apparel. There's a lot you can unlock.
- I liked that there was a game mode where you can spawn with big weapons. I prefer spawning with nothing but it's a nice change up from time to time.
- The rank up system is nice coming from a game like PUBG where you don't get rewarded much for your play. And they always reset your stats.
Negatives:
- The first thing that struck me was the graphics. The game looks incredibly dated. Although not a game breaker for me it affected the feel of the game.
- The shooting and sounds felt very meh. The driving is absolutely terrible. Incredibly stiff steering and wacky drifting. The overall game play feels like its lacking as a whole.
- Due inpart to what I said above, the atmosphere just lacks the thrill you get from a game like PUBG. The fear of dying at any second.
Final thoughts:
The game felt much like a free to play, more fast paced PUBG. Perhaps if I had played this before PUBG I would've had a different outlook. If you have a below average PC I might recommend this to you on sale. As PUBG will probably be not enjoyable for you due to the graphical demands of the game. If you have a average or higher I'd say just save up/buy  PUBG. As the games are similar to the point you most likely will only want to waste time playing one or the other. If you have PUBG like I do, Don't waste your time or money on this game. I myself have refunded already
Edit: Scratch that if you have a below average pc, just go with Fortnite. It's free anyways.

Incredibly fun, and a good challenge. The game itself is a wonderful homage to the 16bit era, and plays amazingly well. If you're a fan of the retro, adventure type games (think combining Super Mario World, Link's Adventure, and some MegaMan style platforming) then I certainly recommend it. The boss fights are tremendously fun and quite the challenge, but not in a cheap or unfair way. The music makes me weep tears of joy, it is some of the best chiptune I have ever heard.
The amount of jokes and references to other internet trends and subcultures is amazing and hilarious. There are jokes ranging from poking fun at Dark Souls, to Team Fortress 2's hat obsession, and even jabbing at the crowd-funding games.
The only thing I don't really like is how easy it becomes to level up your health after the first few bosses. I had a ton of health before finishing the second set of bosses, and it makes the game far less difficult.
Pros:
Amazing platforming
Challenging but Fair Combat
God-like music.
Charming jokes and references
Fun "encounter" sequences
Cons:
Can increase max health very quickly/easily
Difficulty may turn some people off
I don't recommend the use of the keyboard, it's easier to use a controller

is a masterwork of a game, and a quintessential specimen of its genre. There is a perfect balance of pragmatism and ludicrousness inherent to each and every aspect of the game. The mosaic of realistic and ridiculous themes is expertly crafted into one of the most enjoyable games in existence, let alone in the sandbox genre. All but the most extremely discerning gamers should be able to enjoy it.
One of the first features of
that will jump out at you is the fact it is full of preposterous themes, demonstrated not only in the narrative and atmospheric elements, but also the gameplay itself. And so, you definitely aren't supposed to approach this game seriously. That becomes painfully obvious once you learn that you can hop out of a speeding jet and crash face first into the middle of a city with no parachute... only to bounce up and run down the street naked, caving in people's skulls with giant purple sex toys.
Yet despite being a heavy-handed and purposeful parody of itself, the narrative of the game is actually entertaining and logically sensible (by that I mean it adheres to the logic of the gameworld, not real life). And the ludicrousness doesn’t ever get so totally out of hand that it starts to feel like a
game; there is always some semblance of a purpose and direction.
is a good example of how a game doesn’t have to be serious, but also can have an entertaining and somewhat logical narrative.
There is also a number of factors which add a significant layer of customization, progression, and statistics to the game— all of which contribute to increasing the overall
of the experience. For one, there is a wide range of customizing ability, from your character to your vehicles. Many hours can be spent just changing the theme of your gang. There is also a system of XP and level progression, which is uncommon in the genre, but synthesizes perfectly in
. You can use your level-ups to customize certain abilities of your character, and if you devote enough time, you can eventually make yourself invincible purely through the level system (not cheats/codes).
Furthermore, the gameworld in
is a very enjoyable sandbox to play in, and there is a lot of potential for riotous fun to be had. The gameworld is large enough to be interesting, but not so large it becomes a burden to traverse. To keep you busy between campaign missions, there are dozens of side-missions of various gameplay styles which add pleasant diversity. Outside the primary and secondary missions, there are numerous minigames and challenges (stunting, base jumping, racing, streaking, etc.) which all contribute to creating an environment where you can spend hours of gameplay just messing around and having fun, without actively pursuing missions or progressing the game.
And another amazing feature of this game is the ability to play the actual campaign in co-op mode.  Instead of just messing around in the sandbox with friends, you can actually beat the game together.
There is also a lot of DLC, which ranges from cosmetic additions to full-blown extra campaigns. I would say it is definitely worth it to get the GOTY edition right from the start.

I just finished the game a few minutes ago (it took me around a week to finish), and boy was it a good experience.
...Anyway, let's get down the nitty-gritty.
Graphics: The game looked great and I loved all the custom assets, like the portal gun (that paperclip tho)
Voice-Acting: While the voice acting had a few hiccups I liked it for the most part. The Cave Johnson impression sounded pretty off but I liked Virgil and AEGIS' voices.
Music: Harry outdid himself with this man! I loved all the tracks, they felt like something made by the official Portal 2 sound team. Great job!
Puzzles: Really difficult puzzles designed to force you to look outside the box. These aren't your normal Portal test chambers! Some tests actually had me saying to myself, "that was really clever!" after they were over.
Story: This was obviously one of the main focuses for this game. Good writing that made me care about Virgil and Mel. And boy oh boy was that ending good. I'd go as far to say this is almost on par with the main Portal series!
Price: It's free. IT'S FREE.
Verdict: I'd say this is about on par with Portal 2 in almost every way. And the best part? It's free if you own Portal 2!

Im sorry, this wont be the review you will be looking for. Instead, it will be the best pie recipe you will ever learn.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Shovel Knight feels like a late 80s/early 90s NES classic that went under the radar all these years, a game that combined what worked from its peers with its own focused approach to game design and flow and pushed both the NES and game design of the time to their limits. Except, it came out in 2014, but it's every bit as authentic in its heart and focus as you would expect from a true classic. It is completely self-absorbed in its own bubble of influences.
It's action platforming at its tightest, finest tuning. Obstacles are methodical, everything is recognizable, nothing is irrelevant. These levels resemble the kind of methodical level design seen in the likes of Mega Man 2 and 3, whereas the gameplay resembles the careful position-based melee combat of Zelda 2, combined with the platforming approach seen in Ducktales, where enemies often become platforms and movement in combat and movement in platforming often merge together seamlessly.
Don't be fooled by the fantasy setting, this has absolutely no RPG elements aside from an increasing life bar and magic bar (not unlike The Legend of Zelda). Weapon, armor upgrades, and items are designed to expand your options, not make you better at something. Expanding your inventory expands your options on how to approach both enemies and levels, and the brilliant level-design shines at accommodating these added options while at the same time making it possible to finish without them. Some movement items change the way you look at how blocks and enemies are placed, revealing shortcuts and ways to move through the screen that werent there before. It all works.
The game communicates its dangers well, and punishes you for not paying attention, but perhaps its punishment is not enough. Checkpoints are plentiful, there are infinite lives, and your health bar can take quite a beating before you go down, and a certain item in the game breaks it completely beyond repair (you'll know it when you see it), it's not as challenging as you would expect, given its influences. Later stages are designed to set up careful traps and lead you to mistakes, just like in Castlevania, but the punishment just isn't there.
That said, the selection of achievements/feats is above average, containing challenge runs of many kinds and a speedrun achievement that's bound to give anyone a hard (but fun) time, so it does have its challenges.
I could go on forever about the game, but instead I'll end it here and say that this is an excellent game, a time capsule to simpler times in gaming that doesn't just take things from the classics, it stands shoulder-to-shoulder with them.
With no walls of text to read through, or cinematic cutscenes to slog through, this is a very packed and fun game, a joyful adventure that speaks to you through its well crafted levels and designs like only a video game can do, a video game down to its core.

Duck Tales meets Megaman meets Castlevania with a Mario 3 overworld. What isn't to love?
I mean honestly, if the above doesn't sound good to you, then this game probably isn't for you.
For those a bit more on the fence, I suppose I'll elaborate a bit:
In Shovel Knight, you play the titular knight in a battle against the Order of No Quarter. To do so, you travel to various stages and, in classic Megaman style, travel right while fighting enemies, platforming, and finding secrets.
Throughout the level, you gather up Gems and Coins either outright, via slain enemies, or via secrets and chests, in order to gain Gold, which you can spend at the Village on various Health and Armor upgrades or items.
Your shovel is your main weapon, with the ability to outright smack your enemies or pogo on them ala Duck Tales, and similarly can be used against blocks of various types of dirt and/or rock to traverse the screens.
Items work similarly to Castlevania, with a limited resource that drains every time you use it (in Shovel Knight, it's pots, as opposed to Castlevania's hearts), though in Shovel Knight you gain the item permanently and can swap between them at your leisure. Even within the first 3 main stages, the selection of items you get is large enough to accomodate a variety of playstyles and strategies.
The bosses and stages themselves are very remniscient of Megaman, with each stage having a particular theme carried out that matches the Boss. The Bosses themselves have a nice variety of attacks and pattern that, although at first are hard, can be read and manipulated, just like Megaman. Enemy types vary from neat and strange, like the helicopter-rat thing, to fairly standard fare, like the 2spooky skeleton. The music is always wonderfully fitting, and creating a sense of mood and enhancing all of the stages without being distracting.
Movement feels good. Controls are responsive. Hitboxes don't feel wonky.
In essence, this game is great.
If you agreed with the first sentence, you probably already have the game.
If you hate retro and/or have terrible taste, you probably weren't gonna get this game anyway.
If you're interested, but worried $15 is a little steep, let me assure you that based off of the 3 main stages I've played so far and the size of the overworld map, that you are in for a decent amount of gameplay. Moreso if you want to replay anything, which you most likely will. It's absolutely worth it.

As of late, a lot of games have been released which are trying to recreate the feel of games from the NES/SNES era. Some of them are quite good, while most of them don't quite hit the mark. Shovel Knight doesn't belong in either of these categories. It belongs in the category of "nailed it". Upon starting up Shovel Knight (which I had been waiting for for a very, very long time), I was hit by music that reminded me of the music I heard in games I played as a kid. Progressing through the game, the rest of the music got even better, one of the tunes still stuck in my head after I put the game down. Music isn't the only thing the game has going for it, though.
The graphics look just like you'd expect a game inspired by the NES/SNES era to look like: pixelly, and gorgeous. The backgrounds are beautiful, the enemy designs are awesome, and the boss designs are absolutely incredible. The gameplay is tough at times, but the controls are good enoug hthat with a bit of practice, the tough areas can be conquered with ease. The dialogue is hilarious at times (there's an NPC that you can interact with solely for puns), and at other times it can be pretty cheesy. There's plenty to do even after you unlock everything from the shops (collecting the different songs, collecting all relics, New Game+, etc.).
With that all said, that doesn't mean there aren't a couple things I didn't like. The lack of shovel upgrades, for example, is rather disappointing. However, these small qualms are very much shadowed by all the positives that hte game offers. Having already beat Shovel Knight the first time through, I can say I'm already prepared to hop back into New Game+ and continue the adventure. Even after that, there's still perfecting each stage and boss.
Through all of that, I'd say that Shovel Knight is definitely worth the $15 and you should pick it up as soon as you possibly can if you were even remotely interested in it. Any fan of platformers (especially Mega Man) will adore this gem.
To sum it up in just three words: I dig it.

Like another reviewer wrote, "I went in thinking that it wouldn't be like a portal game, but just another palyer mod", and so did I.  However, I completed the game and thought that I played half of a real portal game.
Portal Stories: Mel, is basically a game that is hard to say when it is set due to spoilers possible, but it has the feel of being somewhere in between 1 and 2, or before 1.   Anyway, this review will be short since there is not a whole lot to say, but there is important things to point out.
The Good:
+   It actually feels like a Portal game.  The music, the ambience, the characters, the puzzles, they feel like something that came right out of a Portal game.
+  Actually challening puzzles.  Unlike Portal 1, the challenges start of easy, but then get tricky and then get flatout, hard.  Yes logic will always guide you, but sometimes you have to think 'What is it that I want to do, what is it that I can do, what is it that needs to be done, what is it that does not need to be done", and that will help you.  Various tricks will be reused, but the key is attempting to tie them together.
+  Enjoyable story.   The story is straight forward, not many major plot twists, but its great.
+  The music.  The music, it fits, perfectly.  No other way of putting it.
+  It's free.  You could be a Janitor on 4ch@n, and still be able to afford this.  You do not even need Portal 1 or 2 to play this mod.
The Bad
+  It's pretty short.  It took me about 10 hours, but I was messing around about an hour worth and left my computer afk for a while too, but remove that, and I would say that it would take about a solid 6-7 hours.  If you do a speed run with perfect exection, then 2 hours is about right, but thats ignoring achievements and other things.
+  The ending was nice but it felt like there could have been a possible hint for future things, but it just kind of ended.  Still good, but felt empty.
Overall:  If you enjoyed Portal 1 & 2, then you should like this.  It has all the things Portal games have.  I think it even has one extra liquid, water, that is added which helps to clean things, but I might be wrong.  Anyway, if you have about 6 or 7 hours to burn, then give this game a shot. An amazingly high quality mod considering it was made by a small team of (very dedicated) people, and a brilliant tribute to the Portal series. The visuals and props are of Valve quality, the (lore friendly) writing is mostly great, and the voice acting and music are good. Exploring even more of Aperture was a real treat, and perhaps you see even more of it than you do in the original games (but it's a shame it's not canon).
The only thing is that the puzzle difficulty is sky high. (E: 09/15 - Or at least they were before the new Story Mode came out, reducing puzzle difficulty.) I found the (advanced mode) puzzles fun because I'm familiar with Portal 2 and I like a challenge. Beating them was its own reward though (along with progressing further with the story), and they only use mechanics that the mod introduces to you, or ones that are covered in Portal 1 and 2, so at least the puzzles are fair (so long as you remember all of the mechanics), but I had to use a walkthrough for hints twice.
It is still a brilliant mod though, and well worth looking at if you're a Portal fan.

Calling all adventure enthusiasts, nostalgia freaks, and thirsty gamers! The spaded warrior has arrived! Shovel Knight is a wonderful example of video game love flourishing. The game sports tight controls, unique and intuitive mechanics, and a fair, yet tantalizing difficulty curve. As Shovel Knight, you will have to traverse difficult dungeons to face even tougher bosses. Over all, the game is nearly flawless. In my first 8 hours of play I have never encountered a scenario where the game was at fault for my fumbles; Shovel Knight was painstakingly designed to make sure that the only contributing factors to error are your own, be it your reflexes or a lack of mastery over the game's mechanics. Dynamically, Shovel Knight delivers, with unique and refreshing challenges around every corner for the player to overcome. Finally, Shovel Knight is flawless in its Aesthetics, with Famitracker-composed music that can play on an actual Famicom, and NES-inspired graphics that achieve the nostalgic appearance while taking advantage of new technology. Shovel Knight is definitely a must-play for any fans of old games, and for fans of new as well. Make sure you unearth this gem for yourself!

Rozpoczeła poniekąd moją przygodę z grami RPG, i od mniej więcej 11 lat jest pozycją po którą ze względu na multum modyfikacji, i bardzo klimatycznego świata sięgam. Warto także wspomnieć, że nie przyjeła się aż tak dobrze za oceanem, jak w Polsce, Niemczech czy Rosji, gdzie produkcja ta podbiła serca wielu graczy.

Akcja gry przenosi nas do świata niezwykle brutalnego i niebezpiecznego. Król prowadzi wojnę z wieloletnim i potężnym wrogiem-Orkami. Zdobywali oni coraz to większe tereny, rabując i niszcząc wszytko na swojej drodze. Jedyną nadzieją dla rodzaju ludzkiego były złoża magicznej rudy. Kruszcu, który to pozwalał na wykuwanie oręża, zdołającego przeciwstawić się Orkom. I to właśnie jej król Rhobar II nakazał za wszelką cenę bronić przed najeźdźcą. W tym celu wysłał 12 najpotężniejszych magów królestwa, w celu otoczenia najważniejszego miejsca wydobycia Magiczną Barierą, która to zabezpieczyłaby je przed wrogiem, a niewolnikom wydobywającym kruszec, uniemożliwiła ucieczkę. Jednak procedura tworzenia magicznej kopuły wymknęła się spod kontroli zamykając magów w ich własnej pułapce razem z więźniami i gwardią królewską. Skazańcy pod przywództwem Gomeza szybko wykorzystali nadarzającą się sytuacje, buntując się przeciwko strażnikom. Szybko zajmują zamek, wprowadzając w nim własne prawa i porządki. Król, będąc bezradny w tej sytuacji musiał rozpocząć pertraktacje z Gomezem i jego ludźmi, toteż w zamian za comiesięczne dostawy dóbr z zewnątrz, dostawał kolejne ładunki Magicznej Rudy, która to była mu przecież niezmiernie potrzebna.
Jednak nie wszyscy więźniowie podzielali decyzje Gomeza i jego ludzi, opuszczając zamek, i tworząc własne społeczności. I właśnie w takim świecie dane będzie nam prowadzić rozgrywkę. Sami zdecydujemy, po której stronie się opowiedzieć. W miarę czasu będziemy odkrywać coraz to większe tajemnice kolonii karnej i robić wszystko, aby kiedyś się z niej wydostać narażając się tym samym na wiele niebezpieczeństw.

Shovel knight came out today, and I could honestly say that I was really excited. I wanted to be challenged by something that was brutal, but more importantly fair. Shovel knight is based off of the early NES games like Zelda 2, Super Mario Brothers 3, Megaman, and lots of other games. Unfortunately, the game does not live up to the “Brutal but Fair”. There are moments in the game where I died due to something that was not in my hands. There were moments where the game throws some serious bull♥♥♥♥♥♥at you. Another thing that also pisses me off is the spikes. Sure it makes sense that I would die instantaneously if so much as a pixel on my body touched some lava, but dying instantly by lightly grazing a spike is a whole new story. Plus, combine this with the relatively poor variety in enemies; you have a recipe for a relatively average experience. And deep down that’s what Shovel Knight really boils down to.  Shovel Knight seems to snap out of the matrix though when we reach the boss battles. The greatest thing about the boss battles is that you literally have to “TRY”. There’s no lollygagging’ when you’re here. The boss fights are a true challenge, and every failure is caused because you made a mistake, not because of a cheap spike cop-out for lazy programming. Because I died very so often in the later stages it was really lovely to see a checkpoint system in this game. It works incredibly well, and it’s good to see that they chose this rather than a lives system where you have to start the stage over. Instead, your punishment is similar to dark souls, where you lose your in-game currency when you die. Like dark souls, you can go back and pick the loot back up after you die. Speaking of dark souls, this is probably the one game that gets the closest to being as fair as dark souls. You see, this game did what Dark Souls 2 did not. It brought clever level design, great boss battles, and some relatively fair gameplay along with an incredible soundtrack as well as a great over world and an amazingly simple but charming story. I would probably give this game a 7/10 if the boss battles weren’t so ♥♥♥♥ing awesome, but because of the boss battles, the diversity in stages, and awesome music and story, I give Shovel Knight an 8/10. You see there are games that try all too hard to be like other games, we saw this with Castlevania: Lords of Shadow and that game did not do it right at all. However, Shovel Knight may be something we’ve seen many times all those years ago, but deep down Shovel Knight knew what it wanted to be. Shovel Knight is a homage to old school retro gaming. The game is definitely worth your attention. Watch some gameplay videos on it; I’m sure most of you will find yourself buying the game.

For what is otherwise a very slick and well-done mod, it’s unfortunate that the test chamber design is so lacking.  This is not a knock against the “difficulty” of the chambers, but rather a knock against the way they are made difficult.
Portal, like every other video game, contains a number of player-aids that help make the game friendlier.  Portals are self-centering.  Excursion funnels will tunnel in items from their edges.  Lost cubes are regenerated at their spawn points.  These are small things that help make the game less frustrating and all-around more enjoyable, by accepting intent and forgiving imperfect execution.
Portal Stories: Mel frequently uses these player-aids as test chamber solutions.  One test requires using successive excursion funnels placed close together to move a cube towards the player.  A number of other tests require the player to request a new cube in order to tactically destroy the other.  This is counter-intuitive, because these are never things you would do in the Portal universe.  You are expected to work within the confines of the test, not exploit portions of the game’s design.
The mod also has a fondness for emancipation grids.  It’s not unusual to see at least four or more in a single test chamber, some controllable by buttons, lasers, or switches.  They force the player to “juggle” portals and cubes around them, often an exercise in tediousness itself.  Many of the chambers would have been just as difficult without these emancipation grids, but with the added benefits of being much less tedious and much more fun.
Perhaps the worst quality of the test chamber design is that it tries to “trick” the player into finding solutions that do not exist, and punishes players for experimenting.  One test chamber has a very prominent blue gel pipe for getting to a higher area, but no switch to turn it on.  Another allows the player to extend a light bridge to the exit, but puts an emancipation grid between the ever-necessary cube and the player.  Unlike the original games, the mod also allows players to get “stuck” in an area if they make an incorrect choice, where the only solution is to reload or commit suicide.  All of this is made worse by the fact that many event triggers are obscure, with the connection lines either hidden or poorly marked.
All around, this makes for a frustrating game that feels like it’s trying too hard to make itself difficult, rather than challenging the player to try something new.  Though the story is well done, the test chamber design kills this mod long before it gets on its feet.

A lot of games ATTEMPT to do the whole "Retro" thing, but few actually succeed. This game is one of them.
Graphics;
The game looks just as good in motion as it does in any of the screenshots with great designs and fantastic pixel art. What I love most is the fact that the game isn't held back by any of the palette or sprite limitations one might put upon themselves when developing a game in the style of an NES classic.
Sound:
Without a doubt the music and sound is completely evocative of those old Capcom and Konami classics. From what I could tell this part is actually rather close to being able to run on that old 80's hardware. Obviously, there's not gonna be any competetion for audio channels between music and sound effects, but I really wouldn't be surprised if the soundtrack were totally doable on an NES cart (perhaps with one of those later model sound-chips).
Gameplay:
The game was smartly designed to not just emulate the mechanics of a single game or genre and instead grab elements and ideas from several of the era's best titles. You've got a Mario-3-like overworld, with Mega Man style stages and Bosses. You have an inventory of subweapons and a primary attack with just enough delay on it to take you right back to Castlevania. And hey, how about the pogo stick hop from Duck Tales just for good measure? It's a game that's hard but not too hard with some very clever enemy and stage design.

This game is basically a Portal 3. Not only does it have the length of a portal game (~10 hours), but it also has an outstanding script and voice actors. I feel that Valve should recognize this mod as an official tie-in between Portal and Portal 2.
- Very challenging and interesting puzzles
- Phenomenal voice acting and script
- Ties in great with both Portal and Portal 2
- Exceptional custom textures and storyline
- Music is good and similar to that of Portal 2
- Pre-rendered cutscenes are interesting and are inserted in all the right areas
- Secret achievements are humorous and fun to get
- Somewhat laggy in some areas. Probably just my own computers fault, though.
- Some places in the game have that "find where to place the portal", which isn't my favorite thing in the world, but is mostly just a nitpick
- Steep learning curve in the second half of the game
Overall, Portal Stories: Mel is a fantastic mod that I would recommend to anyone who is a fan of the Portal series. Prism Studios seems to have nailed every aspect of this game to fit the structure of past Portal games. While there are places in the game that can be very frustrating, it is an amazing experience overall.

Seriously very good game. You're doing yourself a disservice by not playing this right now.
R6:S unfortunately has flown under the radar for it's first year or two because of serious crash to desktop bugs that plagued launch.
I say unfortunately because the studio has managed to rectify those issues as well as numerous quality of life issues which has resulted in a game that is VERY worthwhile of your attention. R6:S can be played as an arcadey shooter OR as an intense highly coordinated competitive shooter. Between casual and ranked, group or solo play, there is no wrong way to play R6:S. Just relax and watch your killcams to help learn new tricks all the time.
R6:S has what you could call multiplicative gameplay. Just another way of saying there is lots of variation in experience between every match you play. This is great b/c it keeps you thinking and keeps experiences changing.
There are a lot of wonderfully detailed and crafted maps in R6:S already. Each map is packed with attack angles that change from destruction via explosives or creative hole punching in walls, windows and barricades. Each round randomly places the objectives in a handful of preset locations for even more variation within that one map. Furthermore, each operator brings unique ways to attack or defend the objective.
These components result in a very large variety of outcomes per match. With the season expansions bringing both new maps and new operators each quarter of the year, the game continues to expand and evolve. Even with all of the forward motion brought by the game direction, they continuously have been fixing important things like balance, op low pick frequencies, netcode, bugs AND performance.
So really, if you're curious and have watched some lets plays or live streams and like what you see then it is probably time to scout for your local steam sale and take the plunge. This ocean is deep and vast but don't be scared!

Gothic 1 to gra, którą darzę niesamowitym sentymentem. Rozpoczeła poniekąd moją przygodę z grami RPG, i od mniej więcej 11 lat jest pozycją po którą ze względu na multum modyfikacji, i bardzo klimatycznego świata sięgam. Warto także wspomnieć, że nie przyjeła się aż tak dobrze za oceanem, jak w Polsce, Niemczech czy Rosji, gdzie produkcja ta podbiła serca wielu graczy.
Zarys fabularny.
Akcja gry przenosi nas do świata niezwykle brutalnego i niebezpiecznego. Król prowadzi wojnę z wieloletnim i potężnym wrogiem-Orkami. Zdobywali oni coraz to większe tereny, rabując i niszcząc wszytko na swojej drodze. Jedyną nadzieją dla rodzaju ludzkiego były złoża magicznej rudy. Kruszcu, który to pozwalał na wykuwanie oręża, zdołającego przeciwstawić się Orkom. I to właśnie jej król Rhobar II nakazał za wszelką cenę bronić przed najeźdźcą. W tym celu wysłał 12 najpotężniejszych magów królestwa, w celu otoczenia najważniejszego miejsca wydobycia Magiczną Barierą, która to zabezpieczyłaby je przed wrogiem, a niewolnikom wydobywającym kruszec, uniemożliwiła ucieczkę. Jednak procedura tworzenia magicznej kopuły wymknęła się spod kontroli zamykając magów w ich własnej pułapce razem z więźniami i gwardią królewską. Skazańcy pod przywództwem Gomeza szybko wykorzystali nadarzającą się sytuacje, buntując się przeciwko strażnikom. Szybko zajmują zamek, wprowadzając w nim własne prawa i porządki. Król, będąc bezradny w tej sytuacji musiał rozpocząć pertraktacje z Gomezem i jego ludźmi, toteż w zamian za comiesięczne dostawy dóbr z zewnątrz, dostawał kolejne ładunki Magicznej Rudy, która to była mu przecież niezmiernie potrzebna.
Jednak nie wszyscy więźniowie podzielali decyzje Gomeza i jego ludzi, opuszczając zamek, i tworząc własne społeczności. I właśnie w takim świecie dane będzie nam prowadzić rozgrywkę. Sami zdecydujemy, po której stronie się opowiedzieć. W miarę czasu będziemy odkrywać coraz to większe tajemnice kolonii karnej i robić wszystko, aby kiedyś się z niej wydostać narażając się tym samym na wiele niebezpieczeństw.

For a moment just picture our favorite Blue Bomber Megaman from the NES era. Now replace his Buster Gun with a Shovel Blade, swap out his armor for some plate mail, slap 2 dirty great big horns on his helm and you have yourself the glorious Shovel Knight. After a minor delay (which felt like forever) Shovel Knight has blessed us with its 8-bit grandeur.
I truly dig the game from its 66 piece color palette to its beautiful NES style audio. Its not the most difficult platformer in the world so newbies shouldn't have much trouble but the experienced platform gamer will still find it rather satisfying to play. The controls are simple, easy to learn and reasonably responsive, the level and boss design are awesome and the story is...ahh...so so... But in Shovel Knight's defence, it's more about the gameplay and thats where it shines most brightly.
To sum it all up, Shovel Knight is sure to please anyone who enjoyed NES gaming as a past time, because it takes the best parts of some real classics while still feeling fresh and unique. This review is rather brief but I honestly just want to venture back into gaming history and slay some more Order of No Quarter!

Frictional Games seems to possess the oft-sought-after ability to make a game truly frightening. Using the same talents that produced their Penumbra trilogy, Frictional has honed and tweaked their craft, creating Amnesia: a horror game that instills more fear in me than any other horror game I've played.
The fact that I spend most of the game creeping around corners, afraid of what I might stumble into (or what might stumble into me) is a testament to Frictional's understanding of what is scary: I can honestly tell you that there are moments in the game where I felt genuine fright. The game is well polished, the environments are beautful, and the sound is incredible. Combine this with Frictional's exceptional understanding of what makes a world eery and uncomfotable, and you've got a superb survival horror game.
So, if you're a fan of horror, I highly recommend turning off all the lights, turning up the volume, and delving into Amnesia: it's a horror game that you won't soon forget.

It's way better than I expected. I expected something cheap and short but it feels a bit like it was made by Valve. The voice acting, dialogues and humor are really good and feel exactly like Portal 2. When I saw the title "Mel" I thought it would be based on the prequel idea to Portal called "F-Stop", but it isn't.
It starts looking cheap, re-using Half-Life 2 models, having ugly environment and a Cave Johnson with a different voice actor, but once you get to the testing chambers it's as beautiful as Portal 2 was, feels like the maps were made by professional Valve employees. The game is also pretty long, even longer than the first Portal, and with the puzzles being harder adds more lenght.
The only thing I hate about this game is that puzzles are often badly made. Portal wall and floor positions being inaccurate or the game requiring some really good reflexes and control when in the original portal games it was made so it would be perfectly accurate so that you don't die because your portal was a bit too high. Here you have to force your way into the portals and it's frustrating, and you'll often lose your boxes when trying to portal with them. The is also some useless backtracking at the beggining but it gets better.
Pros :
-Atmosphere exactly like Portal 2
-Great voice acting and usual humor
-Great soundtrack
-Way longer than expected
-Virgil, a new core that talks to you through the game with a personality similar to Wheatley
-It's free
Cons :
-Inaccurate portal walls position
-White walls and floors are hard to find
-First chapter
-Nothing new except a red forcefield that kills you if you try to pass through it

if you enjoyed any of the following, you will likely enjoy this game:
-mega man series
-ducktales (nes)
-super mario bros. 3
-zelda II: the adventure of link.
a veritable love letter to all four and then some, the game features solid gameplay that teaches you through gameplay and not tutorials, a downright boss ost accented by the original mega man 1 composer (!!!), and a goofy, cheesy story that'll at least make you roll your eyes and grin, if nothing else. while i reference the four above as reference material, the game actually plays fairly uniquely and has its own strengths (and weaknesses) by comparison--it's a rare gem among others of its kind that shines in its ability to utilize its tools for its own sake rather than relying on parody and mockery to do its job for it--it's a game that's genuinely fun, rather than only being fun because it makes you think about the fun you had playing the games it takes its cues from.
the game took me about 8-9 hours to complete--rather impressive for an nes-style indie game--and there's a new game+ mode that will probably take a little longer due to increased difficulty. there are also codes you can use to make the game easier/harder/sillier, if you're into that. my main complaints are mainly in difficulty spikes--some areas/bosses are far harder than others, and it can feel a lot like the difficulty takes a sudden dip or jump depending on where you are. i personally had lots of trouble in some of the later stages only to beat the bosses barely getting touched, if at all. the price point may also be an issue for some--$15 isn't terribly cheap, and though i feel the game is worth it for its polish, you might do well waiting for it to inevitably go on sale if you're not sure you'd enjoy it.
all in all, this is a game that has the look of a classic and the feel of a well-constructed platformer--if you enjoy platformers at all, you're missing out if you skip over this game.

After playing the game for 2 hours or so, here are my thoughts:
The developers behind this game "get" what makes a good 2D platform actually GOOD.
+ Responsive controls
+ Stages with diverse hazards in accordance to their theme
+ Memorable boss fights
+ Awesome music
On top of this, they added:
+ A checkpoint system that is both good for beginners and experts alike (for different reasons)
+ Instead of having a finite amount of tries before you get kicked out of a long stage, you lose an amount of your wealth that is retrievable, if you can reach the screen where you died (think Dark Souls)
+ Towns, vendors, minigames, sidequests, upgradable armor and special moves
My only "problem" so far is that with a system that offers you an infinite amount of retries and a very forgiving checkpoint system, they decided to add refillable potions that top up your health and mana to the max and some other stuff that are fairly OP (IMHO, always).
But, given that the developers intended the game to be accessible to beginners and experts alike, the latter can freely choose not to use them (there are also achievements if you don't die at all, break all the checkpoints in the game, don't buy anything with money etc. so for people who crave to be challenged there are plentiful of ways to get their fix).
There's also official word for free content released at a later date such as challenge mode, gender reverse mode, battle mode with the order of no quarter and 3 playable boss campaigns.
tl;dr Just buy it already!

I have been playing this game since it's original android release back in 2009,
and I can tell you with the utmost honesty that it is one of the best tower defense games that I have ever played.
Even 5 years after its original android release, this game still continues to provide great entertainment for myself and many others.
The basic premise of this game is to stop zombies that are invading your yard from reaching your house.
To do this, you need to plant different kinds of plants that you get as you complete each level in the plots around your garden.
The game consists of 5 worlds with 10 levels in each that get harder as you progress, introducing new zombies with new mechanics that means you're forced to choose what the best plants for stopping them are.
Like I mentioned a few sentences up, you get new plants as you progress, this happens as you complete the levels.
Every time you complete a level you get a new plant...unless ofcourse the story needs progressing in some way, then you get an item for that progression.
Their are (in total) 53 different plants & 39 different zombies that all each have there own unique attributes to the gameplay.
All zombies and plants have their own stats, some are strong and some are weak...and some are even suicidal.
Zombies all have unique items that they will be wearing/carrying/using etc.
Some are fast, some slow & some even dance across your yard!
As for plants, they are all unique aswell, in both physical appearance and stats.
Some plants will be more powerful than others, some will shoot peas and some will explode.
But the important thing is that they get the job done!
I personally have taken (on my quickest speedrun of this game) about 6 to 7 hours, just to complete the main story.
And that isnt even a third of the game! When you've completed that, there are actually 3 extra unlockable sections in the main menu called "Mini-Games", "Puzzle" & "Survival", each of which put there own twist on the main gameplay such as making the zombies tiny so theyre faster, or having a bunch of pots in your yard that could have anything from peashooters to gargantuars in them, and giving you an endless wave after wave game of zombies that never ends!
I would say without a doubt that if you like tower defenses and you don't already own this game then you need to get it.

Jesus Christ this game is polarising for me. On the one hand, the people behind it did an amazing job and will without a doubt have bright futures in game design. On the other hand, some of the puzzles are absolute horse pucky, and if you stuff something up, you CANNOT restart the chamber like you can in Portal 1 & 2. So if you stuff up, you can't just restart the chamber. Nope, you'll have to go back to either wherever the last auto-save was or your own manual save. So yeah, that really sucks.
Visually stunning, an audible delight and very well designed and animated this mod is, but gameplay-wise, it will make your head hurt to the point where you might not even care anymore about finishing it. Some of the puzzles are mind-numbingly frustrating. For instance there's Chamber 3 in Chapter 4; lord is this one absurd. I watched Harry101UK's (one of the developer's) playthrough of this chamber where he showed a little trick/shortcut to help bypass it. Unfortunately, I, a player, did not know this trick.
Here's the thing, Harry: If the player doesn't do this "shortcut" as you showed, how are they supposed to do it the "correct" way as supposedly designed? Because at that very point of the puzzle, because I didn't do the shortcut, I found myself utterly stranded with no way of finishing it. That's pretty bad level design right there. And like I said earlier, I can't try again from the start of the chamber.
This mod is really well made for the most part, but it is far from player-friendly and some of the puzzles are ill-designed.
Prepare for migranes.

PSM is excellent! The creators have designed a well thought out game,  balancing the puzzles and plot which fits perfectly into the portal universe.
...  But you won't casually stroll through it! This game is tricky, the puzzles require thought,  but there is always a logical solution. Some other reviews are critical of the puzzles stating that they are illogical,  impossible or confusing.  I'd like to address these criticisms:
- PSM doesn't hold your hand,  you are expected to study the test chamber and work out the solution.
- people used to the obvious visual clues and guidance of portal 2 will struggle with this. PSM is a challenge aimed at those who wanted portal 2 to be more test chamber focussed.
- some knowledge of portal mechanics is assumed.  Although there are no crazy 'ninja' sequences,  there are a few cases where there is a tricky ground fling or a manoeuvre which requires some thought and skilled execution.
- many of the tests require you to work 'out of the obvious order'; ie.  You may need to set things up and then place the appropriate portals for it to work.
- an overall theme of the game is backtracking.  You may need to revisit areas in a chamber (or link sequence) several times before competing it (again,  studying the area and understanding each chamber will help).
I would recommend this for anyone looking for a new portal challenge and willing to think through the Chambers.

If this were made in the 80s, it wouldn't be remembered as a classic, it would be that decent-yet-forgettable title that ripped off everything creative around it. This beautifully crafted game features:
-Tight controls: my character moves exactly where I wish him to go. He does not slip and slide around.
-Unique and challenging bosses: This is the element of this game that really REALLY makes me think of old-school gaming. Each boss has a patterned move-set that you must learn to advance. Each boss has a few moments of vulnerability, allowing you to strike out if you're quick enough. Once you defeat them, you will feel that sense of accomplishment (a la Dark Souls, and other old school games).
-Challenging enemies: they're all different. Challenging, but not impossible to blast through once you learn their techniques.
-Challenging platforming: from large gaps, to bouncing off of enemies to reach high ledges, to very narrow landing spots... this game has all of the platforming you could ask for (and more, which I will not spoil).
-Fun music, old-school style midi/"8 bit" music. It was a pleasure to my ears as a child and certainly fits this game's atmosphere.
-RPG-lite elements. Upgrade your health and magic, acquire new spells, acquire money and buy everything!
-Rewarding and challenging exploration: Need I say more? If you want to explore off of the main path to the boss, you will be  put to the test. However, you will also be rewarded!
-Difficult but forgiving gameplay: There are checkpoints. But you may choose to break the checkpoints to make more money and advance your challenge!
-Superb price point. I would gladly pay more than what I did for this. I'll be getting my money's worth and more.
9/10. Get it. Enjoy it.
