I Dig Shovel Knight!
Shovel Knight
PC, Wii U, 3DS
Who will save the day against the Enchantress and the villainous nights of The Order of No Quarter? Shovel Knight, that's who. The blue knight with the Shovel Blade, a weapon so powerful it can not only dispatch a flying rat foe or enemy knight it can also be used as a real shovel. That comes in handy on your quest to rid the land of evil and rescue Shield Knight, your fellow knight and damsel in distress.
Shovel Knight-who should be in Super Smash Bros, he's so darn likable- is the name of the game and the hero you play. The game is reminiscent of older titles, from the obvious copying of Duck Tales' Scrooge McDuck cane jump; level design and boss fights from Mega Man and some level design from Super Mario. One level was like playing Super Mario World so much I nearly laughed. This is not a carbon copy of those game, oh no, this is a game that took in those games and their best attributes and Yacht Club Games, the developer, made their own, sometimes hard to master, platformer action adventure game.
In the style of 8-bit aesthetic, you'll master Shovel Knight's Shovel Blade and his attacks battling the eight evil knights of the The Order of No Quarter, each in their own themed levels. In the end you'll go off to the Tower of Fate to battle their leader the Enchantress. While on your quest you'll find secrets in every level, gain new items, abilities and powers. You'll meet strange new friends and enemies and be reminded of classic games-if you've played them- while beating each of the bad knights.
By performing the Shovel Drop on most of your foes or swatting them away with your Dig Slash you'll counter the threat of sleeping dragons, wizards firing spells at you and tiny rats with propellers stuck to their bodies. Propeller rats might become your favorite enemy like the Mets from Megaman. These rats vary from the not-as-funny-a-concept exploding green rats in the Explodatorium level ruled over by Plague Knight. Enemies aren't just a way to swat away steam, you"ll need them to make certain jumps and reach certain platforms. Shovel Drop gives you a jump boost to reach higher points, this requires you to master where your heading while you take out enemies. If you get good you might take out multiple foes and never touch the ground. Bringing up the rats without rings, the propeller rats in the Flying Machine level of the gentleman jerk Propeller Knight, are good jumping off points. At parts of the level you make your way to far off hard to reach spots by making multiple jumps on their craniums. Oh, do they fall and their tiny propellers fall off. Better than be electrocuted by the flying Jellyfish you can also bounce off of.
Propeller Rat plushie, when will you come out?
Style and substance, the game offers both with levels centered around the bosses you will engage at the end of each of their levels.

This is for those who enjoy extreamely hard and advanced puzzles.
You may find yourself needing to take a moment or contantly making trial and errors to solve them.

When you get stuck, I recommend you keep trying and then only look up the answer as a last resort.
(As your last resort just watch Harry101UK play it. He's one of the creators of this mod)
There's also a lot of detail,
For those that like to take a moment and look at a scenery to the curiosity "I wanna' be over there!"
You may not notice many easter eggs, just the vast ammount of work put into all these areas, which I found amazing.
I encourage you to take the time to look around and see how hard these artists have worked on this mod.
Now for the story,
You need to play Portal 1 and 2 to understand the story obviously. Optional is Half-Life 1 for a reference.
(There are many references actuatally)
Anyway, you'll realize this is a prequel to Portal 2. Even though it is just a mod, I find it very believeable.
As for the voice acting, Cave Johnson sounds spot on. However the core... you may find distasteful.
Overall,
I'm surprised this was a free mod, and I humbly thank the mod creators for this great experience.
Each puzzle took me about a half hour to figure out, each needed a moment for me to focus.
And every instance through the game kept me wanting more.
I applaud you mod creators for this fantastic experience.

POSTED FROM MY "ShadowHatter Mini Reviews" Blog located here
:
THE GOOD:
- Beautiful pixel art style and chiptune music bring nostalgic gamers back to the small bit era.
- Beautifully done Demon’s/Dark Souls mechanic where you lose gold upon death, having only one chance to go back and collect it where you died, but if you die before you collect your gold it’s GONE FOREVER!
- Wonderful Super Mario Bros 3-like map where even random encounters appear (such as stages to collect more gold and such)
- Impressive character/boss/enemy design filled with unique creativity!
- Tough, but fair difficulty.
- Fun and interesting gameplay with interesting Boss mechanics, Castlevania type gameplay elements (such as chicken and “relics”), and fun items to help you progress through the story.
THE BAD:
- The controls on an Xbox 360 pad feel a bit “slippery” at times when moving Shovel Knight, and you may slip whilst trying to do quick moves such as down-shoveling to propel yourself up through areas where you can fall through to your doom.
- Lack of manual save may be annoying, though I guess in this new age it’s all about auto-save.
Keep in mind ladies and gents, this is a special “mini” review as it’s just a first impressions from playing the first few stages, but it was enough for me to know that this was a WORTHY purchase and I’m glad to have been a Kickstarter backer for this game.
FINAL VERDICT: 9/10 (anybody else tired of numbered ratings? any suggestions for a better system?)

My Review Will Be Comparing Portal Stories: Mel and The Game, Portal 2  IN MY OPINION!
====================================================================================
STORY
-General
In Portal 2 the jist of it is you try to escape but GLaDOS awakens and you do some tests wheatley takes over, do some more tests, and then a boss battle.
In Portal Stories: Mel the story goes so much deeper, and you understand what is happening. Even though you are accompanied by a Core he dosent know everything. Which gives the game depth and realism.
-The Ending --- SPOILERS!!!!
In Portal Stories: Mel, the end has the same boss fight BUT when you escape the facility you leave behind your Core Friend, Virgil, breaking the connection you had with him. Which made me cry, IN REAL LIFE D; | The game also ended with a cliffhanger that makes you miss your companion.
In Portal 2, the game ends with a boss fight, a single tense moment, and then a chorus. There is no cliffhanger, or anything that leads you to want to play the next game.
====================================================================================
GRAPHICS
In Portal Stories: Mel, the graphics are the same as Valve games, BUT has tons of details you wont find in the Portal franchise
In Portal 2, the graphics are great but there are none of the details that you put thought into, which for Valve is suprising!
====================================================================================
PUZZLES
The puzzles in Portal Stories: Mel are quite challenging, which I appreciate Quality over Quantity. Each puzzle has its own variables and its own way to connect to the story.
In Portal 2 you spend little time on tons of tests, and most test's have absolutely no connection to the story, and act more as a filler.
====================================================================================
WORLD
In Portal Stories: Mel, the world has a more open feel, on several mission's you can explore around and see things from different angles. You can move around on catwalks and see previous tests, which makes the world feel more open.
In Portal 2, the world is mostly restricted to test chambers, or puzzles. While few times do you walk around tests and do things out of the test chambers. And when you do, it is strictly on catwalks or in areas that hardly contribute to the story.
====================================================================================
THE GAMES
-The Titles
In Portal Stories: Mel, the title quickly explains the perspective, and  leaves room for many more games in different perspectives.
In Portal 2, the title acts as the order, game one before game two, and will mostly keep the same perspective.
-The Creators
Portal Stories: Mel is a community made game, yet has the quality Valve has in most games.
Portal 2 is made by Valve, and in my opinion lacks the story of the other games they have made.
====================================================================================

One of the best things to come out of indie gaming this year has got to be this mod. Acting as a prequel to Portal 2, Portal Stories: Mel is a mod that throws you into the role of Mel, an Aperture Science Innovators Test Subject whose tests go completely wrong and must work with a new Personality Core, Virgil, in order to leave the facility.
This mod is fantastic for a number of reasons;
Pros:
+Completely original voice acting. Harry101UK does an excellent job as Virgil.
+Soundtrack is great, very reminisisint of Portal and Portal 2.
+Completely new assets, like the Quantum Tunneling Device used by Mel or the new Emancipation Grill that disentragrates people and objects!

Cons:
-Some puzzles were a little too easy in the later part of the game.

-It's common to run into the occassional glitch. That's to be expected though, it is a mod after all.
Overall, it's pretty much Portal 3, and it's very much worth your time to install it and play it RIGHT NOW. I highly reccomend Portal Stories: Mel.

This is a great game, one worth paying for even. You can’t not but appreciate the level of work that went into this mod and from such a small team it’s very impressive. The story is about 10 hours long, and captures all the style from the previous games. I was constantly comparing Portal Stories: Mel to Portal 2, and while on the one hand that can’t be a bigger compliment, on the other you really appreciate what great voice acting, script, characters and level design the original games had by comparison.
The characters in Portal Stories are ok. The script tries it’s best to be funny and while at times it succeeds it unsurprisingly falls short of reaching the heights of its namesakes and the wonderful characters of GLaDOS and Wheatley.
I’ve noticed a number of negative reviews of this game regarding the puzzles. The puzzles in this game I warn you are hard, some verging on obtuse. I consider myself pretty good at puzzle games but I’ve not come across many or any Portal puzzles like some of the ones in Mel. Many of the puzzles are challenging and satisfyingly so, some require a large amount of contemplation, but a few too many push to becoming frustrating. The story levels don’t have the simplistic elegance of Portal 1 or 2 or the replayability. Instead they seem designed to be as difficult and backwards as possible making them a little overcomplicated.
In the end Portal Stories: Mel is for the hardcore, puzzle solving fans of the series; a homage to Valve’s masterpieces but not as accessible for casuals and while I consider myself an experienced ‘puzzle-solver’ if it wasn’t for the guide on a few occasions I would be still stuck frustrated for several more hours.
Portal Stories: Mel is a good game, a great mod, but one that tries too hard to be challenging, rather than focusing more on the joy of being back in that universe and the simplicity and fun of the puzzles that we loved from the originals. If you want a solid puzzler or a taste or the Portal universe again then dive in. Still a worthwhile addition to the series and a stimulating challenge for hardcore fans.

Being closely involved with CS since it's inception,  when I heard that Gooseman had created a new game I was very interested.  This game has a feel of the original CS.  Unfortunately, this game becomes very lopsided in a hurry as equipment and perks are acquired by higher skill level players making them impossible to beat by players on entry levels.  The micro payment system is also difficult to endure, as well as the long delay between maps.  As well, there are too many items that must be purchased with real money and cannot be earned by game points.  I am referring to tactic altering weapons and accessories including supressors, red dot sights, custom skins, and armor - all of which are available if you're willing to spend $7 to $12  per item and for only a limited 30 days use (for all cool items except for skin cheats which only need be purchased once).
What disappointed me quite a bit is the artistic license the devs decided to take with weapons whose character and standard configurations are sacred in the gaming community.  Everyone knows, for example, that the Steyr Aug's receiver casting includes an integrated 1.5x telescopic sight housing fitted for lenses made by Swarovski Optik.  We pretty much all know that the Aug sight contains a simple black ring reticle with a basic rangefinder.  Curiously, the developers of TI decided to remove the integrated 1.5x sight on the only Steyr Aug that you can acquire in-game on a permanent basis.  The REAL Aug equipped with the standard fixed optical sight can only be acquired when  on a temporary basis when playing TI, and this can only be achieved via a micro transaction of real cash - and you will have to buy said Aug as an item in a  weapons crate  containing a bunch of accessories you don't really need or want - tough♥♥♥♥♥♥- but don't worry about acquiring too much clutter in your arsenal cause all items you get in your crate somehow vanish after 30 days.  That's 30 calendar days, not 30 playing days.
Makes me wonder why the developers didn't also program the cars to  transform into pumpkins  at precisely midnight, may as well have the VIP turn into Cindarella holding a mop bucket too.  Which midnight? Good question.  It's midnight once an hour somewhere on the planet.  Insideously,  armor cannot be permanently purchased ever.    What makes me start violently gnashing my teeth is when I am reminded once again --> the items which can only be permanently acquired via micro transaction of real cash are essentially game changing legal cheats.
Yes, I said it, cheats, which I loosely define as advantages that are not available to all players - unless they have cash they are willing or able to hand over via the micro payment system.  Thes advantages these items purchase give players an immediate decided boost, tilting the playing field dramatically.  I can hear many of you now, tsk tsk tsking me, come on now Attrition, do you REALLY want to call these guys out and accuse them of haxoring - they are after all, performing within the framework set up by the developers after all....come on now, I can't imagine it, please, Attrition, describe these cheats of which you speak.
Okay.  I'll touch on one (or two) -  Here's a no brainer: the alternate terrorist skins available for purchase only cause a terrorist appear almost identical to a CT.  Can you look me in the eye and tell me it's cool by you if you're playing as a CT and another CT appears on your screen, when you ignore them since they look like your own team mates and derp derp!! Dead.  You just got PWND. You must be a noob cause you got killed by the guy you mistook for a CT, in a skin that cannot be obtained by game points, only with cash - and once purchased remains in inventory forever.
How about a weapon cheat - you may not call it one but essentially it is when using the Super V SMG.  IRL, Kriss Corporation currently has only built the Vector Super V chambered in .45 ACP with a 5.5" long barrel as the only length availabe in the automatic version. For those of you who don't want to read a full review, here's the summary: Portal Stories: Mel is a good game when considered at its price of 'free'.  It doesn't hurt to try it, and nothing is lost if you don't like it.  However, be advised: there is a video walkthrough posted by one of the developers of the game on the community guides page, which can help with the game's difficulty.
Overall: Worth trying.
For those of you still with me, here's the full review:
Portal Stories: Mel is a game based upon the two games of Valve's Portal franchise, though it draws far more heavily from Portal 2 than the first Portal.  Without going too deeply into the plot, I will say that I enjoyed it overall.  It didn't 'grab' me as much as Portal 2's plot did when I first played, though it did have its moments.  The voice acting, fortunately, was quite well done, with the only notable exception would being Cave Johnson - neither his voice nor his personality really matched the old Cave Johnson from Portal 2.  Barring that, the voice and persona of your companion was very well done, and the villain, while a bit bland, was acceptable.  The plot only really kicked up at the very end, which could be considered a reward for sticking through the tougher parts of the game.  This neatly transitions into...
The gameplay.  You'd think that, in a Portal game that uses the same engine as Portal 2, you'd have some high-quality puzzles - and you'd be right!  For the most part.  The game's puzzles are well done, including some very clever moments that left me grinning when I finally figured them out.  But the game suffers from several problems, one of which is the introduction of gameplay elements.  By this, I mean the game design decision of demonstrating to a player all of the actions that he/she is capable of performing before requiring them to use those actions in a new setting.  For the most part, Portal and Portal 2 did a fantastic job of this - there was narry a moment where the solution to a puzzle was something that never would have occurred to the player, since every mechanic was introduced (consider that the
start of each game involves putting a cube onto a button to open a door; this mechanic is then used in darn near every puzzle in the entire series after that introduction).  A spoiler-filled example follows below.
SPOILERS BEGIN HERE
About halfway through the game, in a room titled "Paint Fling 1", the game introduces three new mechanics with no prelude.  To start, you have the basic cube, and a source of orange gel (from Portal 2 - the gel that makes you run fast when you move over it), and a light bridge (also from Portal 2 - a bridge that can be extended by using portals).  The first new mechanic is having a light bridge that is not at a 90 degree angle.  In Portal 2, light bridges were never in more than two orientations: horizontal and vertical.  Yet here, it is at an angle, which makes it more difficult to manipulate the bridge than if it were not.  The second mechanic is that of covering the cube in the orange gel.  This was never done in Portal 2; the only gel that you ever covered a cube in was the blue gel, which caused the cube to bounce around the place and break things.  Covering the cube in orange gel, by contrast, causes it to lose friction.  These two mechanics - the inclined bridge, and the orange-gel-covered cube - are central to this puzzle, and yet they are used without the game giving you instruction on their nature.  This could be solved with something as simple as a previous room showing an orange-gel-covered cube sliding down a ramp, yet I had to look at the walkthrough to figure out that this mechanic was even possible (and to add insult to injury, neither of these were used in the game again).
Also, did you know that you can shoot the lasers through solid glass?  Me neither.  But the walkthrough sure did!
SPOILERS END HERE
It's not as if the developers did not know to introduce mechanics - there are several points later in the game where new mechanics are demonstrated right in front of you, Valve-style.  This makes it clear to you as the player that these are new things you can manipulate, and also explains what exactly that manipulation will accomplish.  But it's things like these that make the game artificially more difficult.  In a puzzle game, the player should have easy access to all of the pieces, instead of having to figure things out without the proper toolset (as these puzzles are impossible to solve without knowledge of these elements).
Moving past that, the game's puzzles can get exceedingly difficult, even barring the mechanic-introduction issue.
Oftentimes, a given puzzle room would simply be too large for me to assess at the start - leading to lengthy backtracking after I discovered that I needed to bring a long-forgotten cube across the whole chamber for the 10th time.  And the game has an unrequited love for the fields (whose name I forget) that destroy objects and reset your portals, a love that
I've come to hate.  I found myself relying upon the walkthrough too often for my tastes.  The difficulty wasn't uniform, either; I found some of the early puzzles to be just as challenging as the last few in the entire game, and I know I'm not the only one.
As an honorable mention, the soundtrack is fantastic.  Less stuble than Portal 2 (and far less so than the original Portal), but not in a bad way; the music always seemed to fit the atmosphere, and never distracted me from the puzzle solving.  Big points for that!
Overall, it's certainly not a bad game. I feel as though it should have been put through more playtesting - particularly from players that weren't particularly good, or even rather bad at, puzzle solving.  This would have helped highlight the various clarity issues, as well as address the overall difficulty.  Is it good?  Absolutely, especially for an indie effort - the fact that it even was published on Steam means it was better than the vast majority of indie modding projects of this scale.  But it could have been even better, and it's a shame that I have no desire to play through it again to look for secrets or just for the sake of enjoyment.
FINAL VERDICT: Try it/10

"Shovel Knight." I think it is safe to say this is one of the most hotly anticipated indie titles coming out this year... I'm trying to figure out how Yacht Club Games did it. Did they boil a vat of nostalgia stew using "Dark Souls" bones for flavoring; a stew Carl Weathers and Samwise Gamgee themselves would be proud of? No. Did they lock "Dark Souls" and "DuckTales" in a candlelit room with Barry White blasting? Maybe. However they have done it, they did it. The crazy ♥♥♥♥ers did it. They made a fun game, an homage to why we started gaming in the first place. This is not the greatest game in the world, no. It is simply a tribute. A great tribute nonetheless.
It is a simple premise: Shovel Knight and his warrior BFF Shield Knight got their pixelated butts whooped.  Shield Knight is MIA and Shovel Knight took an early retirement. But now a new and evil force is out in numbers - the Enchantress and her Order of No Quarter. Shovel Knight heads out on one last quest, to restore goodness to the land.
You travel from level to level, dispatching enemies and platforming very similarly to "Ducktales," complete with treasure collecting and atypical weapon use. You have two attacks (along with some magics) to deal a variety of enemies, each with their own weaknesses and tactics. It is deceptively challenging. Not "tear your hair out and sacrifice your firstborn" challenging, but a fun challenge. There are secrets to find as well, so keep an eye out for things that look out of place.
The levels are wonderful... each one is unique and beautiful to boot. I am getting tired of pixel games, honestly. All these RPG Maker games... hideous and same-y. But "Shovel Knight" is gorgeous. It reminds me why pixel-style art made a comeback in the first place. Everything flows and you'll find yourself taking dumb damage because you are busy staring at the background and stages.
The gameplay,charming story, and excellent levels are great but the soundtrack, to me, is the star. I equate the "Shovel Knight" soundtrack to that of the "Halo" soundtrack. It is integral. It is inspired. It is catchy as a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
I would be remiss if I didn't mention the boss fights. Amazing. Think "Dark Souls." Every boss has his or her own special style, one that you have to master. Expect a challenge.
This game is cute. It has heart. And it wears its influences on its sleeves, from the bonfire checkpoints to the treasure chest brimming with pixelated treasure. "Shovel Knight" is not a risky game; it is not doing anything new. It is doing something tried and true. But it does it honestly and with its own unique charm. "Shovel Knight" is a blast.

Portal : Stories Mel is a new comunnity made mod that half succeeds and half fails. In this review I will show you whether you want to get this game, or put in the trash like you did with Thinking With Time Machine.
I would start off at the beginning. I loved the train ride. It gave us a little Half-Life memories as it wandered through the halls of Aperture Science in 1952. You actually got see real people, yet sadly not once in the game do you interact with these scientists.
Ok time for the actual review.
Pros:
As for good, I think the visuals in this game are above standard to regular modders. The texture work was fantastic and the scripted scenes were great. The voice acting for Cave Johnson is pretty close to the actual game. And the new portal gun looked AMAZING!
Cons:
For one thing, the new AMAZING portal gun, usually glitches... A LOT. And the frame rate to this game is MADNESS. I have an Intel I7 dual core with (sadly) intel 4000 graphics. It should be able to run fine like Portal 2, but it seems to be even slower than some better looking games. The puzzles are just BAD. First of all, you start off at really difficult puzzles in the beginning (which get harder and harder.) And they're usually just an easter egg hunt to find the portal surface than actual thinking. Luckily this gets better as the levels go on.
Overview:
Overall I would only somewhat recommend this game as of right now. Don't get me wrong, I haven't finished the game so I don't know if it gets better. But I do know that even though it isn't Valve Standards, I still keep going back to it.
UPDATE (5/31/16)
I have a new system with an fx-8350, and a gtx 760 with 8 Gigs of ram. This game now runs like a charm, and that may be that my old system was terrible, or they've updated it. (Probably the former)

"Shovel Knight." I think it is safe to say this is one of the most hotly anticipated indie titles coming out this year... I'm trying to figure out how Yacht Club Games did it. Did they boil a vat of nostalgia stew using "Dark Souls" bones for flavoring; a stew Carl Weathers and Samwise Gamgee themselves would be proud of? No. Did they lock "Dark Souls" and "DuckTales" in a candlelit room with Barry White blasting? Maybe. However they have done it, they did it. The crazy ♥♥♥♥ers did it. They made a fun game, an homage to why we started gaming in the first place. This is not the greatest game in the world, no. It is simply a tribute. A great tribute nonetheless.
It is a simple premise: Shovel Knight and his warrior BFF Shield Knight got their pixelated butts whooped.  Shield Knight is MIA and Shovel Knight took an early retirement. But now a new and evil force is out in numbers - the Enchantress and her Order of No Quarter. Shovel Knight heads out on one last quest, to restore goodness to the land.
You travel from level to level, dispatching enemies and platforming very similarly to "Ducktales," complete with treasure collecting and atypical weapon use. You have two attacks (along with some magics) to deal a variety of enemies, each with their own weaknesses and tactics. It is deceptively challenging. Not "tear your hair out and sacrifice your firstborn" challenging, but a fun challenge. There are secrets to find as well, so keep an eye out for things that look out of place.
The levels are wonderful... each one is unique and beautiful to boot. I am getting tired of pixel games, honestly. All these RPG Maker games... hideous and same-y. But "Shovel Knight" is gorgeous. It reminds me why pixel-style art made a comeback in the first place. Everything flows and you'll find yourself taking dumb damage because you are busy staring at the background and stages.
The gameplay,charming story, and excellent levels are great but the soundtrack, to me, is the star. I equate the "Shovel Knight" soundtrack to that of the "Halo" soundtrack. It is integral. It is inspired. It is catchy as a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
I would be remiss if I didn't mention the boss fights. Amazing. Think "Dark Souls." Every boss has his or her own special style, one that you have to master. Expect a challenge.
This game is cute. It has heart. And it wears its influences on its sleeves, from the bonfire checkpoints to the treasure chest brimming with pixelated treasure. "Shovel Knight" is not a risky game; it is not doing anything new. It is doing something tried and true. But it does it honestly and with its own unique charm. "Shovel Knight" is a blast.

This game is a wonderful trip down memory lane as you head back into Portal 2's version of Aperture Laboratories in the 60s. You are another mute protagonist, as usual, called Mel. You head into Aperture Labs for a test you've been invited for, as you are an olympic athlete.
This doesn't exactly go as planned. You wake up a long while later, awoken in a similar fashion as in Portal 2. Another core with another wonderful adventure to head on, as you start the search for anything to help you escape the desolate laboratories of Aperture back into the outside world.
This is as far as I'll go considering story, as I don't want to ruin the experience for you. The voice actor for the core might be a teeny bit shoddily cast, but the entire rest of the game feels like it could be a real expansion to Portal 2. The gameplay is the same, but more, and a lot more difficult. The custom textures are beautifully made, and the model for the portal gun is gorgeous.
The game runs about as good as Portal 2 does (excellently), has the same (great) options menu, and plays like a dream. The love these fans put into this mod is very apparant, and it makes a wonderful product.
Together with the stunning soundtrack by Harry Callaghan, this game truly feels just like a bit more Portal.

I was a huge fan of the Saints row games, having played the original on xbox 360, and the second on the PS3. So when I saw the third game on sale here on Steam, I had to have it!
The graphics in this one was so much better than the in the second game that it blew me away! The customisation was vastly improved as well, at least in terms of character creation. True, the game lacked any good hairstyles, but other than that? Aces! In fact, I spent a good 40 mins just creating my character!
Once you get in the game, though you see right away how different the game is. It doesn’t FEEL like the past 2 chapters. It’s moved away from urban street gangs, and seems more like organised crime. As such, most of the clothes are flashy and suit like. In fact, your homies wear silk suits, and shaundi looks more like a model instead of the stoner she was in the second.
The game basically leaves the street gang behind, but keeps the slightly over the top feeling of the second and takes it to a whole new level! The game has absolutely NO shred of realism to it, in fact at one point you battle zombies! True, Zombies were present in the first and second game, but they weren’t major plot points, and unless you did certain things to bring dead people to life, you never even knew about it!
So, I am not exactly sure how to review this game. If I view the game as a sequel, it’s bad! It veers too far away from past games, it loses what little realism existed in the game, and turns the whole franchise into a joke.
However, if I review it on its own merits, and force myself to forget that it’s part of the Saints Row franchise, then it’s actually quite good! The over the topness is fun, and makes it difficult to know what’s going to happen next!
Basically, if you are expecting something similar to the previous games, then don’t bother with Saints Row: The Third. If you just want to have fun, doing some insane crazy stuff, then this is the game for you!
Interestingly enough, this is the first game that I would give an overall rating of both 1 Star(Poor) and 5 stars(Best) to.

First of all, let me say this: it's absolutely fantastic. Everything I can think of (price, level design, writing, story, soundtrack, art, voice acting, modeling, animations, etc.) is top-notch. Especially for a mod made by fans, but if you told me it was made by Valve, I'd believe you.
So now that that is out of the way, I'm going to talk about the puzzles. If you've looked at the other reviews, you'll know they are very difficult, and certainly require the player having completed Portal 2. There is no real learning curve; even the very first (actual) puzzle is challenging. But the thing about them is that the puzzles are not cruel. If you make a mistake, you probably won't have to do the entire thing again. Unless you are speedrunning, which you won't be on your first playthrough, literally no fast timings, hard jumps, etc. are needed. It's all logic based, so you can take just about as much time as you need. Finally, if you get stuck (which you will), you can always just look up a video walkthrough. But I would suggest giving everthing a wholehearted, but patient, try. You never know when you just might solve it.

A grate, mind bending, challenging mod. It is hard, and fun, if you like to discover mechanics by yourself. But, it never explains some of it's more advance archaic mechanics, that have never been used in official Portal and Portal 2 maps. This gives the game a huge difficulty curve. But I liked it, because of the satisfaction of discovering those mechanics via examination of subtle visual cues and such. It also mostly does away with the oh so annoying "find the one wall here where you can put a portal through" type of puzzles - gone are the portal walls behind vents -  portal walls are obvious, and it is up to you to understand how to use them.
In terms of story, it fits within the Portal universe canon, and is very Half-Life/Portal esque in it's style - a sagway between parts of gameplay. The story itself is quite well made - Mel, an Olympian that volunteer for a test for Aperture Science in the 50's, gets stuck in a "short term" relaxation chamber to be waken up many years later. What follows is the tale of Mel's attempt to escape Aperture Science (of-course) with the aid of the personalty core Vigle. At the same time, a mysterious entity by the name of AIGES starts working to undermine our 2 companions. It is a good story, if a bit anti-climactic because of it's attempt to connect itself to the story of the official Portal games.
Last but not least, the voice acting and sound design was superb, and the visual design, while not using too many new assets over Portal 2, does use what it has with good cohesion and consistency.
All in all, I recommend this game to any and all Portal fans, who are not afraid to have their minds blown to tiny little pieces at the end of it.

Prism Studios obviously put a lot of effort and work into this, but I cannot recommend it to anyone else.
The problem is with the puzzles. Valve always works hard to make sure their puzzles are elegant and based on thinking, not reflexes. Those playing Portal and Portal 2 rarely (if ever) die as a result of a mistake.
The puzzles in MEL, on the other hand, are brutal and inelegant. Prepare to die
. Worse, dying means you'll often lose several of the many, many steps required to solve each puzzle. MEL's puzzles also require very quick timing in many places, and that's not why I enjoy Portal. (I can get reflex puzzles in Super Meat Boy or Oo.)
I wanted to like MEL -- I really did. But after bashing my head against the walls for more than seven hours, I just decided it's not worth the frustration. Kudos to Prism for taking on such a huge challenge, but unfortunately their love for complexity ran away and left us with a game that's simply not fun to play.

Fiendishly clever game. One of the best that I've seen. It truly is a Portal game.
PROS
1. Clever Map Design
It's so diabolically difficult. You won't notice certain surfaces, secrets are hidden away in cracks, you have to think out of the box and it's so tricky. You would think that you have to go down a certain way then you realise that it was a trap all along. E.g. Determined Achievement.
2. Non-Canon History
So interesting how they show the technology that was basis of the Cores. E.g. Virgil and Aegis. There are so many unanswered questions about Aperture Laboratories E.g. Where did theyget the funding? Why do the Cores have a human pattern? What is the link to Black Mesa? Why oval-shaped portals, not circles? Where did the portal technology come from?
CONS
1. Something Novel
I was hoping for some new feature. There was the Orange and Blue goo in Portal 2 and I was hoping there would have been Green goo or Red Goo, which did something novel. E.g. Green Goo is super-sticky, you could walk upside-down on the ceiling once you coat it with Green Goo. It would turn the game upside down and give a new perspective. Liquid Nitrogen to freeze the water to form bridges and pathways. Red Goo for something.

This mod, just simply amazing. Never have I been so challenged with the puzzles (at least what I can remember), even though some of them were just missing the simple actions needed. - Model Design for that 1950s feel.
- Intro sequence reminded me of Black Mesa. Ironic isn't it?
- Reviving an forgotten character into the world of Aperture.
- The voice actors included.
- Difficult Puzzles.
- New gameplay mechanics to make the puzzles more difficult.
- Music and sounds.
- The entirety of the story. It takes place right between Portal and Portal 2 (at least, not the intro scene anyway)
- Including the ending.
- And lastly, it's FREE!
I don't know what else to say but to try out this mod if you have enjoyed the Portal games. The ending in my opinion was beautiful and made feel emotion for these virtual characters, or maybe that's just me? Anyway, just go play the mod. It's amazing.

Now that I've finished the game, I can give it a full review.
Shovel Knight is that perfect kind of homage to the games you played on the NES. There's a little DuckTales, a little Megaman, a little Zelda II, and even a little Mario 3. Heck, there's even a little bit of Dark Souls thrown in for good measure.
The one thing I do want to immediately draw attention to is the level design. I can sum it up in just one word, "perfection". For the first time in a long time, I found myself learning the game's mechanics without the aid of a tutorial level, and considering the number of games out there that hold your hand through 75% of the game? I find it very refreshing.
I love the music, and considering the composer worked on Contra 4 and Double Dragon Neon, I'm not surprised that it is some of the best. Add in some compositions from a classic Megaman composer, and you have yourself a soundtrack made of pure gold.
In lieu of lives, death takes away some of your gold. You have one life to get that gold back or it is gone forever. This mechanic is very much like dying in Dark Souls, where your souls are taken away and you have one life to get them back.
I felt tthat the game's length was just enough. I'm really looking forward to the additional modes coming in free updates later this year, but for now, I have enough to keep me busy. I feel like the 14.99 price tag is worth it overall.
I have enjoyed my time with Shovel Knight, and I can honestly say, that it never was unfair. Any deaths were because of my own mistakes.
For a first game, Yacht Club Games really knocked it out of the park. I hope to see a sequel someday, but I couldn't be happier to just have this game in my steam library. Proud to be a backer!

I was varsity fencing captain in highschool. I won a lot of bouts in both foil and sabre styles, and I was pretty good at it, just to toot my own horn.
“James, why are you bringing this up? Just to seem awesome to us readers?”
Well, yes. That, and so that I can talk about how a sword feels in the next couple of lines. A sword, let’s say a sabre, feels powerful, and is relatively flexible. It can do both crushing and cutting blows, and is able to cover all five quadrants of your body – Your left shoulder/torso, your right shoulder/torso, your right lower body/leg, and finally your left lower body/leg – effectively and quickly
“James, where are you going with this?”
Patience, dear reader, and you’ll see. Where was I? Ah, yes. The sword has been used by knights throughout history because it’s a versatile weapon for close quarters, as well as agile and powerful. Whereas lower ranking soliders would be given spears, which were easy to use, the sword required finesse and training to use, as well as (due to the level of skill required to use them) showed the stature of the user. Anybody good with a blade gained prestige based on his combat skill. Famous swordmasters are remembered today, such as Bonetti, for his Bonetti’s Defense.
These are great reasons for why a knight would use a sword in combat. Yacht Club Games aren’t paying attention to those, though. They gave the main character of their game a shovel, and it just works. Weapons that are used for a gimmick in games usually turn me off, but in Shovel Knight, it’s used well and feels effectual and powerful to a degree that I greatly admire.
Throwing you into the first level, in a way very similar to Mega Man X, and not teaching you anything about how to play, Shovel Knight has you in the action immediately, and learning the controls as quickly as you can, just to stay alive. It teaches these in a very simple manner, with you having time to learn the controls at to adapt to what is being thrown at you in a way that teaches you as you play. This gets the tedious tutorial portion of the game out in a manner that is both enjoyable and fast. It sets up all of the mechanics that you’re going to need, from basic attack functions, to your ability to jump onto bubbles and use them to jump higher, which becomes incredibly important in later parts of the game, when trying to reach out of reach places.
After you defeat the first boss in this first level, you’re taken to the Shovel Knights camp, where he is dreaming. A woman is falling from the sky, and you get a message saying “Catch her!”. After catching the woman, Shovel Knight wakes up, and he’s off. Little more is said about the falling woman, at this point. After leaving his camp, you’re teleported to an overworld not dissimilar to the overworld of Super Mario Bros., where the gorgeous sprite of Shovel Knight walks between stages. The first is The Village, where Shovel Knight can buy upgrades and talk to members of the civilisation you are trying to save. This is also where the main collectible of the game is introduced; musical pages, which are hidden all over the game, and once unlocked, reward you with gold and the ability to play that song at will from the bard in the main village. In the village, you also have the ability to buy health and mana upgrades, and new items. There’s a lot more to do there, but I want you to discover it on your own, the game is chock full of secrets.
After leaving The Village, you are presented with two levels, both of which are doable immediately. There’s a locked gate that comes down after defeating both of these stages, and two areas that have secrets to them that you can figure out for bonus items and gold.
Each level has you facing off against a boss, and is themed around that boss. The first boss I faced was the King Knight, who fancied himself a king, and lived in a castle with some griffons and knights. His level was pretty straight-forward, with lots of twists and turns to go and find more items, which harkens to the games Metroidvania aspects. It’s possible to find items by exploring, so I highly recommend that, as these can come in extreme handy.
The boss fight against King Knight was again pretty straight forward, but difficult. He has lots of dashing attacks and stuns, and made for a fast paced battle, one that I enjoyed thoroughly. Each boss has his own unique music to his stage, and also to his boss battle, and these were also fantastic.
The boss fights and the stages so far have all been varied and interesting, in their unique styles. The next stage I played, the other one before unlocking the gate, featured levels that were totally dark, and only light up lighting. It was terrifying and challenging, in ways totally different to the first. This variety and change is one of the things that Shovel Knight does so well, and I love the game for it.
Shovel Knight delivers platforming puzzles and combat in a way that is just amazing. It couples of the excitement of dodging a swift attack with the thrill of learning an enemies attack patterns, which leads to a thrilling combat system. As well as this, they incorporate the main characters weapon, his shovel, very well. There are spots that have dig-able dirt on them, which rewards with gems and other rewards. As well as this, Shovel Knight is able to destroy certain walls with his shovel, opening up more avenues to explore, which you need to remember if you’re one of those people that wants every last thing in the game.
As I mentioned earlier, level design is phenomenal, with parts set up to teach you what will be hindering you in a fair manner, so that you’re not standing with your hands on your hand yelling “NO FAIR!” when you’re killed. Everything is telegraphed, with tricky mechanics shown to you before they are really bought into play. One example of this is during the Mole Knight level, where a green gel puts out fires. You see a slime that is on fire jump into the green gel, and he’s instantly put out. This subtle but poignant hint shows how to solve the next couple of rooms, and is only an example of the way that the game teaches you mechanics. Few games do this that well, and it’s fantastic to see ones that do.
Artistically, Shovel Knight looks like an NES game, and it’s awesome. Spirtes are well animated, everything has character, and everything looks like it has been lovingly crafted. Musically, it’s the same. NES-style music, with each zone having it’s own tune, as well as the bosses. Jake “Virt” Kaufman has delivered a masterpiece, as well as Manami Matsumae who also contributed to the project. I would feel amiss if I didn’t mention the sense of humour in this section about the “non-gameplay elements” of the game. The game takes it self in a very self serious way. It stands true to the world it’s created, and treats it as if it’s deadpan humour. One example is the Kickstarter Reward gallery, The Hall of Champions, where you have to pay 5,000 coins to get in, and when leaving, the owner says “That’s what you get for backing something without any knowledge of the end product.” The writers know exactly what they’re doing there, with a subtle wink at the Kickstarter backers in saying “Hey, this is what you guys did. Silly people. ;)”. The story is coming together as I play more and more of the game, but it’s so deep and twisting that I don’t really want to reveal much of it.
Shovel Knight is loving crafted, by people that obviously played the Sigma out of Mega Man X, and that beat the bloody tears out of Dracula in Castlevania. Fans of those sorts of titles owe it to themselves to pick up Shovel Knight at the earliest opportunity, as it does them great justice, and in certain areas, even improves upon them. You can pick up Shovel Knight on Steam, and on the Yacht Club Games website using the Humble Widget for $15.99.

I was varsity fencing captain in highschool. I won a lot of bouts in both foil and sabre styles, and I was pretty good at it, just to toot my own horn.
“James, why are you bringing this up? Just to seem awesome to us readers?”
Well, yes. That, and so that I can talk about how a sword feels in the next couple of lines. A sword, let’s say a sabre, feels powerful, and is relatively flexible. It can do both crushing and cutting blows, and is able to cover all five quadrants of your body – Your left shoulder/torso, your right shoulder/torso, your right lower body/leg, and finally your left lower body/leg – effectively and quickly
“James, where are you going with this?”
Patience, dear reader, and you’ll see. Where was I? Ah, yes. The sword has been used by knights throughout history because it’s a versatile weapon for close quarters, as well as agile and powerful. Whereas lower ranking soliders would be given spears, which were easy to use, the sword required finesse and training to use, as well as (due to the level of skill required to use them) showed the stature of the user. Anybody good with a blade gained prestige based on his combat skill. Famous swordmasters are remembered today, such as Bonetti, for his Bonetti’s Defense.
These are great reasons for why a knight would use a sword in combat. Yacht Club Games aren’t paying attention to those, though. They gave the main character of their game a shovel, and it just works. Weapons that are used for a gimmick in games usually turn me off, but in Shovel Knight, it’s used well and feels effectual and powerful to a degree that I greatly admire.
Throwing you into the first level, in a way very similar to Mega Man X, and not teaching you anything about how to play, Shovel Knight has you in the action immediately, and learning the controls as quickly as you can, just to stay alive. It teaches these in a very simple manner, with you having time to learn the controls at to adapt to what is being thrown at you in a way that teaches you as you play. This gets the tedious tutorial portion of the game out in a manner that is both enjoyable and fast. It sets up all of the mechanics that you’re going to need, from basic attack functions, to your ability to jump onto bubbles and use them to jump higher, which becomes incredibly important in later parts of the game, when trying to reach out of reach places.
After you defeat the first boss in this first level, you’re taken to the Shovel Knights camp, where he is dreaming. A woman is falling from the sky, and you get a message saying “Catch her!”. After catching the woman, Shovel Knight wakes up, and he’s off. Little more is said about the falling woman, at this point. After leaving his camp, you’re teleported to an overworld not dissimilar to the overworld of Super Mario Bros., where the gorgeous sprite of Shovel Knight walks between stages. The first is The Village, where Shovel Knight can buy upgrades and talk to members of the civilisation you are trying to save. This is also where the main collectible of the game is introduced; musical pages, which are hidden all over the game, and once unlocked, reward you with gold and the ability to play that song at will from the bard in the main village. In the village, you also have the ability to buy health and mana upgrades, and new items. There’s a lot more to do there, but I want you to discover it on your own, the game is chock full of secrets.
After leaving The Village, you are presented with two levels, both of which are doable immediately. There’s a locked gate that comes down after defeating both of these stages, and two areas that have secrets to them that you can figure out for bonus items and gold.
Each level has you facing off against a boss, and is themed around that boss. The first boss I faced was the King Knight, who fancied himself a king, and lived in a castle with some griffons and knights. His level was pretty straight-forward, with lots of twists and turns to go and find more items, which harkens to the games Metroidvania aspects. It’s possible to find items by exploring, so I highly recommend that, as these can come in extreme handy.
The boss fight against King Knight was again pretty straight forward, but difficult. He has lots of dashing attacks and stuns, and made for a fast paced battle, one that I enjoyed thoroughly. Each boss has his own unique music to his stage, and also to his boss battle, and these were also fantastic.
The boss fights and the stages so far have all been varied and interesting, in their unique styles. The next stage I played, the other one before unlocking the gate, featured levels that were totally dark, and only light up lighting. It was terrifying and challenging, in ways totally different to the first. This variety and change is one of the things that Shovel Knight does so well, and I love the game for it.
Shovel Knight delivers platforming puzzles and combat in a way that is just amazing. It couples of the excitement of dodging a swift attack with the thrill of learning an enemies attack patterns, which leads to a thrilling combat system. As well as this, they incorporate the main characters weapon, his shovel, very well. There are spots that have dig-able dirt on them, which rewards with gems and other rewards. As well as this, Shovel Knight is able to destroy certain walls with his shovel, opening up more avenues to explore, which you need to remember if you’re one of those people that wants every last thing in the game.
As I mentioned earlier, level design is phenomenal, with parts set up to teach you what will be hindering you in a fair manner, so that you’re not standing with your hands on your hand yelling “NO FAIR!” when you’re killed. Everything is telegraphed, with tricky mechanics shown to you before they are really bought into play. One example of this is during the Mole Knight level, where a green gel puts out fires. You see a slime that is on fire jump into the green gel, and he’s instantly put out. This subtle but poignant hint shows how to solve the next couple of rooms, and is only an example of the way that the game teaches you mechanics. Few games do this that well, and it’s fantastic to see ones that do.
Artistically, Shovel Knight looks like an NES game, and it’s awesome. Spirtes are well animated, everything has character, and everything looks like it has been lovingly crafted. Musically, it’s the same. NES-style music, with each zone having it’s own tune, as well as the bosses. Jake “Virt” Kaufman has delivered a masterpiece, as well as Manami Matsumae who also contributed to the project. I would feel amiss if I didn’t mention the sense of humour in this section about the “non-gameplay elements” of the game. The game takes it self in a very self serious way. It stands true to the world it’s created, and treats it as if it’s deadpan humour. One example is the Kickstarter Reward gallery, The Hall of Champions, where you have to pay 5,000 coins to get in, and when leaving, the owner says “That’s what you get for backing something without any knowledge of the end product.” The writers know exactly what they’re doing there, with a subtle wink at the Kickstarter backers in saying “Hey, this is what you guys did. Silly people. ;)”. The story is coming together as I play more and more of the game, but it’s so deep and twisting that I don’t really want to reveal much of it.
Shovel Knight is loving crafted, by people that obviously played the Sigma out of Mega Man X, and that beat the bloody tears out of Dracula in Castlevania. Fans of those sorts of titles owe it to themselves to pick up Shovel Knight at the earliest opportunity, as it does them great justice, and in certain areas, even improves upon them. You can pick up Shovel Knight on Steam, and on the Yacht Club Games website using the Humble Widget for $15.99.

Came looking for something a bit meatier puzzle-wise than Portal 2, and that's exactly what I got.
Map production values are extremely high, and the puzzle difficulty is tough.  But it's a good kind of tough - I've played some Portal mods where the challenge was in trying the same bloody crouch-fling until you got it pixel-perfect.  Not the case here.  You'll rack your brains, come to the conclusion that the puzzle is bugged or there's a BS trick you missed, and then 10 minutes later you'll be heading through the exit having just had your usual Portal instincts turned on their head.
The bad?  Well, unfortunately, it makes an abortive attempt to match the humour of the originals, and that aspect falls very flat.  The writing, such as there was, wasn't great, and by the end was downright condescending, hand-holding you like some kind of moron who hadn't just cracked a cavalcade of brain-twisters.  Voice acting, for the most part, is also shabby.
However, being that Portal 2 is a puzzle game, this is the most coherent and consistently challenging campaign I've played, and I can easily recommend it to anyone looking for some seriously robust puzzles.
Just try not to listen too hard to anything anyone says.

The sheer thought and effort that went into this game is outstanding and refreshing. A true homage to the original era of Mega Man, Castlevania, Mario, and more. Other games just adopt the "retro" label to excuse pixel graphics or chiptune music, but not this one. Shovel Knight flips things around and uses retro as a RULE, making it so close to the real deal that it could pass for a long-lost NES title save for a few very pleasant improvements. I cannot stress how truly impressed I am: The folks at YCG actually dissected the NES' capabilities and limitations with scrutiny, making sure as many things were consistent to the original system as possible. Incredible music, tight controls, and entertaining writing come together for a real ground-breaking title. I've been with Shovel Knight since the beginning over a year ago and I could not be more proud with what it has become. Well, what are you waiting for? Get digging!

I already have shoveled my way through this game in an entire night, since Yacht Club Games let Kickstarter backers play the game early. I may have missed some stuff, but main game-wise, I've dug up about what's offered here.
As a fellow Kickstarter backer, what do I think of this game? Well, to put it shortly...I ♥♥♥♥ING LOVED THIS GAME! I'm really glad that this game saw the light of day, unlike some other Kickstarted projects out there, and I am content with how it turned out. Yacht Club Games, I applaud your efforts here.
Shovel Knight is pretty much as if someone took Mega Man, DuckTales, and the Metroidvania concept and threw it together in a 2A03 blender set to VRC6, threw in some modern enhancements, and released it out to the world for everyone to try. This game really feels like it could have been on NES, from the graphics to the audio all the way down to the core gameplay. Yes, I know that there are instances of proof that part of the game can't be done on NES, but who cares? I felt like some of the added changes helped with making the game much better, in the long run.
The story itself is pretty much like other NES games: Forgettable. But come on, you're not here for the story. NES games were never recognized for that. The dialogue spoken throughout is also pretty cheesy and full of puns, which I think adds to the charm of the game. You can probably get a good laugh out of it, or at least a smile on your face.
In contrast to that, the gameplay is just excellent. As I said, it's a mix of Mega Man, DuckTales, and Metroidvania stuff. You can slice at enemies with your sharp shovel, bounce off of them to inflict damage and reach higher terrain, and use an assortment of side weapons. The side weapons are definitely built for combat, but most of them are also coded to aid in exploration. There definitely will be levels where you need to use a certain item to advance through, which I think is excellent...though I wish there were more levels/areas in the game that did that, too. But aside from that, you can go through the whole game with just the shovel, like how you can go through all of a Mega Man game with just the Buster.
I think that the difficulty is fairly set. With how the levels are designed and how the gameplay is handled, it's really your fault for failing, which I appreciate with games like this. It also makes you learn the game's mechanics instead of giving you an unnecessary tutorial, which I also like. You can also give yourself a better challenge by destroying the checkpoints, which give you more gold in exchange of having to start from a previous area of the level upon death. With New Game+, you start with your previous equipment/upgrades, but you take more damage, can't find food in the levels, and you have less checkpoints in the level. Definitely for those who want it NES hard.
The level design is superb. Yes, they are linear in nature, like with every NES game. But all the enemies/platforms/items are fairly placed out across the place to synergize with the gameplay. There are also plenty of secrets hidden in each level, which gives an excellent risk vs reward feeling of finding and completing each secret area. They also provide a nice place to test out any relics that you find, if you do find any.
While difficult, I think that the game is also rather forgiving. You don't have a lives system, and you don't get a game over for dying so much or for any other condition. That said, you do lose some of your gold upon death, which you can recover in the same area that you died in, akin to Dark Souls. I like this...but I have a bit of a gripe with it, too (explained at the bottom). I think that the checkpoints are properly spaced out throughout the levels, which aids with some of the forgiveness that the game offers. Either way, if you fall, just get back up and try again. It's not game over unless you make it game over.
I like how the bosses are handled. They don't really have a pattern, but a set list of moves that they choose to execute depending on the situation. These moves are pretty easy to pick up on, and they definitely fit the theme of the boss.
The graphics for the game are just nostalgic glory here. I know that some of the colors in the palette in this game could never show up on a NES game...but I don't care. These added colors really help with the mood and design of the levels/enemies. Yacht Club Games did amazing with making sure that they would work on the NES, similar to how Capcom could get more than three colors on a single sprite. Just great authenticity. The animations are buttery-smooth, too.
The sound...OH MAH RAWR! It's just...too good. The music done in this game was composed with Famitracker, but uses an expansion chip called the VRC6, which was only available in some Konami games for the Famicom, notably Akumajou Densetsu (Castlevania 3). I consider this one of the best expansion chips for the Famicom, and I really was excited to see it being used for this game. Oh, unlike some indie retro games out there, the sound effects in this game really do sound like they could have came from the NES, so kudos to that, as well.
If I had one complaint about this game, it would be how the money bags are sometimes spawned upon death. I've had moments of not being able to reach any floating bags, all because they would be in an area that's impossible to return back to safety, especially over bottomless pits. I hope that a future patch can resolve that.
One play session will vary on your skill level. For me, I beat the game in a bit over 7 hours with 84% item completion for my first playthrough, though it seems like it's an average of 4-6 hours for everyone else...and less than 1 1/2 hours if you're really that good at the game. There's New Game+ for those who want to extend their time with the game with a better challenge. But either way, with the quality of the final product, I say the price is justified.
Overall, as a PC gamer, a NES gamer, and a Kickstarter backer, I really enjoyed this game. It's by far one of the greatest games I've played this year, and I'm really happy that this game was completed. I can't wait to see what else Yacht Club Games has in store soon, either for this game or for another. If you're a fan of retro games (especially the NES), you owe it to yourself to pick this game up.

Portal Stories: Mel is a good community mod, the story is quite interesting, with the plausible, but, sadly, non-canonical characters and story development. The puzzles are nice overall, though sometimes they are not intuitive and other times require an extremly precise control and timing, Frustration can be a recurring issue throughout the course of the mod. Yes, I've heard the complaints about "it's not a puzzle, it's a searching game", but, in my point of view, limited resources are what makes the puzzle solving fun. the tools provided to you are really powerful, so, to add up the challenge, limited portal surfaces are a must. The story, although with few characters, gives you the drive to move on and finish the mod. The voice acting is decent, not something professional like the original Cave Johnson voice actor, but I admit that the mod's voice actor came closer than the majority of people that tried to impersonat Cave Johnson that I've ever seen. Achievements and full closed captions (with almost 100% precision with what's written and what's said, the meaning is the same, just a tiny bit choice of words that are different from the text). So, not to make this an overly long review, this mod is fully recommended, since it adds up some story to the already story rich Half-Life universe, even though it's not canonical.

I'll start off by saying if you haven't beat Portal and Portal 2, you should probably beat those first, because this mod is going to use EVERYTHING you learn in those games and you will also need to have a solid understanding of the mechanics and physics that make the game work. The puzzles in this mod are VERY difficult, but not impossible if you understand how everything interacts.  If you are not good at thinking in three dimensions then this is not the mod for you.  Unlike the main game, the puzzles here are quite long and many require you to manage a lot of steps in the correct order to solve.  You will need to be able to understand what the problem is before solving it, and in many cases this is going to require you to reverse engineer your environment in order to find the correct starting point.  Understanding the physics of the game can also allow you to solve some of the puzzles in ways not intended, if you are looking for a little extra fun/difficulty.  There are very few ques for solving the puzzles, which could be improved upon so a few of them are a bit less nightmarish to complete, but it's still fun to struggle every now and then.  My first run was about 6 hours of actually playing and solving, plus another couple hours looking for easter eggs and trying to break the game.  If you are like me and thought the main game was a bit too easy, then this is the mod for you.  If you struggled with the main game  but still want to tackle this mod, then I would suggest practicing a few puzzles first, reading up on the mechanics of the game, and finding some inner peace, because you WILL get frustrated with some of the puzzles.

Plants vs Zombies, GOTY Edition is a must-have game if you like the Tower Defense genre. Basically, the idea is very simple: defend your garden(s) against the relentless attacks of Zombies, trying to get into your house. The means you have at your disposal to do so, are ... plants. Plants in all varieties: from the basic grunt (aka the Pea Shooter) through the basic defense plants such as potatoes (halting zombies for awhile) up to plants that are capable of doing great amounts of damage, even inclusing kamikaze-like jumbing plants. Which is needed too: the Zombies come in different varieties and are more resilient than you'd expect from your average Zombie. But they are pretty brainless as well and just rugh at you, in ever growing numbers. There is a bit of strategy involved, however, first of all by choosing the 8 possible plants for a given level, and secondly by the actual planting. Since you have zes different lanes through which the Zombies come Marching In, it's important to keep everything well-covered.
You have one resource at your disposal: sunlight, which comes naturally (except in the night-levels) or, mostly, by means of planting sunflowers. The more sunlight you collect, there more plants can grow at the same time. No water needed. Simple, isn't it? Furthermore, the Zombies drop coin (they seem to go on a stroll with some plan...) which you can use to buy new slots for your plants, or some upgrades with a crazy neighbour.
And that's it,  really. There is an extensive adventure mode, slowly revealing all the plants (over 40!!) and zombie-types, and there are great mini-games that give you an extended challenge. It's all so well done with vivid graphics, and so humourish that it's difficult to resist. It comes with a bunch a Steam achievements which I recommend heartily, since they let you discover some possibilities of the game you otherwise wouldn't have thought about.
There are some techical shortcomings which did bother me. The Steam-version is basically a port from the mobile platform versions, and to be honest, it's very badly done. There is only one fixed resolution (800x600 I think), no widescreen support, so the game uses only the middle portion of the screen if you happen to have a widescreen (which I guess most of us have by now). This is really appaling, and should long have been fixed by now. Some graphics configuration options might come in handy as well.

I'll start off by saying if you haven't beat Portal and Portal 2, you should probably beat those first, because this mod is going to use EVERYTHING you learn in those games and you will also need to have a solid understanding of the mechanics and physics that make the game work. The puzzles in this mod are VERY difficult, but not impossible if you understand how everything interacts.  If you are not good at thinking in three dimensions then this is not the mod for you.  Unlike the main game, the puzzles here are quite long and many require you to manage a lot of steps in the correct order to solve.  You will need to be able to understand what the problem is before solving it, and in many cases this is going to require you to reverse engineer your environment in order to find the correct starting point.  Understanding the physics of the game can also allow you to solve some of the puzzles in ways not intended, if you are looking for a little extra fun/difficulty.  There are very few ques for solving the puzzles, which could be improved upon so a few of them are a bit less nightmarish to complete, but it's still fun to struggle every now and then.  My first run was about 6 hours of actually playing and solving, plus another couple hours looking for easter eggs and trying to break the game.  If you are like me and thought the main game was a bit too easy, then this is the mod for you.  If you struggled with the main game  but still want to tackle this mod, then I would suggest practicing a few puzzles first, reading up on the mechanics of the game, and finding some inner peace, because you WILL get frustrated with some of the puzzles.

I can't wait to see what else Yacht Club Games come up with in the future!

This game is very competative, and that's it. It doesn't really have anything other than it's competativeness, and that's just ONE of it's many mistakes.
This game had so much potential when it was original announced/released, but it quickly diminished. The lack of things you can do in this game make it very hard to enjoy. There are only two different game modes to play (besides the tutorial-based "Situations"), Terrorist hunt and Operations. Terrorist hunt is basically Operations, but with NPC's, so it's barely different from the rest of the game. Operations (the main part of this game) is very annoying becuase despite the fact that you can pick Casual over Ranked, it's basically the same ridulousness. Unless you spend hours studying every single tactic or trick (or taking advantage of the broken mechanics) that should really only be necessary for ranked, you're not gonna make it far in this game (unless you get lucky, like 50% of players). Most games have some other aspect that let's you at least enjoy the gameplay/mechanics/style of the game through a different game mode or a story, but this game unfortunately doesn't. It's not very fun (in my opinion) doing the same thing over and over again, experiencing the same horrible mechanics and not being able to find a better agngle of the game. One of the main issues is that this game doens't have a decent matchmaking system that matches players based off skill. There were never any fun games that were actually balanced. I either played against a team who practically majored in FPS or R6S, and then I get annihilated. Or I play against a bunch of people who never even touched an FPS, and then I might win.
Bottom line is, this game is ONLY fun if you have a very competative nature, and if you want to spend countless hours studying the maps, positionings, tricks, and tactics neccessary to even win ONE game. This game wasn't fun on Console, and it's nowhere near better on PC. Please do not buy or recomment this game if you share even the slightest of similar opinions/views.

I posted this review on one of the forums I'm on. I did edit it at certain points because I assume we all know what's going on here.
Story: Portal 2 is always praised for its fantastic combination of story and gameplay. PS:M's story is simple but still pretty good! It only have two voice actors and they do a good job throughout! PS:M does well in terms of bridging the two Portal games.
Puzzles: PS:M isn't easy. This game was designed to be challenging and feature the best puzzles the community had to offer. For many of them I was stumped and I admit I needed walkthrough assistance for a few of them - only to learn that I had been duped by something which wasn't excessively difficult. And it's here where I found the most standout aspect of PS:M: it's puzzles are intelligent. They require thought and planning and when you solve them (without aid) you feel like a genius! Almost all of the puzzles feature multiple steps, each with a different challenge and each individually well-designed. Towards the end some did get frustratingly difficult. But, I say again, they were intelligent - not unfair. Emancipation grids everywhere, though!
Graphics: It's not next-gen. But it is also the first 'game in the series' to feature such external environments as it did and they were all really well done and beautifully made.
Portal Stories: Mel is a mod designed by hardcore Portal fans who wanted to give more Portal to the world. And thank Valve they did! It does have its faults, but considering the small team that worked on it, they're minor. And if I'm honestly, it's one of the best games I've played this year. It is challenging. It is smart. It was made with love.

This game is very competative, and that's it. It doesn't really have anything other than it's competativeness, and that's just ONE of it's many mistakes.
This game had so much potential when it was original announced/released, but it quickly diminished. The lack of things you can do in this game make it very hard to enjoy. There are only two different game modes to play (besides the tutorial-based "Situations"), Terrorist hunt and Operations. Terrorist hunt is basically Operations, but with NPC's, so it's barely different from the rest of the game. Operations (the main part of this game) is very annoying becuase despite the fact that you can pick Casual over Ranked, it's basically the same ridulousness. Unless you spend hours studying every single tactic or trick (or taking advantage of the broken mechanics) that should really only be necessary for ranked, you're not gonna make it far in this game (unless you get lucky, like 50% of players). Most games have some other aspect that let's you at least enjoy the gameplay/mechanics/style of the game through a different game mode or a story, but this game unfortunately doesn't. It's not very fun (in my opinion) doing the same thing over and over again, experiencing the same horrible mechanics and not being able to find a better agngle of the game. One of the main issues is that this game doens't have a decent matchmaking system that matches players based off skill. There were never any fun games that were actually balanced. I either played against a team who practically majored in FPS or R6S, and then I get annihilated. Or I play against a bunch of people who never even touched an FPS, and then I might win.
Bottom line is, this game is ONLY fun if you have a very competative nature, and if you want to spend countless hours studying the maps, positionings, tricks, and tactics neccessary to even win ONE game. This game wasn't fun on Console, and it's nowhere near better on PC. Please do not buy or recomment this game if you share even the slightest of similar opinions/views.
